Appendix A
Environment Construction and Quality Evaluation
The appendices provide protocols, implementation details, per-site results, and source inventories for the completed experiments.
A.1
Historical Construction and Cost Records
Construction reports for the historical 85-site subset record 59 passed sites, 15 source-blocked sites, 6 failed sites, and 5 sites with missing reports. These statuses reflect different versions of acceptance criteria, visual algorithms, and thresholds and serve to trace historical construction processes. After initial setup and authorization, this subset contains no recorded per-site manual implementation, debugging, or repair. Conclusions about human intervention and pricing are restricted to this historical subset and the recovered calls.
This construction experiment used the Full Coverage policy. In the recovered SDK records, the Builder and Verifier primarily used
gpt-5.6-sol
with
xhigh
reasoning; some Builder calls used
gpt-6-astra
, so the entire batch did not use a single model.
Recovered model-call and partial cost records cover 84/85 sites. Input tokens, including cached tokens, total 11.207 billion, of which 10.672 billion are cached input tokens; output tokens total 38.4318 million. Recorded, quantifiable model costs total $220.62, with recorded Builder and Independent Verifier costs of approximately $142.52 and $78.11, respectively. Across the 84 sites with records, the mean recorded per-site cost is approximately $2.63 and the median is approximately $1.60. Independently rounded components sum to $220.63, differing from the total by $0.01 due to rounding. Seven sites additionally contain unpriced Astra calls. These costs therefore provide only a lower bound for recovered, priceable model calls. They exclude unpriced calls, browser execution, and other system overhead, are not extrapolated to the total cost of 244 sites, and are not interpreted as the marginal cost of the Verifier under a controlled ablation.
Costs distinguish system development, initial authorization/setup, per-site implementation/debugging/repair, and research auditing. Neither the 244-site artifact pool nor the historical 85-site subset has a complete attempt cohort under uniform acceptance criteria, so we do not compute a unified construction success rate.

All 244 startup records in the frozen inventory contain HTTP 200 responses and homepage screenshots, but these do not represent complete functional acceptance. The 113 additionally reviewed sites comprise 70 without confirmed anomalies, 9 with flagged presentation issues, 26 with signals awaiting diagnosis, and 8 other special records. The remaining 131 sites received no additional review.
SHA-256 and 256-bit difference-hash diagnostics across all frozen screenshots found byte-identical blank homepage screenshots for Cohere and United Airlines. Fifteen screenshot pairs with difference-hash distance at most 12 are used to locate low-content pages, not to identify duplicate implementations.
The historical Best Buy artifact contains 184 programmatically generated SVGs, and its homepage explicitly uses locally synthesized product and store data. This confirms that some colored blocks are synthetic resources rather than loading failures. Fictional business data do not themselves imply functional invalidity, nor do they establish the pool-wide prevalence of templated implementations. Presentation diagnostics are reported separately from source fidelity and interaction tests; test results for other candidate versions are not reassigned to the current resource pool.

Appendix B
System Implementation and Verification Feedback
B.1
Propagation of Evidence, Candidates, and Feedback
The Builder reads existing source materials, candidates, and the latest repair package in the workspace, preserving valid captures and implementations when resuming execution. The independent verification runner reads construction reports and evidence directories and returns verification reports and repair requests. The outer controller records execution statuses and sends failed reports back to the Builder; source blocking and authorization requirements are handled separately. Task generation, interaction collection, and evaluation use frozen environments.
B.2
Version Association
Sites, source snapshots, candidates, and release packages have separate stable identifiers. Version associations for tasks, trajectories, and evaluation results should identify specific implementations, resources, initial data, and runtime configurations rather than relying solely on site names. Training and evaluation protocols and data-overlap checks appear in Appendix
E.1
.
B.3
Site Contracts and Verification-Report Fields
The inspected contracts associate sites, coverage configurations, viewports, page paths, workflows, and acceptance requirements, with optional interaction contracts and state assertions. Specific checks are determined by the corresponding execution reports.
Independent verification reports record conclusions, candidate digests, page and workflow checks, source limitations, and evidence. Repair packages associate issue locations, expected and observed outcomes, corresponding evidence, and repair suggestions. The model determines diagnostic actions using the reports and existing source evidence.
B.4
Construction-Stage Verifier Implementation and Versions
The construction-stage Verifier uses site contracts, model-executed browser tests, and site-specific assertions. Visual comparison may combine screenshots, DOM, element geometry, and auxiliary scripts. Historical versions did not use a unified SSIM, LPIPS, or L1–L4 composite score. Fidelity v19 introduced normalized RGB pixel similarity, but algorithms and thresholds still differ across sites.
Reset prechecks include programmatic hard checks dependent on
WebAnything
’s Flask/SQLite architecture; they are not stack-independent external-baseline scorers. Earlier runners did not enforce positive- and negative-case calibration acceptance criteria for evaluators. Task-evaluation calibration therefore requires independent evidence.
Reports preserve concrete check evidence, with top-level conclusions distinguishing passed, failed, and source-blocked outcomes. The outer runner consumes reports rather than recomputing a unified four-layer score. The historical artifact pool contains candidates from different versions with passed, failed, source-blocked, and missing-report statuses. The independent evaluation harness retests frozen artifacts without reading these historical verification conclusions.
B.5
Resumption Prompt for the Explorer and Builder
The Builder Agent directly receives a real website URL and manages exploration, evidence collection, and local reconstruction within the same context. The historical resumption template requires preserving existing source evidence, candidate implementations, and repair records, reading the latest check feedback, and continuing repairs from failed or unfinished items. It returns to the source for targeted recapture only when existing evidence cannot answer a concrete question. Its final submission comprises the candidate implementation, local resources, and a self-check report containing actual check results and limitations. This template resumes checkpoints after timeouts; it is not the sole initial prompt shared by all construction batches.
The complete historical English template appears in the separate prompt supplement; this description does not replace the original instructions.
B.6
Independent Final Verifier Prompt
The Independent Verifier inspects frozen candidates in a separate context without modifying the Builder’s candidate code. Appendix C
Task Supply and Data Statistics
C.1
Interfaces for Downstream Task Generation, Evaluation, and Collection
Task and training-data construction use released environments. This section describes the implementation interfaces for task specifications, runtime recovery, evaluation, and data binding.
From environment capabilities to tasks.
The task pipeline reads the pages, visible objects, native operations, and seed data of a specific mirror to formulate goals such as retrieval, filtering, detail verification, comparison and aggregation, and state modification. Existing planning materials record whether the required facts reside in lists, detail pages, or other pages, and organize applicable operations into task specifications. Natural-language instructions express user goals, while answers, evidence supporting the operations, and evaluation materials remain hidden. The executable scope of a task is bounded by the capabilities and initial state actually supported by the environment.
Initial states and success conditions.
Public task records contain task identifiers, instructions, sites, starting URLs, and login and reset requirements. Task specifications record capability tags, action and step budgets, and successful and unsuccessful terminal states. Hidden specifications associate required objects, query parameters, source evidence, expected results, and output contracts. Success conditions for information tasks may specify fields, sets, orderings, or comparison results in normalized answers. State-changing tasks check application states after saving, creating, modifying, or restoring objects; tasks admitting multiple solutions use sets of state predicates. When necessary, fictional test records are prepared in private copies of native data structures, while original environment assets remain read-only. Task answers are grounded in the task’s initial data. Task text or a nonempty answer file alone does not establish evaluability: corresponding executable checks must exist.
Evaluator construction and execution-based verification.
During generation, site-specific scripts first check native routes, evidence visibility, and applicable answer, state, and reset conditions. A visual agent then receives instructions and observations in the initial state of the corresponding mirror through the fixed harness and performs browser operations. An independent task evaluator checks the final answer against hidden success conditions and determines goal completion using the terminal DOM, screenshots, and applicable state evidence. Model-based evaluation is used for applicable semantic conditions and is separated from agent execution. Tasks with evaluation materials become end-to-end accepted tasks only after actual interaction and outcome checks, rather than receiving a pass solely because specifications exist.
Recovery, binding, and training entry points.
Task execution packages locate native implementations, immutable seeds, and starting routes through runtime descriptions. When login is required, they restore fictional seed identities while isolating real user sessions. Before task execution, mutable databases are restored from seeds, and site-specific reset and startup checks verify applicable states. Tasks whose runtime prerequisites are not met are recorded as blocked. Task identifiers, source-data versions, and specification digests connect public tasks to hidden evaluation materials. Collection packages record implementations, resources, initial data, runtime configurations, and archive digests to associate the complete environment identity.
The pipeline separately records task generation, evaluator construction, execution-based acceptance, trajectory collection, and training-sample export. Saved successful trajectories are used for training after quality filtering, format conversion, and step-level sample export. The 6,172 accepted tasks in the earlier source collection, the 5,856 trajectories used for SFT, the 5,167 unique training task IDs obtained by deduplicating task IDs in the training manifest, and the 60,517 step-level samples are counted in their respective units. The relationship between the separate batch of 6,812 new tasks across 229 sites and the 74 source sites follows the set definitions in the experimental setup.

Appendix D
Human Blind Audit: Protocol and Results
The human blind audit evaluates historical source-state fidelity in RQ2-A. All five sites and 14 page states in the WebHarbor-matched historical-state subset are included: Apple, arXiv, Cambridge Dictionary, ESPN, and Hugging Face Papers. There is no sampling or selection based on automatic scores. Each sample simultaneously displays the historical source reference, anonymous mirror A, and anonymous mirror B, with A/B order randomized per sample. Three annotators participate, forming final labels through discussion. Annotators do not know system identities or see Pixel, SSIM, or Text F1.
Rating questions.
Q1 (overall source-state fidelity) asks which mirror is closer overall to the designated historical source page, with choices A better/tie/B better. Q2 (information fidelity) asks which mirror more completely preserves visible information that may affect agent observation or decisions, using the same choices. The target is always the designated historical source state. Annotators are not asked to infer functional correctness for operations that were not executed.

Runtime coordinates use CSS pixels relative to the current viewport; image coordinates in the training exports are normalized to 1000.

article.headline: 把真实网站自动改造成智能体训练场
article.lede: WebAnything 从真实 URL 全自动重建可执行、可重置的网站环境，并配套生成任务与交互轨迹。
article.problem: 网页智能体需要多样、可执行、可重置的网站环境，才能进行可复现的训练与评测，但直接在真实网站上运行会让状态初始化、复现和安全隔离变得困难。现有人工镜像方案要对每个站点单独工程化，生成式建站容易偏离指定网站，抓取回放方案的交互覆盖又受限于已抓取内容和回放能力。
article.method: 作者提出 Explorer–Builder 流水线：从真实 URL 采集浏览器可观测的页面结构、计算样式、资源依赖，以及交互前后的状态变化，形成页面结构与外观、资源与依赖、交互前后观察三类证据，据此实现本地可执行路由与状态转移。独立验证器在单独上下文中检查已冻结的候选实现，不得修改代码；若证据足以判定期望结果而候选未复现，则触发局部修复，若证据不足则生成具体的观察请求进行定向重采集，更新后重新冻结并复验。
article.results: 资源池包含 244 个网站产物，覆盖 14 个应用域、53 个细类，支持 12,984 个已执行且通过验收的任务。在五个 WebHarbor 匹配站点、14 个历史状态上，自动指标为 Pixel 0.9240 对 0.8083、SSIM 0.7904 对 0.6260、Text F1 0.8541 对 0.2617，盲审为 12 胜 2 平 0 负；但同一子集的交互测试中，WebAnything 的能力覆盖率为 75%、全部测试通过率为 63.3%，低于 WebHarbor 的 80% 和 76.7%。另一组五个 VeriEnv 站点上，选定产物通过 29/33 项测试，VeriEnv 为 21/33。85 站点历史集合记录无逐站人工实现或修复，84 个站点可计价模型调用合计 220.62 美元（均值 2.63、中位数 1.60，为下界）。用 5,856 条轨迹对 Qwen3.5-9B 做 SFT 后，REAL 成功率从 22/91 升到 31/91（+9.9 个百分点），Odysseys-Easy 的 Rubric Avg 与 Task Avg 分别提升 6.25 和 6.32 个百分点，WebArena-Verified Overall 由 16.41% 升到 29.74%（+13.33 个百分点），但其中 Retrieve 子项下降 8.75 个百分点。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「真网站多样性」和「本地可复现执行」拼在一起，为网页智能体提供了一条少依赖逐站人工工程的规模化环境与轨迹供给路径。
article.limitations: 训练验证只在 Qwen3.5-9B 这一规模上做，未系统评估更大模型、其他后训练方法与更长训练预算；站点会持续变化，论文未评估镜像的时效性与长期维护成本，且高保真复现涉及版权、商标与服务条款，公开分发受授权约束。此外，验证分析属事后观察性质，219 对报告里只有一对严格匹配同一候选，且交互覆盖在 WebHarbor 子集上实际落后于基线。
article.figure_caption_zh: WebAnything 的重建流程：源证据约束可执行构建，独立验证器检查冻结候选，并把差异分流为局部修复或定向重采集。

email_papers.title: Attention as Lattice Gauge Theory: Relations Interact Only Through Wilson Loops
email_papers.abstract: Relations compose through the entity they share - Alice is Bob's mother and Bob is Carol's father, so Alice is Carol's grandmother - and the order matters, since a father's mother is not a mother's father; verifying a composed relation means closing the loop. We show that if each entity's coordinate frame may be rotated independently (per-entity frame freedom), three things follow. In the pure-gauge sector, relations that share no cycle cannot interact at all. The only gauge-invariant score of a triangle is a class function of its holonomy $H = T_{ij} T_{jk} T_{ki}$ - a Wilson loop. And the only equivariant update of an edge is $U = Ψ(H)\, T_{ij}$ with $Ψ$ conjugation-equivariant. Edge attention by Wilson loops is therefore not one design among many but the unique form the symmetry permits. Three communities hold pieces of this form: the commuting-operator embeddings of knowledge graphs are its abelian (commuting) sector; AlphaFold's triangle update and the Edge Transformer have its shape - an edge updated through the third vertex - without its constraints; and lattice QCD builds it equivariantly on lattices. We instantiate the equivariant sub-family on general relational graphs as holonomy attention. With no training and composition alone, it infers unobserved $S_4$ relations on sparse graphs at 0.88 with a fifth of the edges corrupted, at or slightly below specialist synchronization algorithms, where every commutative architecture is capped at 0.083; its holonomy score flags corrupted triangles at AUC 0.99 where commuting scores are capped at 0.76 by a second selection rule, and it separates clusters without labels.

article.headline: 框架自由迫使关系注意力成为Wilson环
article.lede: 每个实体可独立旋转坐标系时，关系只能沿闭环（Wilson环）组合：作者证明这唯一决定了边注意力的更新形式。
article.problem: 注意力如何让关系算子相互作用，通常被当作设计选择。但如果实体嵌入的坐标系本身没有意义——新出现的实体没有内在框架——预测就必须对逐实体的坐标旋转不变。论文追问：这一对称性是否唯一地约束关系与关系之间的交互形式。
article.method: 作者把每条关系看作连接两个实体的O(d)平行移动，规范变换在每点独立作用，并沿生成树做规范固定。由此证明：不含闭环的边集合之间完全没有交互；三角形的唯一规范不变分数是holonomy H=T_ijT_jkT_ki的类函数，即Wilson环；边的唯一等变更新为U=Ψ(H)T_ij。据此实例化holonomy attention：以Wilson环为分数、经共享顶点组合、用极投影回到O(d)，不学习任何参数，仅在S_4置换表示上运行四轮。
article.results: 在14个实体、度8、四轮的S_4群同步任务上（每格1000个实例），20%的边被随机置换破坏时，holonomy attention对未观测关系对的准确率为0.988，稀疏度5图为0.886；只走单条路径分别为0.645和0.625，交换算子架构的上限为0.083。损坏率0.3和0.45时准确率降至0.937和0.700，比均匀权重分别高0.026±0.004和0.078±0.006。holonomy分数区分干净与损坏三角形的AUC为0.993，交换分数在S_4上的上限为0.759；无标签区分两个簇的三角形AUC为0.98。
article.why_it_matters: 这为边注意力给出了一条可由对称性推出的设计规则，并把知识图谱的交换嵌入、AlphaFold的三角形更新与格点QCD放进同一框架，压缩了关系推理的架构空间。
article.limitations: 它并不是更好的同步器：Singer特征向量法与之持平或在0–5点内领先，cycle-edge message passing在n=12试点上最多领先11点。实验限于S_4等有限群和14个实体的小图，且算子需从群库中取用，尚不能由上下文生成。

email_papers.title: WeVisCut: The Whole Editing Room in One Agent From Narration to Long-Form Video
email_papers.abstract: Producing long-form videos from narration requires interdependent decisions that remain coherent across shots. Existing agentic editors often use multi-stage workflows driven by general models, leaving the quality-cost trade-off of compact, task-adapted policies unclear. We address this gap with WeVisCut, a long-form script-to-video system that connects tool execution with policy learning. Its agent harness maintains shared production state so that tool feedback informs subsequent decisions and repairs. Because finished videos do not expose these decisions, our four-stage data pipeline combines editing inversion with verified replay to turn recovered editing intent into executable supervision. Applied to 3,750 finished videos, this pipeline yields over 130K training examples. We use this supervision to train a single 9B policy that coordinates production and recovers from failures within the same harness. Moreover, we introduce a 100-task benchmark and five metrics assessing editing quality and delivery reliability. Under a shared tool environment, WeVisCut substantially outperforms its base model and achieves comparable performance to Claude Opus 5 while using nearly 33x fewer generated tokens per successful output minute. It also outperforms task-matched native editors on our proposed metrics.

Abstract
Producing long-form videos from narration requires interdependent decisions
that remain coherent across shots. Existing agentic editors often use
multi-stage workflows driven by general models, leaving the quality-cost
trade-off of compact, task-adapted policies unclear.
We address this gap with
WeVisCut
, a long-form script-to-video system
that connects tool execution with policy learning. Its agent harness maintains
shared production state so that tool feedback informs subsequent decisions
and repairs.
Because finished videos do not expose these decisions, our four-stage data
pipeline combines editing inversion with verified replay to turn recovered
editing intent into executable supervision. Applied to 3,750 finished videos,
this pipeline yields over
130K
training examples.
We use this supervision to train a single 9B policy that coordinates
production and recovers from failures within the same harness.
Moreover, we introduce a 100-task benchmark and five metrics assessing editing
quality and delivery reliability.
Under a shared tool environment, WeVisCut substantially outperforms its base
model and achieves comparable performance to Claude Opus 5 while using nearly
33
×
\times
fewer generated tokens per successful output minute.
It also outperforms task-matched native editors on our proposed metrics.
1
Introduction
“The whole eloquence of cinema is achieved in the editing
room.”
— Orson Welles
Creating a narrated long-form video involves turning a script into a
sequence of coherent shots. Planning, visual retrieval, narration synthesis,
and timeline assembly are interdependent. Changing a shot’s duration affects
later timestamps, while unsuitable visual material may require both retrieval
and planning to be revisited across the affected shot sequence.
Recent agentic editors coordinate production through specialized agents and
tool workflows
[
48
,
39
,
47
,
49
,
21
,
44
]
. Several systems use general
models with feedback or graph refinement. Yet orchestration alone does not
specify how to train a compact policy that maintains video quality at low
token cost. Crayotter trains a 9B editing model using final-video preferences
on manually constructed tasks
[
38
]
.
Such a policy needs a stateful environment for execution and recovery, together with
supervision grounded in that environment. Finished videos, however, omit the
tool calls, intermediate artifacts, and failures needed for such supervision.
The challenge is therefore
to connect stateful execution, executable supervision, and policy learning.
To address these challenges, we present WeVisCut, which integrates a
script-to-video agent harness, executable data construction, and a task-adapted
policy. The harness (Figure
2
) maintains shared production
state and validates tool actions. It exposes execution feedback for inspection,
bounded repair, and replanning while preserving unaffected artifacts
from earlier successful production steps.
Within this harness, we construct executable supervision through the
four-stage pipeline in Figure
3
. We first recover script–shot
intent through editing inversion and execute it through verified replay.
When replay reveals defects, we apply observe–reflect–repair for bounded
corrections that preserve successful artifacts. We then use trajectory
materialization to organize the recorded executions into training examples
with tool feedback and repair outcomes. From 3,750 video projects, this
process yields over 130K examples.
Using these examples, we train a single 9B policy across production roles in
three phases (Figure
4
). In Phase 1, we establish tool use
and recovery through unified supervised fine-tuning
[
46
]
and runtime-verified rejection-sampled fine-tuning
[
45
]
.
In Phase 2, we apply Guided-OPD
[
12
]
to learn recovery on
policy-reached states while phasing out teacher intervention.
In Phase 3, we use
RCF-DAPO
, our role- and context-factored
DAPO
[
43
]
, to optimize decisions by comparing runtime outcomes
within matched roles and contexts.
Moreover, we introduce a benchmark of 100 script-to-video tasks and five complementary
metrics to evaluate editing quality and delivery reliability. These metrics
relate rendered videos to their scripts and production plans, so evaluation
goes beyond successful rendering alone. In a shared tool environment, our
policy improves over its base model by
16.0
points in Overall Score
and achieves comparable performance to Claude Opus 5 while using nearly
33
×
\times
fewer generated tokens per successful output minute.
Our complete system also outperforms task-matched native editors.
We summarize our contributions as follows.
1.
We design a script-to-video agent harness that maintains shared
production state, validates tool actions, and supports inspection,
bounded repair, and final delivery.
2.
We build a four-stage data pipeline based on editing inversion and
verified replay, converting finished videos into executable training examples.
3.
We train a unified 9B policy for tool use and recovery through
sequential SFT, runtime-verified RFT, Guided-OPD, and
RCF-DAPO
within a shared production harness.
4.
We introduce a 100-task benchmark and five metrics. WeVisCut improves
its base policy, outperforms task-matched systems, and achieves comparable
quality to Claude Opus 5 at markedly lower cost.
2
Related Work
Tool agents and long-horizon post-training.
Producing long-form videos requires agents to choose tools and revise plans
from execution feedback. Earlier methods range from interleaved reasoning and
action
[
41
]
to learned API calls
[
29
,
23
,
22
]
and runnable
tool dialogues
[
13
]
. To
train such behavior, researchers curate interactions and synthesize
instructions or tool calls
[
46
,
2
,
20
,
16
]
. Reflection and reusable skills also
support recovery
[
32
,
35
]
. Closer to our
data pipeline, AgentTrek builds verified web trajectories from
tutorials
[
37
]
. Finished videos, however, do not record
editing actions. We therefore infer script–shot intent and replay it with
production tools to obtain executable trajectories. Long-horizon training
also needs to handle policy-generated states. DAgger
[
28
]
collects expert labels for
learner states, while generalized
knowledge distillation trains on student-generated sequences
[
1
]
. Guided-OPD mixes teacher and student
turns, while TurnOPD and Step-Level OPD refine supervision at turn and step
boundaries
[
12
,
51
,
33
]
. We apply
Guided-OPD with truncated teacher logits. For reward optimization, GRPO and
DAPO build on PPO-style updates with group-relative comparisons
[
30
,
31
,
43
]
. We adapt DAPO for
our multi-role policy as
RCF-DAPO
, comparing
rewards only within matched roles and decision contexts.
Video editing.
Video editing systems range from user-assisted tools to autonomous agents.
LAVE keeps users in the editing loop
[
34
]
. In more automated
settings, CutClaw and CineAgents handle music-synchronized editing and
cinematic compilation
[
48
,
47
]
.
The original Crayotter uses a traceable multi-agent workflow, while VideoAgent
assembles specialists dynamically
[
39
,
49
]
. Beyond
workflow design, task-specific training has also been explored. “The Script
is All You Need” trains a ScripterAgent but uses a separate DirectorAgent
[
21
]
. Aurora trains a planner for local edits
[
44
]
. Building on the Crayotter environment, subsequent work
trains a 9B policy with final-video preferences on manually constructed
tasks
[
38
]
. In contrast, WeVisCut learns one role-routed
policy for fixed-narration production from executable trajectories built
through editing inversion, verified replay, observe–reflect–repair, and
trajectory materialization.
Agent and video evaluation.
Evaluation of narration-driven video production needs to consider both the
rendered video and the production process. VBench, VideoScore, and VMBench
assess generated-video quality and motion
[
9
,
6
,
15
]
, while Goku-Bench
tests instruction-based edits
[
14
]
. Script–video timing has
also been evaluated
[
21
]
. Complementary agent evaluation
ranges from recorded web and mobile trajectories
[
3
,
27
]
to interactive shopping, browser,
and desktop environments that validate action outcomes
[
40
,
50
,
11
,
4
,
36
]
. Software-repair benchmarks use repository
tests
[
10
]
, while multi-turn and tool-oriented suites
measure progress, valid transitions, and task constraints
[
17
,
19
,
18
,
42
]
.
We combine these perspectives in a benchmark of 100 script-to-video tasks,
linking scripts, shot plans, tool trajectories, and rendered videos. Five
metrics are introduced to assess script fidelity, visual–narration alignment, timeline plan
realization, long-horizon consistency, and end-to-end delivery success.
3
WeVisCut Agent Framework
Figure

script-to-video production. A shared policy makes editing decisions, while a
stateful runtime executes tools and maintains the resulting production
artifacts. Their interaction connects the narration script to a rendered video
through an inspectable process that supports revision when execution reveals
problems. We first define the task and policy–runtime interface, then describe
the harness that implements this process.

3.2
Harness Design
The harness in Figure
2
implements the interaction in
Equation
1
through a shared tool space, persistent production
state, and runtime checks. Each orchestrator turn selects one tool, which may
process multiple shots and invoke generator or critic calls. Tool selection
depends on the current production state, including available artifacts and blockers,
rather than a predetermined sequence.
Production flow and tool system.
Starting from the narration script
S
S
, segmentation produces production
segments, and shot planning expands them into the shot plan
P
P
. Shot records
connect narration spans to visual queries, target durations, and spotlight
assignments. Visual retrieval and text-to-speech (TTS) tools use these records
to obtain shot assets and narration audio. For spotlight shots, decoration
tools select verified
HyperFrames
templates
[
7
]
and
fill typed slots, allowing the policy to control presentation through
structured content rather than raw layout code. Music search supplies
background music (BGM) for the final mix. Timeline composition combines shot
assets, narration audio, and decorations, while final rendering produces the
shot videos required for stitching. Quality judging and repair tools allow
the policy to revisit these intermediate products before delivery. This
progression describes artifact dependencies, not an obligatory ordering of
every tool call.
Persistent state and selective context.
These tools communicate through the production state
s
t
s_{t}
. Global records
track narration coverage, shot order, and timing, while per-shot records
associate assets, audio, templates, renders, and unresolved issues with shot
IDs. Planned content remains distinct from artifacts that have actually been
produced. Episode memory retains these artifacts, and the event trace
preserves calls, returns, and failures. The initial observation exposes the
full production state. Subsequent role contexts
c
t

contain the latest
runtime observation, state changes, a progress summary, and relevant local
records. Separating persistent storage from model context avoids repeatedly
serializing the entire project while preserving the information needed for
later inspection and repair.
Validated execution and actionable feedback.
Given a tool action
a
t
a_{t}
, the runtime identifies the tool contract
u
t
u_{t}
and
checks argument schemas, artifact references, and execution prerequisites.
When structured content or inspection is required, it supplies this contract
in the generator’s or critic’s role context. Only the runtime commits
validated results to the production state, whereas
rejected calls return typed blockers that identify what must be corrected or
produced next. For example, a stitching request cannot substitute for missing
shot renders or background music. The runtime reports these missing
prerequisites, allowing the orchestrator to select the necessary production
tools before retrying. This separation keeps model decisions grounded in
execution evidence rather than treating a proposed plan as completed work.
Artifact-grounded inspection and bounded repair.
Execution feedback also determines when revision is needed. Quality inspection
combines structured checks of shot records, timing, and render status with a
VLM-Judge over spotlight renders. The critic identifies affected shots and the
defects that a repair should address. Repair tools then revise the relevant
content and recheck affected downstream artifacts while retaining still-valid
results. For example, correcting a decoration need not regenerate unchanged
narration audio. Repair limits bound repeated correction attempts, but
exhausting this budget does not remove the artifact prerequisites for delivery.
Quality warnings and missing production artifacts therefore remain distinct
conditions. The representative trajectory in Appendix
D
illustrates how inspection, blocked calls, and targeted follow-up actions
interact within this loop.
Verified delivery and trace retention.
When the required artifacts are available, the policy requests final
stitching. Reaching the call limit also triggers a delivery attempt from the
available production state. Before stitching, the runtime checks the required
shot renders, narration audio, and background music. After stitching, it
validates the video and delivery manifest. Missing prerequisites are returned
as blockers while further calls are available. A run that terminates without a
validated final video is recorded as incomplete, with its execution trace
retained for diagnosis. The resulting production records support executable
data construction in Section
4
and policy training in
Section
5
. This production harness is separate from the
read-only evaluation harness in Appendix
B.2
.
4
Data Construction
The harness records execution, but finished videos expose only narration
and shot structure, not the tool calls, feedback, and repairs that produced
them. To train the shared policy, we recover editing intent and replay it
under the same state and action contract, constructing role-specific
examples grounded in real tool returns from executing the recovered intent.
Our source data consists of finished narration-driven videos collected from
Bilibili, spanning technology and digital products, business and finance,
natural science, and social sciences and humanities. The admitted set contains
3,750 video projects.
4.1
Executable Trajectory Construction
To convert these videos into executable supervision, we use a four-stage
pipeline comprising editing inversion, verified replay, observe–reflect–repair,
and trajectory materialization (Figure
3
).
Figure 3:
Executable data construction through editing
inversion, verified replay, observe–reflect–repair, and trajectory
materialization. (A) Editing inversion recovers aligned narration and shot
evidence from a finished video. (B) Verified replay executes this intent
with deployment-aligned production tools. (C) Observe–reflect–repair
performs bounded inspection and targeted repair to preserve successful
artifacts. (D) Trajectory materialization organizes recorded tool
interactions, feedback, and repair links into role-specific training
examples and rollout records.
Editing Inversion.
We first recover script–shot intent from the source videos
(Figure
3
A), including timestamped narration, shot structure, and
complete sentence–shot alignment for every admitted project. Narration
provides temporal anchors, while aligned shots indicate how the content is
organized visually. Together, this evidence forms a structured storyboard
describing what each shot should communicate, how long it should last, and
which production constraints it should satisfy. This process recovers the
intended video structure, not the original editor’s tool actions.
Verified Replay.
The recovered storyboard specifies what to produce, but does not provide
execution feedback. Verified replay (Figure
3
B) therefore executes
this intent through a production toolchain aligned with the deployment state
and action contract.
Schema-checked tools maintain a shared production state across planning
(article segmentation, shot planning, and self-reflection), asset production
(visual retrieval with TTS, spotlight decoration, music search, and severity
ranking), and timeline execution (composition with judging, final rendering,
and stitching). Each real tool
return updates this state before the next decision. The runtime verifies
asset references, audio durations, template inputs, timeline positions, and
rendered outputs against the artifacts actually produced. Spotlight shots use
verified
HyperFrames
templates
[
7
]
that separate
layout, motion, and visual style. The policy selects a template and fills
typed slots instead of generating raw HTML, CSS, or JavaScript.
Observe–Reflect–Repair.
During replay, quality inspection combines structured shot, timing,
decoration-slot, and render-status checks with a VLM-Judge over spotlight
renders. Using these inspection results, we locate production problems,
apply bounded local repairs supported by the toolchain, and verify these
changes while preserving successful artifacts (Figure
3
C).
Trajectory Materialization.
These executions produce trajectories that retain pre-action states, tool
names and arguments, real returns, created artifacts, quality verdicts, and
failure–repair links. Missing arguments, unresolved references, invalid stage
order, and failed delivery checks remain visible rather than being rewritten
as successes. We then organize these trajectories into role-specific examples
and rollout records (Figure
3
D).
4.2
Training Examples and Data Split
These examples provide role-specific supervision under the framework in
Figure
2
. Orchestrator samples supervise tool selection and
structured arguments, while generator samples cover script segments, shot
plans, retrieval queries, and template content. Critic samples provide failure
localization, repair requests, and verification decisions. Runtime
observations remain context, with loss applied only to model-authored tokens.
We partition by source project, keeping all its examples and repair
records together. Held-out projects supply the benchmark in
Section
6.1
and are excluded from training. The
134,771 examples supervise a single Qwen3.5-9B policy with shared production
state and tool vocabulary across all three roles.
5
Training WeVisCut
The executable examples provide initial supervision, but WeVisCut also needs
to handle the states produced by its own decisions. Figure
4
summarizes three training phases, comprising unified SFT and runtime-verified
RFT, recovery learning with Guided-OPD, and decision optimization with
RCF-DAPO
. The policy interaction and agent harness are defined in
Section
3
.
Figure 4:

6
Experiments
We evaluate whether task-specific training improves script-to-video production
and whether these gains extend to complete editing systems. We first compare
policies in a shared tool environment, then compare WeVisCut with editors using
their native workflows. Separating these comparisons distinguishes policy
performance from differences in tools and orchestration. We further examine
the cumulative training stages and assess the rendered videos through blinded
human evaluation.
6.1
Experimental Setup
Benchmark and implementation.
We construct a fixed benchmark of 100 script-to-video tasks from the held-out
source projects in Section
4
. Each task specifies a
narration script, source pool, target duration, and aspect ratio. All systems
receive identical task inputs and delivery constraints. Our
trainable variants share the Qwen3.5-9B backbone, training split, decoding
configuration, tool registry, and rendering budget. The Guided-OPD and
RCF-DAPO
training configurations are given in Appendix
Table
5
.

For the policy comparison, all models use the same instructions, tool schemas,
runtime, and rendering budget. We evaluate Qwen3.5-9B, Qwen3.6-27B, and

[
5

Claude Opus 5 snapshot. These reference models receive no task-specific

We compare WeVisCut with Crayotter

Appendix Table
6

Evaluation metrics.
We propose five complementary metrics for script-to-video production that
assess the relationship between the source script, editing plan, execution
trace, and rendered video. All scores lie in
[
0,100
]
[0,100]
, with higher values
indicating better performance. Script Content Fidelity (SCF) measures
the coverage, faithfulness, and ordering of narration claims relative to the
source script. Visual–Narration Semantic Match (VNSM) assesses whether
rendered visuals support the concurrent narration. Timeline Plan Realization
(TPR) compares planned and realized shots in presence, duration, and order.
Long-Horizon Consistency (LHC) measures late-stage shot-health retention and
asset diversity. End-to-End Rendering Yield (ERY) is the fraction of held-out
tasks producing a decodable, sufficiently complete video with the required
non-silent narration. Overall Score is the equally weighted mean of the five
reported metric means, used only as a descriptive summary
for comparing aggregate task performance.
Production Cost Efficiency (PCE) is reported separately as tool calls and
generated tokens per successful output minute. For native systems, we instead
report wall-clock minutes and estimated USD per successful output minute,
since the underlying tools and services differ. Both measures include failed
attempts in the cost numerator, and lower values are better. Definitions,
eligibility rules, and missing-data treatment are given in
Appendix
B
.
Evaluation protocol.
Each system is evaluated in five independent runs over the 100 tasks. We
report across-run means and standard deviations for the five component
metrics, with no uncertainty estimate for Overall Score. Permissions and
retry limits are fixed within the shared environment, and thresholds,
adapters, and evaluator settings are selected on development tasks.
Semantic evaluation uses timestamped contact sheets in a read-only,
network-free environment with access restricted to metric-specific evidence.
The held-out evaluator, its prompts, and the five reported metrics are not
used as post-SFT training signals. The metric-validation protocol is described
in Appendix
B.1
, and evidence collection and
isolation within the read-only evaluation environment are detailed in
Appendix
B.2
.

We first compare policies within the shared production environment to examine
the effect of task-specific training without changing the tool pipeline.
We report task performance and policy-generation cost for each evaluated policy variant
in Table
1
.
Task-specific performance.
WeVisCut improves the Overall Score from 74.5 to 90.5 over its Qwen3.5-9B
initialization, a gain of 16.0 points, with improvements in all five metrics.
The gains extend beyond successful delivery to script fidelity and visual
grounding, as SCF and VNSM increase by 18.6 and 15.4 points, respectively.
By comparison, the unadapted models show less uniform improvements over the
9B base policy. Qwen3.6-35B-A3B gains 9.0 points on ERY but loses 2.5 points on
VNSM, illustrating that delivery success does not necessarily imply better
visual–narration alignment. WeVisCut also obtains higher means on all five
metrics than Qwen3.5-397B-A17B and Gemini 3.1 Pro.
Comparison with Claude Opus 5.
WeVisCut achieves an Overall Score of 90.5, compared with 89.9 for Claude
Opus 5. Its mean scores are higher on four metrics and slightly lower on
VNSM, with no component differing by more than 1.3 points. Yet it uses
2,377 generated tokens per successful output minute, compared with 78,763
for Claude Opus 5, or approximately one thirty-third as many. Relative to
its base policy, WeVisCut also reduces token usage from 11,883 while
maintaining 3.1 tool calls per successful output minute. These results
show that the task-adapted 9B WeVisCut policy achieves mean task scores close
to those of Claude Opus 5 at substantially lower generation cost. We next
examine quality and cost in complete editing workflows with each system’s native tools.

7
Conclusion
We presented WeVisCut, a system for long-form script-to-video production built
around a single 9B policy shared by the orchestrator, generator, and critic.
Our four-stage data pipeline combines editing inversion and verified replay
to recover executable supervision from finished videos. Training progresses
from executable imitation to recovery learning and reward-based decision
optimization. Our 100-task benchmark connects source scripts, editing plans,
execution traces, and final videos through five complementary metrics.
The trained policy improves all five metrics over its base model and achieves
mean scores close to those of Claude Opus 5 while using approximately one thirty-third
as many generated tokens per successful output minute. Native-system
comparisons and blinded human ratings also favor WeVisCut. Broader template
coverage and more robust retrieval are needed to extend the system to a wider
range of editing tasks.

This trajectory exhibits the target inference pattern end to end. The policy
constructs a long-horizon production plan before acting, executes real tools,
and treats every runtime failure as a structured observation rather than a
terminal condition. The invented issue identifiers of step 6 are corrected by
running reflection first. The blanket quality failure of step 5 is resolved into

Appendix E
Visual Inputs to the Evaluation Harness
Figures
7
and
8
show two representative
contact-sheet inputs provided to the evaluation harness. Each contact sheet
contains temporally sampled video frames annotated with source-frame indices
and timestamps, allowing the judges to inspect local visual consistency,
timeline progression, long-range coherence, and rendering quality. These
inputs are exposed through read-only, network-free tools and archived together
with their metadata, ensuring that metric decisions are grounded in traceable
visual evidence rather than evaluator-side assumptions.
Figure 7:
Visual Input to the Evaluation Harness: Case 1.
A contact sheet of temporally sampled and timestamped video frames used
for evidence-grounded diagnostic evaluation.
Figure 8:
Visual Input to the Evaluation Harness: Case 2.
Appendix F
Limitations
WeVisCut is limited by the current
HyperFrames
template library, so uncommon
visual languages may be approximated using the closest available structure,
motion, and style. Expanding the library through automatic template generation could
broaden the design space. The dataset and project-disjoint split cannot cover
all domains, editing conventions, runtimes, or asset distributions, while
verified replay guarantees executability only within the registered runtime.
The quality of long-form videos also depends on the stability of the video
retriever, particularly for instruction-based retrieval. Integrating a trained
video generation model could reduce this dependency and improve robustness.
Finally, VNSM relies on a VLM. Although evidence isolation, frozen anchors,
agreement reporting, and human calibration improve auditability, they cannot
eliminate judge bias or service drift, motivating broader blinded studies and
cross-family audits.

article.headline: 9B智能体从解说稿直出长视频，比肩Opus 5
article.lede: WeVisCut用单个9B策略从解说稿生成完整长视频，总评90.5，接近Claude Opus 5的89.9。
article.problem: 从解说稿生成长视频，需要在规划、素材检索、配音与时间线之间做互相牵制的决策：改一个镜头时长会牵动后续时间戳，素材不合格又要回头改检索和规划。现有智能体剪辑系统多是把通用模型串成多阶段工作流，紧凑且任务适配的策略在质量与成本之间如何取舍仍不清楚。成品视频里看不到工具调用、中间产物和失败记录，因此也难以直接拿来做监督。
article.method: 作者搭了一套共享生产状态的智能体框架：同一个9B策略（Qwen3.5-9B）轮流扮演调度者、生成者和批评者，运行时校验工具参数与前置条件，失败时做有界修复并保留已成功的产物。数据侧用四阶段流水线，先对成品视频做“编辑反演”恢复解说与镜头的对应意图，再用与线上一致的工具集做验证回放、观察—反思—修复，最后物化成带真实工具返回的角色级训练样本。训练分三步：统一SFT加运行时验证的拒绝采样微调，再用Guided-OPD学习从自己造成的错误状态中恢复，最后用角色与上下文分组的RCF-DAPO比较同一决策下的不同候选。
article.results: 从3,750个成品视频项目构建出134,771条训练样本。在100个留出任务上，WeVisCut把基础模型的Overall从74.5提到90.5（+16.0），五项指标分别为SCF 88.4、VNSM 74.6、TPR 94.0、LHC 98.8、ERY 96.7。与Claude Opus 5（Overall 89.9、VNSM 74.8）相比，它的Overall均值接近，但每成功输出一分钟只生成2,377个token，Opus 5为78,763，约为前者的1/33。端到端原生流程对比中，WeVisCut的Overall为90.5，Crayotter为84.9，VideoAgent为82.5；每成功输出一分钟耗时2.1分钟、成本0.09美元，对应为8.6分钟和0.97美元、10.4分钟和0.58美元。三名标注者的盲评总体偏好为4.56，Crayotter为3.48，VideoAgent为3.46。
article.why_it_matters: 这项工作把“状态化执行环境+可执行监督+策略学习”连成一条链路，说明一个9B的任务适配策略在固定工具环境下可以用远低于通用大模型的生成成本拿到相近的剪辑质量；对那些在意推理开销的长视频生产管线，这条路线值得参考。
article.limitations: 效果受限于HyperFrames模板库，少见视觉风格只能用最接近的模板近似；数据集与项目级切分无法覆盖所有领域、剪辑惯例和素材分布，验证回放只能保证在注册运行时内可执行，长视频质量仍依赖检索器的稳定性。评测层面也有保留：Overall是五项均值的描述性汇总，论文明确不给出标准差、置信区间或显著性检验，人工评分只是描述性均值；而VNSM使用Claude Opus 5（同时是论文的对比基线）作为留出评判器，作者自己也承认证据隔离与冻结锚点无法消除评判偏差和服务漂移。
article.figure_caption_zh: VNSM的评判路径：镜头包绑定解说窗口、时间戳、视频与清单摘要、采样器/提示版本和评判快照，Opus 5评判器必须先记录可见证据，再从锚定档位中选一个分数并输出符合schema的JSON。

figure.caption: Auditable VNSM evaluator path. A shot packet binds the narration window, timestamps, video and manifest digests, sampler/prompt versions, judge snapshot, and decoding configuration. The frozen sampler exposes four timestamped frames and, only when motion is necessary, one bounded clip. The held-out Claude Opus 5 evaluator must first record visible evidence, then choose one anchored grade and emit schema-validated JSON. Aggregation excludes unavailable calls rather than converting infrastructure failure into a zero-quality judgment.

email_papers.title: EditAgent: Rethinking Agentic Image Editing
email_papers.abstract: Agentic image editors decompose complex requests into steps, but when a step fails, they mostly retry with the same narrow set of tools and a judge that scores each output by eye directly. We argue that such agents are bounded by two spaces: the action space of what the agent can do, and the observation space of what its judge can see. On our expert-annotated benchmark, a general-purpose editor yields no usable result in over 40% of the cases, and no judge is reliable across edit types. We present EditAgent, which expands both spaces. It routes each step to general editors and specialized methods, and attaches to each candidate a verification record. With these records, off-the-shelf VLM judges outperform finetuned reward models. Candidates are generated in parallel and judged in one listwise call: experts prefer this to sequential refinement in 78.5% of decided comparisons, at no more than half the judge calls. EditAgent improves two open-weight editors on three benchmarks and serves as a data engine for training stronger editors.

Abstract
Agentic image editors decompose complex requests into steps, but when a step fails, they mostly retry with the same narrow set of tools and a judge that scores each output by eye directly. We argue that such agents are bounded by two spaces: the action space of what the agent can do, and the observation space of what its judge can see. On our expert-annotated benchmark, a general-purpose editor yields no usable result in over 40% of the cases, and no judge is reliable across edit types. We present EditAgent, which expands both spaces. It routes each step to general editors and specialized methods, and attaches to each candidate a verification record. With these records, off-the-shelf VLM judges outperform finetuned reward models. Candidates are generated in parallel and judged in one listwise call: experts prefer this to sequential refinement in 78.5% of decided comparisons, at no more than half the judge calls. EditAgent improves two open-weight editors on three benchmarks and serves as a data engine for training stronger editors.

Instead of trying again with the same editor, EditAgent generates candidates with different editing methods in parallel, and a judge (off-the-shelf VLM) compares them in one call with a verification record (evidence) for each candidate, without judge finetuning.

Introduction
Instruction-based image editing models can now perform a wide range of edits from a single text instruction
[
4
,

26

. Real requests, however, rarely ask for a single edit. Given “move me to the left of the frame, widen the shot to show more of the beach, remove the people walking behind me, and make it look like sunset,” today’s editors tend to complete some parts and silently drop others
[
67
,
57
]
. Agentic editing systems
[

30

address this by decomposing the request into steps and running a plan-edit-judge loop on each. Yet when a step fails, they mostly try again. The step is refined, retried, or rolled back with the same tools and judge. Here we ask the question:
when an editing agent fails, is another attempt really what it needs? If not, what does the agent really needs?
Consider how a professional retoucher would handle the same request: pick a different tool for each part, and check each result by zooming in and comparing before and after. A retoucher does not simply try again but acts differently and looks more closely. We argue that an editing agent is likewise bounded by two spaces: its
action space
, what it can do, and its judge’s
observation space
, what it can see.
Existing agents
[
15
,
30
,
49

keep both small. Each attempt runs one tool, often a general editor
[
23

26

63

43

14

To explore how each space should be designed, we introduce a diagnostic benchmark of 600 candidate sets over 30 edit types, labeled blindly by professional Photoshop editors (
Fig.
2
). We find that the general editor yields no usable result in 42.7% of the sets, mostly in geometry, tone and enhancement edits, and a specialized method recovers 175 of these 256 failures. Meanwhile, no judge we test, including finetuned reward models
[
35
,
65
]
, is the most accurate across edit groups.
We therefore rethink agentic editing by expanding both spaces. Our system,
EditAgent
, shown in
Fig.
1
, expands the action space by routing each step to general-purpose editors and specialized methods, including masked local editing, object removal and movement, photometric and geometric operators, and so on. It expands the observation space by attaching to each candidate a verification record (evidence), such as a change map, close-ups of the edited region, and measured color and geometry, together with the outcomes of programmatic checks, so that the judge knows what code has verified and what remains for visual judgment. Instead of refining one result round after round, EditAgent thus generates candidates from all selected methods in parallel from the same source image, and the judge compares them with their records in a single listwise call. Unlike in text-to-image generation
[
17
]
, professional editors prefer this parallel search over sequential refinement in 78.5% of non-tied comparisons, with at most half the judge calls (
Sec.
3.3
). With verification records, off-the-shelf VLM judges outperform finetuned reward models without finetuning.

and FLUX.2-klein-9B

[

Our contributions are threefold.
•
We identify the agent’s action space and its judge’s observation space as two bottlenecks of agentic image editing, and analyze both with an expert-annotated diagnostic benchmark spanning 30 edit types.
•
We propose EditAgent, which expands the action space with specialized editing methods and the observation space with verification records, and couples them through parallel candidate generation and listwise judging. With these records, off-the-shelf VLM judges outperform finetuned editing reward models.
•
EditAgent consistently improves strong open-weight editors on three multi-turn and complex-instruction benchmarks, and the sessions it accepts yield training data that further improves standalone editors.

Rethinking Agentic Editing

3.1
Diagnostic Benchmark
We construct a benchmark of 600 editing sets covering 30 fine-grained edit types, with 20 sets per type. The types span six groups:
Content
,
Style & Effects
,
Scene
,
Photometric
,
Geometry
, and
Enhancement
. Each set contains a source image, an instruction, and 2-4 candidate edits from two sources: samples of a general-purpose editor (FLUX.2-klein-9B) and specialized methods such as masked local editing, object removal, and photometric operators. Five professional Photoshop retouchers sit together and select every usable candidate,
i.e.
, every candidate that completes the instruction acceptably. We call the selected candidates the winner set.
3.2
Is One Editor Enough?
We categorize the 600 sets by their winner sets (
Fig.
2
a). The winner set contains only general-editor candidates in 254 sets (42.3%), only specialized candidates in 175 (29.2%), and both kinds in 90 (15.0%). In the remaining 81 sets (13.5%), no candidate is usable. Since every set includes a general-editor candidate, the general editor fails in 256 sets (42.7%), and a specialized method recovers 175 of them. The outcomes also vary strongly across edit groups. The winner set contains only general-editor candidates in 73.8% of
Style & Effects
sets, but only specialized candidates in 72.5% of
Enhancement
and 66.7% of
Geometry
sets.
More samples from the general editor do not recover these failures. For every request, the general editor produces several samples and one of them is delivered,
i.e.
, parallel sampling with a verifier
[
17
]
. A second pool also includes the specialized methods, and the same VLM judge selects the delivered edit in both pools. Both delivered edits are among the labeled candidates of the set. Although the general-editor pool contains more samples, its delivered edit is usable in only 45.2% of the sets, compared with 68.2% for the pool with specialized methods. In the 296 sets where exactly one delivered edit is usable, it comes from the pool with specialized methods in 217.
These results show that one editor is not enough, even when sampled more often.
3.3
Refine Sequentially or Search in Parallel?
While sequential refinement has been shown to improve text-image alignment in image generation
[
17
]
, we observe that it can suffer from error accumulation in image editing, as errors introduced in earlier iterations may propagate to later edits. To investigate this, we compare two strategies using the same editor (FLUX.2-klein-9B) and judge (Qwen3.8-27B), each with a budget of 4 image generations. Sequential refinement iteratively edits the previous result using prompts revised based on VLM feedback, requiring 3 feedback calls and 1 final selection call. Parallel search, in contrast, generates two candidates independently from the original image. If neither is accepted by the judge, it revises the prompt and generates two more candidates from the original image before selecting the best result. This requires at most 2 VLM calls.
In a blind comparison on 144 Complex-Edit samples
[
67
]
at complexity levels 1, 4, and 8, five professional Photoshop editors preferred parallel search in 102 cases and sequential refinement in 28, with 14 ties. Parallel search thus wins 78.5% of the non-tied comparisons with at most half the VLM calls. Unlike generation, editing must stay faithful to the source image. Sequential refinement keeps editing its own output, so small errors can accumulate, whereas parallel search edits every candidate directly from the source.
Thus, for editing, parallel search uses the budget better than sequential refinement.
With several candidates available, the delivered edit then depends on what the judge can see.

4
EditAgent
Given a user request, a planner decomposes it into ordered editing steps (
Fig.
3
). For each step, an analyzer specifies the editing operation and its target, a grounder localizes the target with a VLM and SAM 2.1
[
46
]
when a method needs a mask, and a router selects the applicable editing methods, each of which generates at least one candidate in parallel (
Sec.
4.1
). An off-the-shelf VLM judge evaluates the candidates together with their verification records (
Sec.
4.2
), either accepting one candidate or returning feedback for a retry. Each accepted image becomes the source of the next step, and the requirements it satisfies are carried forward so that subsequent turns can verify that they still hold (
Sec.
4.3
).
4.1
Expanding the Action Space
Candidate Construction.
Given an executable instruction and its source image, the analyzer specifies the editing operation and recommends candidate methods, and the router turns the recommendation into a set of methods that each contribute at least one candidate. Different methods explore different realizations of the request, while repeated sampling explores variation within a method.
Action Space.
Besides the general editor, the capability pool contains: 1) masked local editing and recoloring, which run the general editor inside a SAM 2.1 mask, 2) object removal with OSOR
[
80
]
, 3) object movement with a dedicated model, 4) subject scaling by segmentation and compositing, 5) global and local photometric operators, 6) style filters and neural style transfer, 7) flips, rotations, and rotation to level, and 8) zoom-in by cropping with super-resolution and zoom-out by outpainting. Details can be found in
Tab.
S5
.
4.2
Expanding the Observation Space
Comparative Judging.
Inspired by
Sec.
3.4
, we provide the judge with all candidates in one call. It only needs one VLM call per step, whose comparison yields feedback for the next attempt if a retry is needed.
Verification Records.
Just as a professional retoucher uses different tools to judge an editing operation, we argue that different edits require checks of different properties (
Fig.
4
). For example, a localized edit requires checking both the target change and the preservation of unrelated content, whereas a geometric transformation requires assessing its direction and extent. Some of these properties can be checked by code during execution, some require visual judgment. For each candidate, we collect these checks into a verification record, together with what remains for visual judgment. EditAgent collects the verification record and gives to the judge, so the judge no longer judges by eye alone. Therefore, after all, the judge will receive the edit instruction, the source image, all candidates and their records in one call.

4.3
Planning and Preserving Edits across Turns
Figure 6
:
The history check extends what the judge observes to earlier turns.
Letting in more daylight in turn 2 clears the frosted glass from turn 1. The history check detects this and repairs.
The planner splits a request into dependent steps when its parts need separate execution, and each accepted step becomes the source of the next. Because the step judge sees one step at a time, a later edit can undo an earlier one unnoticed. After every turn, a history check therefore shows the VLM the original image, the results of earlier turns and the current image, and asks whether each earlier request still holds. On a confident violation, EditAgent runs one repair turn and adopts it only if its step judge accepts it (
Fig.
6
).

Experiments
5.1
Experimental Setup
Benchmarks.
We evaluate EditAgent on three benchmarks covering multi-turn and complex-instruction editing. EdiVal
[
6
]
comprises 572 three-turn sessions and assesses editing quality as successive requests accumulate. Complex-Edit
[
67
]
comprises 8,496 real and synthetic examples spanning different levels of instruction complexity. ComplexBench-Edit
[
57
]
comprises 763 examples with compositional instructions, including parallel constraints and multi-step chains. Together, they assess performance across editing turns, complexity, and compositional structure.
Backbones and Baselines.
We instantiate EditAgent with two general-purpose editors, Qwen-Image-Edit-2511
[
63
]
and FLUX.2-klein-9B
[
27
]
. For each backbone, we compare standalone editing with its integration into EditAgent. We also compare it with seven agentic editors (
Tab.
5
). On EdiVal, both backbones edit at the 512 px input resolution. Because most closed-source editors generate at 1024 px or more, we also run Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 at 1024 px and resize back to 512 px for fair comparison. The comparison with agentic editors and all ablations use the 512 px setting.
Evaluation.
We follow the evaluation rubrics of each benchmark. EdiVal uses its released judges, and Qwen3.8-27B
[
56
]
replaces GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking on Complex-Edit and ComplexBench-Edit. As it is also our internal judge, to avoid potential bias, we additionally evaluate EditAgent using Gemma-4-31B
[
55
]
(
Tab.
S8
).
Implementation Details.
Qwen3.8-27B serves as the planner, analyzer, grounder and judge, and SAM 2.1
[
46
]

5.3
EditAgent as a Data Engine
Because EditAgent flags every edit that its judge did not accept, its fully accepted sessions can serve as training data. Using FLUX.2-klein-9B as the general editor, EditAgent produces about 25.7K sessions, averaging four turns each. Each session yields one training sample consisting of the source image, a session-level instruction, and the final edited image. For comparison, we use FLUX.2-klein-9B to directly edit the same sessions, keeping the training inputs identical and varying only the final images. We fully finetune Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 and FLUX.2-klein-base-9B on each dataset for one epoch and evaluate them as standalone editors.
As shown in
Tab.
6
, training on EditAgent data improves both editors across all three benchmarks. On EdiVal-O at turn 3, Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 and FLUX.2-klein-base-9B gain 1.95 and 2.00 points, respectively, while their ComplexBench-Edit averages increase by 3.17 and 2.14 points. More importantly, EditAgent data consistently outperforms directly generated FLUX.2-klein-9B data under the same training recipe.
Notably, direct FLUX.2-klein-9B data degrades FLUX.2-klein-base-9B on all three benchmarks, whereas EditAgent data improves it.
These results suggest that EditAgent provides higher-quality training supervision rather than merely additional training examples.

, where restricting EditAgent to the general editor lowers the share of usable delivered edits. Expanding the observation space further improves performance by 3.09 points.
5.5
Qualitative Results
Figure
7
compares standalone FLUX.2-klein-9B with EditAgent. For multi-turn editing, each turn edits the previous output, so an error carries into every later turn. Standalone editing drops the dog of turn 1 when it adds the old man in turn 2. When turn 2 asks for two baguettes, it adds three, which remains in turn 3. Instead, EditAgent judges each step against its source image, which already contains the earlier edits, and checks that they remain. More qualitative comparisons is provided in
Sec.
I
, further demonstrating the overall advantages of our method, even over GPT-Image-2.
6
Conclusion
We presented EditAgent, which rethinks agentic image editing as expanding two spaces: the action space of the agent and the observation space of its judge. It routes each step to general-purpose and specialized editing methods, generates their candidates in parallel, and lets the off-the-shelf VLM judge compare them with verification records. EditAgent improves two editing backbones across three benchmarks, and functions as a robust data engine, leveraging its accepted sessions to improve standalone editors through fine-tuning.
Limitations.
EditAgent incurs roughly 10
×
\times
the inference time of standalone editing models, and its performance is inherently bounded by the capabilities of its underlying editing methods. Nevertheless, EditAgent can serve as a data engine for finetuning stronger and more efficient standalone editors, potentially amortizing its computational cost.

A
Diagnostic Benchmark
Requests.
The benchmark covers 30 edit types in six groups, with 20 requests per type (
Tab.
S1
). Source images are drawn from COCO val2017
[
31
]
, and each image is used in one set only. A VLM (Qwen3.8-27B) screens each photograph so that every edit type is assigned only to photographs that support it, and then writes one natural instruction of the assigned type, following the type’s definition in
Tab.
S1
. Requests are written before any candidate exists.
Candidates.
Candidates come from two runs of EditAgent on each request, one with the full capability pool and one restricted to the general editor. Both runs use FLUX.2-klein-9B as the general editor and Qwen3.8-27B in all VLM roles. All distinct images generated in these runs form the pool of a set, from which we keep up to four, giving priority to the delivered results and to methods not yet represented. This yields 2 to 4 candidates per set and 1,995 candidates in total.
Annotation.
Five professional Photoshop editors label each set together in a shared interface and agree on one label, so each set has one consensus label. The interface shows the source image, the instruction and the candidates under neutral keys (C1 to C4), in an order fixed by a hash and without any indication of their method. For each set, the editors select every usable candidate,
i.e.
, every candidate that completes the instruction acceptably. A usable candidate is selected even when another candidate is better, so an unselected candidate is unusable, not merely second best. The editors can also mark the set as all usable or all unusable. Of the 600 sets, 248 have one selected candidate, 155 have several, 116 are marked as all usable and 81 as all unusable.
Winner-Set Hit@1.
The winner set of a set contains its selected candidates, or all candidates when the set is marked all usable. It is thus the set of usable candidates, and Winner-Set Hit@1 measures how often a judge’s top choice is usable. We exclude the 81 sets without a usable candidate. Of the remaining 519, we also exclude 4 in which one candidate has no verification record, so that every judge is compared on the same 515 sets. A judge that scores candidates separately selects its top-scoring candidate. When several candidates share the top score, the tie is broken uniformly at random, and we count the expected outcome,
i.e.
, the fraction of the tied candidates that are in the winner set. An invalid output, or a missing score for any candidate of the set, counts as 0. Accuracy is computed per run over the fixed set of sets and averaged over three runs. The random baseline is the mean over sets of the winner-set size divided by the number of candidates. It is 59.32% on the 515 sets and 47.10% on the 396 sets with at least one unusable candidate.

Refine Sequentially or Search in Parallel
Requests.
We sample 48 requests at each of the complexity levels 1, 4 and 8 from the real-image split of Complex-Edit
[
67
]
, each with its own source image. A request at level
k
k
chains
k
k
atomic instructions, so the three levels range from a single edit to a long compound request.
Policies.
Both policies use FLUX.2-klein-9B, Qwen3.8-27B as the VLM, and at most four images per request. Sequential refinement generates the first image from the source with the original instruction. After each of the first three images, it asks the VLM for a corrective request for the latest image and applies it to that image, and a final selection call picks among the four images (3 feedback calls and 1 selection call). Parallel search generates two images from the source with the original instruction. If the VLM accepts neither, it revises the instruction and generates two more images from the source before a final selection, using at most two VLM calls. The VLM sees the source, the candidate images and their difference maps, in a shared random order. Sequential refinement re-edits the latest image, as iterative editing agents commonly do, whereas the retries of EditAgent re-edit the source of the step with a revised instruction (
Sec.
D
).
Human Study.
Five professional Photoshop editors view the final images of the policies blindly, next to the source and the request, in random positions and without labels, and assess instruction following, preservation of unrelated content, and artifacts. For each comparison of parallel search with sequential refinement, the editors either choose the better policy or mark the two as equal. Parallel search is preferred in 102 comparisons and sequential refinement in 28, with 14 ties, so parallel search wins 78.5% of the 130 comparisons in which the editors prefer one policy.
Cost.
With at most four images per request for both policies, parallel search needs at most two VLM calls per request, and sequential refinement always needs four.

State.
EditAgent stores each session as a version graph. Every node holds one image state together with its parent, the step that produced it, its candidates, the judge’s report, and whether it needs review. Accepted states are never modified. A later step adds a child node, and a user correction branches from the parent, so every accepted state remains available. The requirements that an accepted state satisfies, such as the requested change and the regions that had to stay, are carried into the prompts of the planner, the analyzer and the history check in later steps and turns.
Turn.
Algorithm
1
runs one user turn. The planner decides the number and order of the steps (
), and each step starts from the state accepted by the previous step. When a step uses up its attempts, the re-planner either replaces the failed and pending steps or keeps the best attempt, which is then marked as needing review. After the turn, the history check verifies every earlier turn against the current image. On a confident violation, EditAgent runs one repair turn and keeps its result only if the judge accepts it.
Step.
Algorithm
2
runs one step. The analyzer rewrites the step into an explicit instruction for a mask-free editor, stating both the requested change and what must remain, sets the parameters of the applicable methods, and suggests how many candidates the step needs. The router selects the methods (
Tab.
S4
), each of which contributes at least one candidate. Every candidate receives a verification record, candidates that fail a code check are removed, and the judge compares the remaining candidates in a single call, in a shuffled order. An accepted candidate becomes the new state. Otherwise, the judge’s feedback is passed back to the analyzer, which revises the step for the next attempt.

Acceptance.
The judge returns one JSON object (
) with a short note, a pass/fail verdict and a score from 1 to 10 for every candidate, followed by the best candidate and a complete ranking. Only the judge can accept a candidate. The step accepts the best candidate when the judge passes it, and otherwise passes the notes back to the analyzer as feedback for the next attempt.
Robustness.
A method that fails, for example because grounding finds no target, loses only its own candidate, and a step that never produced a candidate leaves the state unchanged. EditAgent keeps the best candidate across the attempts of a step.

Routing Rules.
The router is deterministic code (
Sec.
4.1
of the main paper). It turns the recommendation of the planner and analyzer, that is, the operation, target, executor and parameters of a step, into the methods of
Tab.
S4
, which
Tab.
S5
describes. Every masked method is raced against the general editor, so the judge can fall back to the general editor when a mask is imperfect.
F
Verification Records
Definition.
A verification record holds, for one candidate, the checks that code runs on its pixels (
Sec.
4.2
of the main paper). These are the share of visibly changed pixels, a change map, a close-up of the region that the request names, the measurements that the step calls for (
Tab.
S6
), and the outcomes of code checks, which state what code has verified and what remains for visual judgment. Every record is computed in the same way from the source image and the candidate, and it names no method. What code cannot decide, such as whether an edit looks real, the judge assesses from the photographs (
).
Close-Up.
For a localized step, the grounder names the region of the source image that the request refers to, such as “the man’s shirt” or “the sky behind the house”, and localizes it once, with a VLM box refined by SAM 2.1 and reviewed. Every candidate then gets a
BEFORE
|
AFTER
close-up of this same region, both halves at a height of 448 px, so that all candidates are inspected at the same place and scale, whichever method produced them.
Change Map.
The change map shows where and how strongly each candidate differs from the source, on one fixed scale for all candidates, so that the judge can compare the extent of the changes across candidates. It is not a photograph, and the judge does not assess color or realism from it.
Measurements.
The visible change counts the pixels whose CIELAB color differs from the source visibly (
Δ
​

>
8
\Delta E>8
), after a light blur that suppresses compression noise. For sharpening, deblurring, denoising and blur requests, no blur is applied, since these edits change exactly the fine detail that a blur would hide. The other measurements depend on the operation of the step (
Tab.
S6
), such as the brightness, clipping and color shift in
Fig.
4
(b) of the main paper.
Code Checks.
Each method also declares what it guarantees by construction or verifies by code, such as unchanged pixels outside its mask or an exact pixel permutation for a flip (
Tab.
S5
). A candidate that fails such a check is removed before judging. The record of every remaining candidate lists the checks it passed under
VERIFIED
and what code cannot decide under
TO JUDGE

The judge receives one message with the instructions of

VERIFIED

Backbones.
Each backbone uses the same checkpoint and sampler with and without EditAgent. Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 runs 40 steps with CFG 4 in BF16, and FLUX.2-klein-9B uses its distilled 4-step sampler. Within EditAgent, the backbone is the general editor. It therefore also runs inside the masked methods, the refinement and harmonization of Subject Scaling, the Multi-Reference Editor and the fill of Canvas Extension, which all call the general editor. OSOR, FLUX.1-Fill for the rotation ring and the outpainting fallback, Swin2SR, neural style transfer and the closed-form operators are the same for all backbones. Compute.
Generation runs on nodes of 8 H200 GPUs. With speculative decoding (DFlash2
[
1

), the 40,726 sessions take about 400 GPU-hours. Every 10,000 sessions take about 100 GPU-hours, and about 70% of them are kept as high quality.
Training Pairs.
Each kept session gives one training pair, made of the source image, one instruction for the whole session and the final image. A pair ends before the first turn that changes the image size and needs at least two applied edits. This gives 26,251 pairs with 3.9 edits per pair on average. Qwen3.8-27B composes the instruction from those of the delivered steps, resolving the final intent by dropping overridden or cancelled edits. The pairs are split by source image into 25,753 training and 498 validation pairs. The same pairs train the students for all three benchmarks.
Baseline Data.
For the matched baseline, FLUX.2-klein-9B edits every turn of the same sessions directly with the original per-turn instructions, each turn on its own previous output, without planning or judging. Its pairs use the same kept sessions, split and instructions as the EditAgent pairs, with the final image taken from the FLUX.2-klein-9B chain, so the two datasets differ only in their images.

article.headline: EditAgent：扩展智能体的动作与观察空间
article.lede: EditAgent 让每个编辑步骤并行调用多种方法生成候选，再由现成 VLM 带验证记录一次性比较挑出可用结果。
article.problem: 现有智能体式图像编辑器把复杂请求拆成步骤后，一旦某步失败，往往仍用同一套狭窄工具重试，评判模型也只对着单张输出「用眼睛」打分。作者认为这类系统受限于两个空间：智能体能做什么（动作空间），以及评判模型能看到什么（观察空间）。在自建的 600 组、30 类编辑的诊断基准上，通用编辑器有 42.7% 的组里没有任何可用结果。
article.method: EditAgent 把每一步路由到通用编辑器与专用方法（掩码局部编辑、物体移除与移动、光度与几何算子等），各方法从同一源图并行生成候选。每个候选附带一份验证记录，包括变化图、局部放大图、颜色与几何测量值，以及代码检查结论，让通用 VLM 评判时知道哪些性质已验证、哪些仍需目视判断。评判以一次 listwise 调用完成全部候选的比较，接受其一或返回反馈；多轮场景还加入历史检查，检测后续编辑是否破坏了早期编辑并执行一次修复。
article.results: 诊断基准上，在含至少一个可用候选的 515 组中，加入 listwise 比较与验证记录把 Qwen3.8-27B 的 Winner-Set Hit@1 从 71.6% 提升到 81.3%，比最强的微调奖励模型 EditScore-72B 高 6.5 个点；七个现成 VLM 评判器提升 6.3 至 9.3 个点，Qwen3.8-Flash-Next 达到 82.8%。在 144 个 Complex-Edit 样本的盲评中，专业修图师在 130 次有偏好的比较里 102 次选择并行搜索、28 次选择顺序精修，即 78.5% 偏好并行，且 VLM 调用不超过后者的一半（至多 2 次对 4 次）。以 Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 与 FLUX.2-klein-9B 为骨干，EdiVal-O 第三轮分别从 47.64 升到 55.46、从 53.20 升到 59.45（1024 像素设定的 Qwen 骨干从 59.80 升到 62.58），ComplexBench-Edit 平均分分别提升 6.43 与 3.06 分；专用方法贡献了 19% 至 31% 的被接受步骤。作为数据引擎，用其约 25.7K 条全接受会话微调，EdiVal-O 第三轮分别提升 1.95 与 2.00 个点。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「换方法、换看法」变成可操作的工程原则，说明在图像编辑里扩大工具池与给评判模型提供证据，比反复精修同一个输出或微调专用奖励模型更划算。被接受的会话还能当作数据引擎，反哺更强的单模型编辑器。
article.limitations: 推理时间约为单体编辑模型的 10 倍，且性能本质上受限于底层各编辑方法的能力上限；此外论文内部评判与两个基准的自动评测都使用 Qwen3.8-27B，虽然作者用 Gemma-4-31B 复测缓解了偏差疑虑，诊断基准的请求也是由 VLM 生成、仅 600 组。
article.figure_caption_zh: EditAgent 流程示意：底层是一个请求被拆成有依赖的步骤、每步接受的结果成为下一步的输入；上层放大第一步，规划器排序，分析器与路由器选出适用方法，各方法从同一源图并行生成带验证记录的候选，现成 VLM 一次性比较后接受其一或返回反馈。
