email_papers.title: Co-Design Bench: Multimodal Collaborative Coding Evaluation for Agentic Models
email_papers.abstract: Evaluating human-AI co-design requires testing whether coding agents can translate real users' multimodal requests into working application revisions. We introduce Co-Design Bench, a reference-free benchmark of 273 tasks curated from 37,463 deduplicated queries across 26,314 real user coding sessions. Its two tracks, Multimodal Editing (ME) and Repository Editing (RE), cover localized edits with optional image, audio, video, or document inputs and coordinated repository revisions. Tasks span three capability dimensions: Grounded Understanding, UI Transformation, and Functional Implementation. The tasks pair normalized requests and runnable pre-edit applications with 2,331 hidden expert-authored acceptance criteria. Our judge-then-refute protocol grades criteria using source and browser evidence, challenges positive verdicts with a separate LLM verifier, and audits visual and interaction claims without gold code or target screenshots. Under a shared agentic harness, the strongest of ten model endpoints passes an average of 69.9% of criteria per task but fully satisfies only 26.4% of tasks. All ten endpoints achieve lower criterion completion on repository edits spanning three or four change types than on those spanning one or two. Co-Design Bench provides a testbed for studying the gap between partial requirement satisfaction and complete task success under agentic execution for real-user application revisions.

1
Introduction
Web application co-design follows an iterative cycle of inspecting an existing artifact, requesting changes, and assessing the result
(
Schön, 1983
)
.
Coding agents can participate in this cycle by inspecting visual context, modifying source files, and executing applications
(
Yang et al., 2024a
;
Anthropic, 2025
;
OpenAI, 2026a
;
Qwen Team, 2026b
)
.
Success requires translating user intent into working revisions of the current application.
A request may combine image, audio, video, or document inputs with changes to layout, interaction, and application state, requiring the agent to connect multimodal evidence to dependent revisions across the application’s interface and behavior.
Existing benchmarks capture important parts of this problem: reference reconstruction
(
Si et al., 2024
;
Lai et al., 2025
;
Chen et al., 2025
)
, synthetic or predefined edits and repairs
(
Li et al., 2026
;
Lei et al., 2026
)
, edits extracted from version histories
(
Xiao et al., 2025
)
, and implementation of repository issues or freelance requests
(
Jimenez et al., 2023
;
Yang et al., 2024b
;
Miserendino et al., 2025
)
.

1
).
For example, the sports clip editor request in Figure

Such a request ties success to the behavior of the edited application across several interacting requirements at once.

We introduce
Co-Design Bench

273

2,331

We recover and validate runnable pre-edit applications, retain available session context and attachments, and consolidate user requests into bounded editing tasks.
The benchmark covers two complementary settings:
Multimodal Editing (ME)
evaluates localized visual, structural, and content edits with optional image, audio, video, or document inputs;
Repository Editing (RE)
evaluates coordinated UI and feature changes across components, routes, state, and data flow.
Both tracks pair the starting application with a normalized request and hidden acceptance criteria that specify the requested changes while allowing multiple valid implementations.
A document-grounded edit can require consistent updates to a displayed value and its dependent summaries, while a repository request can couple visible controls with state transitions across components.
The shared task formulation captures these dependencies as auditable requirements, connecting the interpretation of user evidence to observable visual changes and state transitions in the edited application.
Evaluating these tasks requires checking whether requested features are reachable and behave correctly in the edited application.
Our
judge-then-refute
protocol first grades hidden criteria using source code and browser execution evidence.
A separate LLM verifier challenges
Pass
and
Partial
verdicts against the collected evidence, checking for stubs, hardcoding, unreachable functionality, and requirement mismatches.
Audits require successful renders and screenshots for visual claims and recorded browser actions for interaction claims; missing evidence aborts evaluation before score aggregation.
The pre-edit application grounds the requested changes, enabling reference-free acceptance without gold code or target screenshots, while retained verdicts and traces link each criterion judgment to its supporting evidence for inspection.
We evaluate ten model endpoints under a shared agentic harness.
The strongest endpoint passes an average of
69.9
%

of criteria per task but fully satisfies only
26.4
%
26.4\%
of tasks.
Model rankings vary between tracks, and all ten endpoints achieve lower criterion completion on repository edits spanning three or four change types than on those spanning one or two.
These results show that substantial coverage of individual requirements can coexist with limited complete-task success, motivating evaluation of both criterion satisfaction and complete delivery.
Contributions.
(1)
We construct a benchmark of real-user application revisions spanning localized multimodal edits and coordinated repository changes, with runnable starting states and expert-authored criteria.
(2)
We develop a reference-free evaluation protocol that combines code and browser evidence, a separate refutation pass, and mandatory evidence audits to assess requested changes.
(3)
We characterize the gap between criterion satisfaction and complete task success across ten model endpoints, with analyses of input modality and edit breadth.

2
Related Work
Multimodal web generation and editing.
Design2Code, WebSight-Test (from WAFFLE), and WebRenderBench evaluate screenshot-to-code reconstruction against reference pages
(
Si et al., 2024
;
Liang et al., 2024
;
Lai et al., 2025
)
. IWR-Bench extends reconstruction to interaction videos, using annotated action replay and reference screenshots
(
Chen et al., 2025
)
. WebGen-Bench and FrontendBench add browser- or sandbox-based functional tests for websites generated from scratch
(
Lu et al., 2025
;
Zhu et al., 2025
)
. Editing benchmarks instead revise an existing artifact. DesignBench extracts adjacent-version pairs from V0/Vue0 histories for before/after screenshot assessment
(
Xiao et al., 2025
)
. MT-Web2Code synthesizes repair trajectories by corrupting reference pages
(
Li et al., 2026
)
, while WebCompass constructs tasks around predefined edit operations
(
Lei et al., 2026
)
. FronTalk studies conversational front-end generation with multimodal feedback
(
Wu et al., 2026
)
. Co-Design Bench instead fixes a bounded revision recovered from a production coding session, retaining its runnable starting application, context, and attachments; hidden criteria specify requested changes without gold code or a target screenshot as supervision.
Repository-level coding.
SWE-bench evaluates changes for real GitHub issues through executable tests
(
Jimenez et al., 2023
)
. SWE-bench Multimodal covers frontend JavaScript software with visual tests
(
Yang et al., 2024b
)
, and SWE-Lancer evaluates real freelance implementation requests through browser-based end-to-end tests
(
Miserendino et al., 2025
)
. Co-Design Bench focuses on compound design and feature revisions within coding sessions. Its repository track covers coordinated changes to components, routes, state, and data flow. A shared task interface and acceptance protocol connect this setting to localized multimodal edits, allowing both requirement coverage and complete delivery to be measured on a common scale across the two tracks.
Agentic artifact evaluation and verification.
Agent-as-a-Judge assesses generated artifacts against user requirements using agent capabilities
(
Zhuge et al., 2024
)
. WebCompass uses browser interaction and adaptive tests for generation; its editing and repair settings use checklist-guided judgments from code, logs, and screenshots
(
Lei et al., 2026
)
. Structured LLM evaluation can improve agreement with human judgments, yet evaluators can exhibit self-preference and benchmark-dependent reliability
(
Liu et al., 2023
;
Panickssery et al., 2024
;
Lù et al., 2025
)
. For application revisions, source presence alone does not establish reachability or correct behavior. Our
judge-then-refute
protocol therefore combines source and browser evidence with a separate verifier; mandatory audits require screenshots for visual claims and recorded actions for interaction claims. Retained evidence makes positive credit traceable, though it cannot eliminate judgment error.
3

Recovering executable starting states.
We reconstruct applications from session logs, repository archives, or HTML bundles. Candidates must pass dependency, build, container launch, and Playwright rendering checks

Selecting requests and authoring acceptance criteria.

Evidence and primary grading.
The candidate is built and rendered in an isolated environment. A fixed agentic evaluator

Evidence must match the claim: source inspection can establish a static property, a screenshot can support a visual requirement, and recorded actions can establish an interaction and its resulting state. Failed builds or missing DOM nodes invalidate render-dependent criteria; a handler in source code alone cannot establish that users can reach and operate the requested functionality through the rendered interface.

5.4
Ablation and Robustness Studies
We conduct systematic ablations across three critical experimental axes.
Execution Regimes:
Comparing single-shot against agentic execution on
150
150
WebCompass-edit tasks demonstrates the necessity of iterative agentic loops (Appendix
A
).
Evaluator Sensitivity:
Swapping the underlying judge model confirms that relative model rankings and score distributions remain highly robust across different evaluators (Appendix
C
).
Scaffold Robustness:
Evaluating identical solvers across three distinct harnesses reveals strong model
×
\times
harness interactions and highlights the decisive role of closed-loop verification (Appendix
H
).
6
Conclusion
Co-Design Bench evaluates
273
273
real-user application revisions with runnable starting states and
2,331
2{,}331
hidden acceptance criteria. Its two tracks span localized multimodal edits and coordinated repository changes under a shared protocol of source evidence, browser execution, and adversarial review. Across ten endpoints, the strongest model reaches
69.9
%
69.9\%
mean strict completion but fully satisfies only
26.4
%
26.4\%
of tasks. Track-specific rankings, edit-breadth differences, and harness sensitivity show where reliable delivery remains difficult. Runnable baselines and criterion-level evidence support analysis of failures in request grounding, change propagation, and final-state verification. The benchmark provides a common setting for measuring progress toward complete delivery by coding agents, while retaining the task context and execution evidence needed to analyze unmet requirements and compare future solvers.

Appendix D
Implementation and Resource Accounting
Execution constraints.
Each trajectory has a three-hour wall-clock limit and a
120
120
-turn cap. A wall-clock timeout terminates execution and is recorded as an infrastructure failure. Reaching the turn cap instead triggers a build, render, and evaluation of the final workspace state.
Telemetry and token accounting.
Resource totals come from request-level API logs and include retries. For Anthropic routes, token totals sum prompt, completion, cache-creation, and cache-read entries. For OpenAI routes, reported prompt usage already includes cached input. The evaluated trajectories contain
135,370
135{,}370
tool calls. These accounting conventions distinguish actual requests from a count of unique attempted actions.
Trace integrity and final-state evaluation.
Tool invocations and returns are paired sequentially within the same assistant scope. This prevents identifiers reused by nested agents from merging unrelated events. Intermediate renders and edits remain available for inspection. Scores use the final candidate: earlier behavior earns credit only if it remains present in the final workspace.

Representative Benchmark Cases
Figures
5
and
6
connect solver inputs to evaluator checks. Each row shows the runnable page and relevant detail on the left, a summarized request in the center, and three selected acceptance criteria on the right. Full-page views establish the surrounding application; detail views locate the edit or its supporting evidence. The checks cover requested changes, dependent updates, and explicit preservation constraints, illustrating why a plausible local modification may leave part of a task unresolved. These panels illustrate the task interface; quantitative results use the full task pool and complete rubrics, which remain hidden from the solver.
Figure 5:
Representative ME cases: grounded local edits.
The examples cover cross-source reconciliation, cross-view consistency, and
visual-reference grounding. Numbered markers organize the visible evidence;
the right column visualizes three selected evaluator targets as value flows,
compact charts, and state transitions. The complete rubric may contain additional criteria.
What the ME examples test.
The receipt case requires a value to be reconciled across a source document,
an editable row, and multiple dependent summaries. The click-audit case tests
whether externally supplied counts propagate consistently without disturbing
unrelated link metadata. The video-grounded case combines visual-reference
transfer with localized preservation: one product card must adopt evidence from
the clip while neighboring cards, ordering, price, and rating retain their specified values and positions.
Across the three rows, the selected checks follow a common pattern: establish
the authoritative evidence, verify every requested dependent update, and test
that unrelated content remains stable. The checks assess whether a local patch also satisfies the requested relationships among totals, linked views, and neighboring components.
What the RE examples test.
These repository-level tasks require behavior to remain coherent beyond a
single screenshot. The partner-page case combines navigation restructuring,
new content sections, responsive styling, and accessibility requirements. The
clip editor couples duration and count limits with recovery, timeline accuracy,
export, and keyboard control. The theme case adds persistent color modes,
working routes, and a GSAP-driven mega menu while preserving the site’s layout
and existing motion behavior.
Across the three rows, the checks distinguish visible content, executable
interaction, and baseline behavior that must remain intact. The checks cover the requested interface together with the state transitions that make its controls and routes usable.
Figure 6:
Representative RE cases: coordinated repository edits.
The examples span navigation and page construction, clip editing under
resource limits, and theme-aware motion with a morphing mega menu. The
selected targets use route flows, thresholds, token palettes, and interaction
states to make the behavior and preservation constraints explicit.

article.headline: 真实用户改码基准：最强模型仅完整通过26.4%
article.lede: 从26,314个真实编程会话筛出273个改码任务，最强模型平均通过69.9%的验收标准，全部通过仅26.4%。
article.problem: 现有网页编码基准多基于参考页面重建、合成编辑操作或版本历史抽取的改动对，缺少从真实用户编程会话中回收、同时覆盖局部多模态编辑与跨组件仓库协同修改的复合修订任务。论文还指出，执行方式会显著改变测得的完成度：在同样的150个WebCompass-edit任务上，qwen3.7-plus从单次执行的73.6%提升到agentic执行的95.1%，相差21.5个百分点，因此只报单一分数容易误读。
article.method: 作者构建Co-Design Bench，含273个任务与2,331条专家撰写、对解题者隐藏的验收标准，分多模态编辑（ME，100个任务）与仓库编辑（RE，173个任务）两条轨道，每个任务都配有可运行的编辑前应用、归一化请求和可选附件。评测采用judge-then-refute协议：先由固定的agentic评估器依据源码差异、渲染页面和Playwright轨迹对每条标准给出Pass/Partial/Fail，再由独立的LLM验证器专门反驳正向判定（查桩代码、硬编码、不可达入口等），最后做证据审计——视觉类声明必须有成功渲染与截图，交互类声明必须有录制的浏览器动作，缺证即在聚合前中止。
article.results: 在统一使用Claude Code harness、限时3小时与120轮的前提下，十个模型端点跑满2,730个模型–任务对。最强的gpt-6-astra平均严格完成度为0.699（69.9%），但只有26.4%的任务全部标准通过；分轨道看ME为0.754、全通过41.0%，RE为0.667、全通过17.9%，也就是说约73.6%的任务至少残留一条未满足的标准。RE轨道上，跨三或四种编辑类型的任务汇总严格完成度为0.591，低于只跨一或两种的0.654，差6.3个百分点，且十个端点在宽编辑组上无一例外更低。评估器敏感性检查中，换用三个替代评判模型后绝对分数最多偏移0.053，kimi-k3与Qwen3.8-27B在两条轨道上的相对顺序保持不变。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「通过多少条要求」与「整个任务是否交付」拆成两个指标同时报告，说明高分覆盖度可以掩盖大量未完成交付，为真实用户应用修订场景下的coding agent提供了可追溯到证据的评测口径。
article.limitations: 评分主体仍是LLM评判加LLM反驳，论文自承无法消除判断错误，人工只由两位前端专家抽查了200个任务–模型输出；任务使用固定请求，不模拟执行过程中的进一步用户反馈。此外跨harness实验显示模型排序会随执行框架反转（ME上Spearman ρ=-1.00，两模型差距在10.0至16.2个百分点间摆动），分数与harness强耦合；模态与编辑广度的分组比较也被明确称为描述性而非因果。
article.figure_caption_zh: 从产物到判定：先构建并渲染候选、采集源码与浏览器证据并给隐藏标准打分，再由独立验证器挑战正向判定、审计必需证据并聚合分数，并行的基线与可解性检查用于失败归因。

figure.caption: {Evaluation from artifact to verdict.} (a) Build and render the candidate, collect source and browser evidence, and grade hidden criteria. (b) Challenge positive verdicts, audit required evidence, and aggregate scores. Parallel baseline and solvability checks diagnose failures for supplementary attribution analysis.

email_papers.title: VibeGame: Prompt-to-Game Development with AI-Native Engine and Self-Evolving Adversarial Agent Team
email_papers.abstract: Large language model agents have enabled software development through natural-language interaction, but extending this paradigm to end-to-end game development remains challenging. Building a playable game requires coordinating code, scenes, assets, animations, physics, and configurations, while allowing developers to validate their integrated behavior through interactive testing. We introduce VibeGame, a framework for creating complete 2D game projects from natural-language prompts and optional reference images. Its AI-native game engine represents project state as schema-validated structured text and provides frame-synchronous runtime control, enabling agents to inspect game states, execute actions, and verify behavior at their own pace. Built upon this interface, we design an Adversarial Agent Team of eight specialized agents to separate implementation from review, so that problems are found and fixed through multi-round loops. For each conducted and accepted project, we further introduce a training-free self-evolution mechanism to distill it into reusable skeletons, modules, and collaboration contracts for future development. We evaluate prompt-assets-to-game (PA2G), where agents are given an asset library, and prompt-to-game (P2G), where agents generate their own art. On a GameCraft-Bench subset, VibeGame in P2G consistently outperforms a range of agent harnesses in either P2G or PA2G with the same underlying model, including GPT-6.1-Sol.

Abstract
Large language model agents have enabled software development through natural-language interaction, but extending this paradigm to end-to-end game development remains challenging.
Building a playable game requires coordinating code, scenes, assets, animations, physics, and configurations, while allowing developers to validate their integrated behavior through interactive testing.
We introduce VibeGame, a framework for creating complete 2D game projects from natural-language prompts and optional reference images.
Its AI-native game engine represents project state as schema-validated structured text and provides frame-synchronous runtime control, enabling agents to inspect game states, execute actions, and verify behavior at their own pace.
Built upon this interface, we design an Adversarial Agent Team of eight specialized agents to separate implementation from review, so that problems are found and fixed through multi-round loops.
For each conducted and accepted project, we further introduce a training-free self-evolution mechanism to distill it into reusable skeletons, modules, and collaboration contracts for future development.
We evaluate prompt-assets-to-game (PA2G), where agents are given an asset library, and prompt-to-game (P2G), where agents generate their own art.
On a GameCraft-Bench subset, VibeGame in P2G consistently outperforms a range of agent harnesses in either P2G or PA2G with the same underlying model, including GPT-6.1-Sol.
1
Introduction
Games are among the most demanding types of software to develop: they must sustain interactive worlds in real time, maintain a coherent visual identity, and enforce consistent, balanced rules.
Meeting these requirements has traditionally required months of collaboration among designers, programmers, and artists using game engines such as Unity
[
1
]
, Unreal Engine
[
2
]
, and Godot
[
3
]
.
The required time and resources put game development out of reach for many creators.
Artificial intelligence (AI) has begun to lower this barrier from two directions, yet neither fully supports practical game creation.
World models such as Genie
[
4
]
generate interactive experiences directly from video but produce no editable source code, while large language models (LLMs) integrated into commercial engines, as in DreamGarden
[
5
]
for Unreal, face project state scattered across graphical interfaces and binary assets that agents cannot consistently inspect or modify.
Neither produces a complete game project that can be built, played, inspected, versioned, and iteratively revised.
Meanwhile, LLM-based coding agents
[
6
,
7
]
have made “vibe coding” increasingly accessible, allowing non-programmers to describe software in natural language and refine it through iterative feedback.
Games are the natural next step, and we formulate this challenge as
Prompt-to-Game (P2G) Development
: given only a natural language description and optional reference images, the system must produce a complete playable game project, discovering and fixing its problems along the way.
Recent systems and benchmarks have made progress toward this goal.
AutoUE
[
8
]
and OpenGame
[
9
]
build games end to end with agents, and GameDevBench
[
10
]
and GameCraft-Bench
[
11
]
evaluate such abilities, the latter also with a provided asset library, a setting we call Prompt-Assets-to-Game (PA2G).
However, most of these efforts reserve runtime checks for final evaluation or limit them to verifying that a game builds and runs.
Yet many game issues emerge only during play, making interactive testing and refinement essential to playability.
Additionally, fixing one project artifact can introduce inconsistencies across interdependent code, scenes, assets, animations, physics, and configurations.
Addressing these challenges reliably and carrying validated solutions forward to future projects requires three tightly coupled capabilities.
First, an
agent-operable project state
must expose the structure and dependencies among scripts, scenes, assets, animations, physics, and configurations, because direct file access alone cannot prevent a seemingly local edit from violating hidden relationships elsewhere.
Second,
interaction-grounded verification
is needed because a structurally valid project can still fail at runtime when player input, physics, animation, and game logic interact; since execution unfolds faster than an agent can reason about it, verification requires controllable execution that can be paused, advanced, and examined.
Third, the system must
preserve validated development experience
: so that reusable project structures, features, and coordination procedures can guide subsequent work, while unverified or project-specific content must remain isolated.
To address these requirements together, we introduce
VibeGame
, a unified framework that connects project construction, runtime verification, and experience reuse within a development loop, as illustrated in Figure
3
.
(1)
An
AI-native game engine
exposes scenes, nodes, assets, scripts, and configurations as structured text with explicit references and schema validation, and its frame-synchronous runtime control lets agents inspect game states, inject actions, and observe their consequences.
(2)
Built upon this interface, an
Adversarial Agent Team (AAT)
separates implementation roles from auditor, player, and reviewer roles, which challenge the game from structural, behavioral, and project-level perspectives; the team iterates review and revision until the project satisfies the intended design and functionality.
(3)
Once the project is accepted, a
training-free self-evolution mechanism
distills its reusable experience into project skeletons, verified modules, and collaboration contracts (Section
3.3
), which subsequent projects adapt and revalidate rather than reuse blindly.
Figure 2
:
Games created by VibeGame from prompts across diverse 2D game genres.
Figures
1
and
2
present some examples produced by VibeGame.
And with the same underlying model, VibeGame in P2G outperforms a range of agent harnesses in either P2G or PA2G. Ablation studies further show that removing either the AI-native engine or the adversarial review roles substantially lowers the overall score, and that the experience distilled through self-evolution with a stronger model can be transferred to improve a weaker one.
In summary, our contributions are three-fold:
•
We introduce VibeGame, a framework for
prompt-to-game development
that transforms natural-language prompts into complete, playable game projects, enabling rapid game creation and subsequent iterative refinement.
•
At the core of our method is an
AI-native game engine
that enables coding agents to directly inspect and modify project state and control runtime execution without relying on graphical editors. Building on this engine, we introduce an
Adversarial Agent Team
that separates implementation from review, together with a
training-free self-evolution
mechanism that distills validated development experience into reusable knowledge for future projects.
•
We comprehensively evaluate VibeGame against other mainstream agent harnesses in both P2G and PA2G settings, demonstrating superior performance over all of them.
2
Related Work
Agentic software development and vibe coding frameworks.
Coding agents such as Claude Code
[
6
]
, Codex
[
7
]
, Cursor
[
12
]
, OpenHands
[
13
]
, and SWE-agent
[
14
]
, often with ReAct
[
15
]
-style reasoning and evaluated on benchmarks such as SWE-bench
[
16
]
, have moved LLM-based programming to repository-level development.
Vibe coding frameworks such as Trellis
[
17
]
externalize specs, tasks, and memory as persistent repository artifacts, and ChatDev
[
18
]
and MetaGPT
[
19
]
introduce role specialization into software development.
VibeGame extends these directions to game projects, where code, art assets, scene configurations, and runtime behavior must be maintained jointly and verified by running the game.
Engine-integrated game generation.
Prior work connects LLMs and generative models to game engines and 3D tools: Sketch2Scene
[
20
]
builds 3D game scenes from sketches; UnrealLLM
[
21
]
and DreamGarden
[
5
]
generate content and environments in Unreal Engine (UE); 3Dify
[
22
]
uses the Model Context Protocol (MCP)
[
23
]
or computer use to call Blender
[
24
]
, Unity, and UE toolchains, enhanced by retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)
[
25
]
; and
Hassan [26]
generate Unity templates from design documents.
AutoUE
[
8
]
chains five agents to generate 3D games in UE and uses play-testing for the final evaluation.
These systems mostly work around the graphical user interface (GUI) workflows of commercial engines, whereas web frameworks like Phaser
[
27
]
express projects fully in text.
OpenGame
[
9
]
builds on Phaser with templates and a debug protocol, generates its own assets from the prompt alone, i.e., the P2G setting, and repairs build and test failures until the game builds and runs.
VibeGame further adds an agent-oriented project representation, runtime control, and visual verification, and lets independent roles verify the running game inside the development loop.
3
The VibeGame Framework
Figure 3
:
System overview of VibeGame.
(a) The Adversarial Agent Team turns a user request into an accepted game through intention alignment, parallel development, and adversarial correction. (b) The AI-native game engine exposes a structured project representation and frame-synchronous runtime control for implementation and play-testing. (c) Training-free self-evolution extracts skeletons, modules, and collaboration contracts from accepted projects and returns them to future development as project priors.
VibeGame takes a natural-language request and optional reference images as inputs and produces a complete 2D game project that can be run, inspected, and modified through later requests.
Figure
3
presents the project lifecycle.
The AI-native engine provides the shared project representation and runtime interface on which all agents operate (Section
3.1
).
On top of it, the Adversarial Agent Team, eight specialized agents coordinated by an
orchestrator
, turns the request into an accepted game through intention alignment, parallel development, and adversarial correction (Section
3.2
).
After acceptance, the training-free self-evolution mechanism distills the project into skeletons, modules, and collaboration contracts that initialize future runs (Section
3.3
).
3.1
AI-Native Game Engine
A game engine provides the foundation on which a game project is constructed and executed, but traditional engines are designed for human-operated workflows.
We define a game engine as
AI-native
when it has three properties that remove the resulting barriers for coding agents.
(1) GUI-Independent
: the entire project is represented as plain-text files that agents can inspect and edit directly, rather than engine-specific identifiers or binary files that require graphical editors.
(2) Runtime-Accessible
: agents can pause, step through, observe, and intervene in the running game through code rather than GUI-based debugging tools, turning an asynchronous real-time system into a synchronously verifiable process.
(3) Source-Available
: agents can inspect the engine’s uncompiled source code rather than relying on documentation that may lag behind version changes or omit implementation details.
GUI-Independent.
We build our engine on Phaser because it expresses projects fully in text (Section
2
).
However, Phaser imposes little structure on how a project is organized, which makes agent-generated projects prone to fragmentation.
We therefore represent each game as a collection of scenes whose configurations are stored in type-checked JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) files.
Each scene is a hierarchy of nodes, the basic building blocks of the project; a node groups its visual appearance, collision geometry, behavior scripts, and configuration into one unit, declared explicitly in JSON fields rather than hidden inside constructors.
Nodes shared across scenes are stored as standalone definition files and instantiated at runtime.
This scene-node-asset hierarchy gives every artifact a clear location and makes cross-file dependencies explicit, so schema validation can detect invalid references, such as missing assets, before execution rather than as runtime failures.
Runtime-Accessible.
A structurally valid project may still fail when player input, physics, animation, and game logic interact during execution.
We therefore expose the running game through a frame-synchronous programmatic interface: agents can pause and resume execution, advance a specified number of frames, inspect or modify runtime properties such as node positions and velocities, inject semantic actions such as “press jump”, and capture screenshots.
With these controls, agents verify runtime behavior at their own pace through frame-by-frame inspection, scripted test sequences, or heuristic bots that react during real-time play.
Source-Available.
Even with structured project files and runtime control, agents may still encounter engine behavior that the documentation does not fully explain, particularly after an interface change or in uncommon functionality.
We therefore copy the engine’s complete, uncompiled source code into the project directory at initialization, so agents can look up the exact application programming interfaces (APIs), assumptions, and implementation details needed for the current task.

3.2
Adversarial Agent Team
The engine provides the interfaces required to construct and test a game, but it does not determine what should be built, how development should be organized, or when the result is satisfactory.
Assigning these responsibilities to a single agent would also require the same role to both produce and evaluate its own work, making behavioral failures and visual defects during gameplay easier to overlook.
VibeGame therefore introduces an
Adversarial Agent Team
(AAT) comprising eight specialized roles: orchestrator, designer, artist, architect, programmer, auditor, player, and reviewer.
We define each agent’s responsibilities through role-specific prompts and execution hooks, and use persistent project artifacts to preserve decisions and communicate them across the team.
As shown in Figure
3
(a), the team organizes development into three stages:
Intention Alignment
,
Parallel Development
, and
Adversarial Correction
.
Throughout this process, the orchestrator maintains the development state and coordinates the specialized roles.
3.2.1
Intention Alignment
Before development begins, the designer draws on game-design principles and genre conventions to expand requests such as “make a Hollow Knight-style boss fight” into a complete Game Design Document (GDD) that defines gameplay mechanics, progression rules, and numerical systems.
In parallel, the artist uses image-generation models to create concept art that establishes a consistent visual direction for subsequent assets.
After user confirmation, the GDD and concept art form the shared ground truth for all downstream development and evaluation.
During development, any task that introduces or changes a design decision returns to the designer, who drafts it, confirms it with the user, and merges it into the GDD.
3.2.2
Parallel Development
Code Workflow.
Code is implemented by a pipeline of four agents: architect, programmer, auditor, and player.
The orchestrator first decomposes the game into parallel components, retrieves relevant skeletons, modules, and contracts from the self-evolution repository (Section
3.3
) as project priors, and prepares a Product Requirements Document (PRD) that defines the scope and acceptance criteria of each component.
The architect then plans the implementation strategy and its verification procedure, and after the orchestrator approves the plan, the programmer implements it.
The auditor checks the result statically with the engine’s consistency-checking tools and against the design specification.
Finally, the player runs the game through the engine’s runtime interface under frame-synchronous control and uses a vision model to assess whether the rendered result matches the intended appearance.
A sub-task is complete only after it passes both static auditing and runtime play-testing.
Artist Workflow.
The artist agent converts visual requirements from the orchestrator into engine-ready assets.
It invokes image-generation models, including GPT-Image-2
[
31
]
and Nano Banana Pro
[
32
]
, to create the initial artwork, then applies post-processing operations such as background removal and size normalization.
It then registers the processed assets with the engine, recording their paths, dimensions, and usage.
3.2.3
Adversarial Correction
After all sub-tasks are completed, an independent reviewer acts as the final quality gate and evaluates the complete project on
functionality
(whether the game behaves as specified),
visual quality
(asset completeness, stylistic consistency, and screen clarity), and
playability
(e.g., control responsiveness and the clarity of combat feedback).
If the project fails any criterion, the reviewer rejects it with specific reasons, and the orchestrator converts them into new repair tasks; this build-review cycle continues until the project satisfies all acceptance criteria.
The process runs automatically by default, and the orchestrator incorporates any user feedback into subsequent development.
3.3
Training-free Self-Evolution
The AI-native game engine and AAT produce accepted game projects that reflect both agent-side implementation and user feedback.
VibeGame distills reusable experience from these validated projects with a training-free self-evolution mechanism and uses it to initialize future development runs, preserving implicit development knowledge that general-purpose agents lose across independent runs.
We organize the experience into three complementary forms: skeletons, modules, and contracts.
Skeletons.
A skeleton is a runnable project template associated with a particular game type.
It removes project-specific art assets but preserves the code architecture, tuning values, visual proportions, scene flow, and runtime structure of the original project.
Each skeleton also includes error notes and an art pack.
The error notes summarize recurring failures and their verified fixes, while the art pack records reusable visual-production recipes, including asset-generation prompts and post-processing conventions for the corresponding game type.
Modules.
A module is a self-contained behavior script that can be attached to any node (Section
3.1
) and implements functionality reusable across game types.
In addition to the underlying behavior, a module may include self-checking logic that converts previously observed runtime failures into static validation rules executed before the game starts.
Contracts.
A contract is a document that adapts the general AAT workflow to a recurring feature or development pattern.
It specifies the role-specific inputs, outputs, dependencies, and verification criteria required to implement that feature, enabling agents to coordinate through a validated procedure rather than relying only on the generic build-and-review loop.
For example, a map contract defines how the designer specifies map requirements, how the programmer represents the map in project files, how the artist supplies the required assets, and how the auditor and player verify the completed result.

Main Results.
As shown in Table
1
, under the same underlying model, general coding agents perform similarly to one another in the PA2G setting, with gaps of at most 2.50 points, and GPT-5.6-Luna
[
35

does not turn image generation into a visual advantage in the P2G setting.
OpenGame, although designed for game development, does not outperform general coding agents, suggesting that it may not generalize to tasks beyond its built-in templates or adapt well to the demo-recording requirements of GameCraft-Bench.
In contrast, with GPT-5.6-Luna, VibeGame leads in all four categories and improves the overall score over the strongest baseline by 11.70 points, showing that our harness substantially strengthens weaker models.
With the frontier model GPT-6.1-Sol, VibeGame trails Codex (P2G) by less than one point in Core Mechanics and Functional Visuals but leads it by 4.76 and 7.72 points in Content Depth and Art & Presentation, outperforming it by 4.19 points overall.
This suggests that frontier models can already implement core mechanics and reasonable visuals on their own, but still fall short in building games with deep content and polished presentation, which is where VibeGame adds its value.
Across game types (Figure
4
(a)), VibeGame outperforms the strongest baseline of each model on 13 of the 15 types.
User Study.
We further conduct a blind user study with 30 participants of diverse backgrounds, including students from fields such as mathematics and bioinformatics, information technology practitioners, and game enthusiasts. We pair VibeGame with each of the five GPT-6.1-Sol baselines on all 30 tasks, giving 150 pairs, and collect two judgments per pair, 300 in total. In each judgment, a participant reads the game description and the full evaluation rubric of the task, plays the two anonymized games, and picks the better game in each of the four rubric categories and overall. As shown in Figure
4
(b), human preferences broadly agree with the GPT-6.1-Sol judge, whose pairwise results come from comparing the two games’ scores on each task: under both, VibeGame wins against every baseline in every rubric category, with an average overall human win rate of 72.7%.

2
reports the effect of the three coupled components. Removing the AI-native engine or the adversarial review roles of AAT lowers the overall score by 10.33 and 4.63 points, respectively, indicating that both the structured project representation with runtime control and the adversarial review substantially help prompt-to-game development. Adding the engine alone to Codex with GPT-6.1-Sol also raises its overall score by 2.69 points (Appendix

Qualitative Analysis.
We select the qualitative cases from GameCraft-Bench (Figure
5
).
The left case is Sports Skateboard Park, where the agent needs to implement a trick system in which the player chains flip, grind, and grab tricks into combos.
VibeGame presents aerial tricks such as board flips in a consistent and appealing visual style, while Codex (PA2G) draws the character and environment with programmatic shapes (i.e., simple shapes drawn in code), which gives the game a crude art style.
Codex (P2G) generates a coherent background, but its user interface (UI) overlaps the character, which is also assembled from programmatic shapes.
The right case is Sports Boxing Gym, where the task requires the opponent to telegraph each attack with a visible tell so that the player can read it and respond.
VibeGame fulfills this requirement with complete attack animations and mechanics that include wind-up tells.
Codex (PA2G) also draws its boxers with programmatic shapes and represents each punch by stretching a rectangular arm, which looks abstract rather than like a punching animation.
Codex (P2G) also produces polished visuals but does not show the opponent’s wind-up.
5
Conclusion
We present VibeGame, a framework for end-to-end prompt-to-game development that integrates an AI-native game engine, an adversarial agent team, and training-free self-evolution.
Under the same underlying model, VibeGame, without any provided assets, outperforms all evaluated agent harnesses; even with the frontier model GPT-6.1-Sol, it improves over the strongest baseline, Codex (P2G), by 4.19 points.
Limitations
While VibeGame delivers strong results across diverse game genres, we recognize that several directions remain open for future work.
First, we focus on 2D games and have not yet validated the framework in more complex 3D scenes or used it to develop complete commercial games that sustain long-term play.
Second, our AI-native design principles are implemented on a web-based 2D engine; bringing them to established engines such as Godot
[
3
]
, so that agents can also operate existing game projects, is a promising extension.

Experiment Details
8.1
Setup
Every harness, including VibeGame, has a 24-hour budget per task and runs its model at the xhigh reasoning effort. In the P2G setting, harnesses without a native image generation tool are given GPT-Image-2

For w/ Experience, we let VibeGame with GPT-6.1-Sol build and self-evolve on 5 tasks randomly sampled from outside the ablation set, using the task rubrics and the vision-language model (VLM) judge scores in place of user feedback. We then add the evolved artifacts to the initial project of VibeGame with GPT-5.6-Luna and let it build the ablation tasks.

9
Demonstrations
We demonstrate VibeGame in two scenarios: creating a game from a new request (
Game Creation
), which corresponds to the P2G task defined in Section
1
, and continuing to edit an existing project (
Game Edit
).
Unless otherwise noted, the demonstrations use the automatic-by-default setting described in Section
3.2.3
: after the user approves the request, the orchestrator continues development until reviewer acceptance, while the user may still interrupt the process with feedback.
The prompt boxes in the figures report the final user-approved request rather than interface commands or intermediate clarification turns.
Figure 9
:
Game creation demonstrations.
Top: Pixel Sekiro, a pixel-art boss fight created from a text prompt. Bottom: Hollow Knight boss slice, a side-scrolling boss fight created from a gameplay prompt and a concept image.
Figure 10
:
Game edit demonstrations.
Top: intellectual property (IP) transfer, replacing the visual theme while preserving gameplay logic. Middle: genre transfer, converting a turn-based card game into a real-time boss fight while preserving its visual identity. Bottom: rule transfer, swapping the player and boss roles while preserving their abilities and animations.
9.1
Game Creation
Game creation starts from a text request and optional reference images and exercises the full loop from intention alignment to project delivery. In this paper, we report results for both text-only and multimodal requests.
9.1.1
Text Input
To test creation driven by a compact text request, we asked the system to build a Sekiro-style 2D boss fight: a retro pixel-art duel recreating the reed-field battle between Sekiro and Genichiro.
The request specified the combat rules in a few sentences: the player can defend, perform frame-perfect deflections, attack, step-dodge, jump, slash in the air, and execute a deathblow once the boss posture is broken; the boss can defend and deflect, and special attacks are made readable through delayed wind-up frames.
The system started from an existing side-scrolling action skeleton, inheriting its scene structure and UI modules.
However, Sekiro’s core is a deflection-posture system entirely different from the skeleton’s simple hit-point-based combat, requiring the system to build the combat layer from scratch: both sides have independent posture gauges, defense distinguishes regular blocking from frame-perfect deflection, boss attacks are divided into blockable normal attacks and perilous attacks requiring specific responses, and a full posture gauge triggers a multi-stage deathblow animation.
The final output comprised 12 scripts, 2 character asset packs, 11 visual effect entities, and 1 UI asset pack.
This case demonstrates how a short request that names a genre convention is expanded into a complete, correctly tuned combat system.
The first row of Figure
9
shows the request and resulting combat sequence.
9.1.2
Multimodal Input
To test multimodal creation, we provided a text request together with an author-created concept image for a Hollow Knight-style 1v1 boss fight.
The text request specified the mechanical scope: the player has a basic attack, a charged attack, a dash, a jump, and an aerial attack, while the boss combines two melee skills with a ranged attack on a side-scrolling arena 1.5x the camera width.
The concept image anchored the character designs, the ruined-cathedral arena, and the overall visual atmosphere, which the generated assets were required to match.
The second row of Figure
9
showcases the multimodal input and resulting game.
We can observe that the delivered slice realizes both sides of this specification.
The boss gates its melee sweep, ground slam, and arcing projectile on the player’s distance, keeps its preferred range, and can be staggered out of idle; the player’s five actions cover the full movement-attack loop, including dash invincibility frames and aerial slashes; hit feedback combines screen shake, flash, and spark particles, with mask-style health icons and a full-width boss bar completing the heads-up display (HUD).
All character and arena art was generated to match the concept image, preserving its silhouette language and cold palette.
This case demonstrates how text can specify gameplay rules while the concept image anchors visual identity.
9.2
Game Edit
The next cases begin from accepted projects and alter different layers of the existing game.
Specifically, in this paper, we report three types of editing:
(1) intellectual property (IP) transfer that changes visual assets while preserving mechanics;
(2) genre transfer that replaces the central gameplay while preserving visual identity;
and (3) rule transfer that changes the roles of existing characters while reusing their abilities and animations.
9.2.1
IP Transfer
Starting from a completed side-scrolling boss fight project, we ask the system to replace the entire game’s visual theme with a Kung Fu Panda IP.
The system regenerates all art assets (including characters, effects, UI, and background), and then adjusts configurations for the new sprite size and frame counts. The delivered project retains the original combat logic, illustrating an edit concentrated on the asset and configuration layers. See top row of Figure
10
.
This validates the code-asset decoupling in the engine: when the project structure is well designed, IP transfer is accomplished primarily through asset replacement, with no need to rewrite core logic.
9.2.2
Genre Transfer
Starting from a completed turn-based card game project, we ask the system to change the core gameplay from card strategy to a real-time action boss fight.
This is a deep transformation: the turn-based card-playing mechanic was completely replaced with real-time melee, dodging, and shooting, while the system preserved the original project’s cyberpunk visual style and character designs.
Unlike IP transfer where only assets change, genre transfer requires the system to judge what can be preserved and what must be rewritten, demonstrating the system’s ability to perform selective deep modification while maintaining overall consistency (Figure
10
, middle row).
9.2.3
Rule Transfer
Starting from the Hollow Knight-style boss fight created from multimodal input in Section
9.1.2
, we tested the system’s ability to handle unconventional creative requests by asking it to swap the player and boss roles, requiring only that each character keep its existing abilities and animations.
In that source game, the player controlled a small horned warrior, while the antlered boss moved autonomously with a melee slam, a lunge, and a ranged thorn volley.
The edit enlarges the former player character into an AI-driven boss and shrinks the former boss into the player-controlled character, so the player now wields the former boss’s moveset while the former player character fights autonomously with its own dash, charged slash, and aerial attack.
This request is not a simple asset exchange: the system must convert the former boss AI into a player control scheme, turn the former player’s manual controls into autonomous boss AI, rebind inputs, and remap the HUD and win/lose flow, all without adding any new art or moves.
Our system completed this transformation (Figure
10
, bottom row), demonstrating that it can restructure gameplay roles in response to non-standard edit requests.
10
More Demonstrations
Beyond the cases analyzed in Appendix
9
, we used VibeGame to build a broader range of games spanning multiple genres and input modalities. Each game was produced from a natural language prompt, some accompanied by a reference image, exercising the same pipeline described in the main text. Together they illustrate the breadth of game types the system handles, from real-time action and arcade games to turn-based strategy and an LLM-driven social-deduction game.
Fruit Ninja
A fruit-slicing arcade game built from a text-only request (Figure
11
). Each fruit splits into two physically simulated halves with fruit-specific weight, bounce, and juice effects; the game includes pointer-driven slicing, combo scoring, missed-fruit indicators, and a game-over state.
Figure 11
:
A three-fruit combo sliced mid-air with split halves and juice effects.
The King of Fighters
An arcade fighting game generated from a single-sentence prompt requesting a King of Fighters remake, with no reference image (Figure
12
). Two fighters trade combos under health bars, a round timer, and a neon-lit stage.
Figure 12

Two fighters trade blows with an impact spark on the neon stage.
Dungeon Roguelike
A Soul Knight-style dungeon-shooter roguelike (Figure
13
). The map is built from rooms and corridors; entering a room seals the doors and starts combat. The player picks up weapons from chests, carries up to two at a time, and aims toward the mouse, with health, shield, and mana as stats.
Figure 13
:
The player fires a spread of projectiles at an enemy inside a sealed combat room.
Parkour Platformer
A cartoon parkour platformer (Figure
14
). The protagonist runs and dashes across a field of floating balloons; stepping on a balloon pops it and launches her upward, and the level is cleared by chaining precise balloon landings.
Figure 14
:
The protagonist floats above a balloon, with the goal flag on its platform.
Civilization prototype
A simplified Civilization-style 4X strategy game on a hex map, rendered in a cartoon hand-drawn style with city management and unit combat (Figure
15
). It runs on a separated frontend and backend with multiplayer support.
Figure 15

A selected warrior unit and its stats beside a city on the hex map.
AI Werewolf
A single-player Werewolf game driven by the engine’s built-in LLM module (Figure
16
). Eleven AI players fill a 12-role setup (villagers, werewolves, seer, hunter, witch, idiot), conducting sheriff elections, day discussions, and night actions; each AI’s speech is rendered as on-screen text.
Figure 16
:
The round-table layout with AI player portraits and live speech text during the sheriff election.
Hollow Knight to Demon Slayer
An IP transfer applied to the Hollow Knight-style boss-fight prototype from Appendix
9.1.2
: the system restyled the entire game into a Demon Slayer theme, recreating the Mugen Train battle between Tanjiro and Upper Rank Three while keeping the underlying combat logic unchanged (Figure
17
).
Figure 17

Tanjiro faces Upper Rank Three under the moon on the Mugen Train night field.

The PRD asks the player to tap “when the timing indicator is inside its acceptance band” (beats at 1, 2, 4, and 5 s,

To isolate the effect of the AI-native engine, we equip the native Codex harness with the engine of VibeGame.
Both settings use GPT-6.1-Sol on all 30 tasks in the PA2G setting with the same asset library.
With the engine, the overall score of Codex rises from 64.44 to 67.13, with gains in all four categories (Table

Limitation of Self-Evolution
We observe that when VibeGame continuously develops games of different types, the experience accumulated by self-evolution can instead lower agent performance.
Future work should analyze this phenomenon further and separate general experience from genre-specific experience, so that each can be injected adaptively.
This observation is also one of the motivations for our experimental design: the main experiments use VibeGame without any accumulated experience, and we evaluate self-evolution separately in the ablation study.

article.headline: VibeGame：从提示词生成可玩2D游戏
article.lede: 南京大学等提出VibeGame，用AI原生2D引擎和对抗智能体团队，把提示词变成可运行、可编辑的游戏项目。
article.problem: 游戏开发需要同时协调代码、场景、素材、动画、物理和配置，还要通过实际试玩验证整体行为。现有LLM智能体多把运行检查留到最终评估，或只验证游戏能否构建和启动，难以发现只有在游玩中才暴露的问题。
article.method: VibeGame把项目状态表示为带模式校验的结构化文本，并提供逐帧同步的运行时控制，让智能体暂停、步进、注入动作和截图检查。其八角色对抗智能体团队把实现与审计、试玩、评审分离，并在项目通过后以免训练自进化提炼骨架、模块和协作契约。
article.results: 在GameCraft-Bench子集30个任务上，以GPT-6.1-Sol为评审时，VibeGame（P2G）总体得分72.99，高于最强基线Codex（P2G）的68.80，提升4.19分；用GPT-5.6-Luna时总体49.99，比最强基线38.29高11.70分。消融显示去掉AI原生引擎总体从53.45降至43.12，去掉对抗评审角色降至48.82；加入GPT-6.1-Sol进化经验后GPT-5.6-Luna升至56.37（+2.92）。30人盲测共300次判断，总体人类胜率平均72.7%，15类游戏中13类超过各自模型最强基线。
article.why_it_matters: 它把“可运行、可检查、可迭代”的游戏项目作为智能体输出，并用运行时试玩补足静态代码检查看不到的问题，为游戏生成基准提供可复现的工程路径。
article.limitations: 仅在2D游戏上验证，未覆盖复杂3D场景或可长期游玩的完整商业游戏；作者也观察到连续开发不同类型游戏时，自进化积累的经验反而可能拉低智能体表现。此外，评审模型从GPT-5.5换为GPT-6.1-Sol会改变绝对分数和排名，且因引擎改为Phaser，结果不能与原始GameCraft-Bench直接比较。
article.figure_caption_zh: VibeGame从文本或多模态提示生成并编辑多种2D游戏类型的示例。

email_papers.title: AskStream: When and What to Ask Proactively under Uncertainty in Streaming Video Understanding
email_papers.abstract: Recent advances in multimodal large language models have increased interest in interaction paradigms for video understanding. The evolution from offline to streaming and proactive interaction has gradually shifted models from passive responders toward more proactive agents that can decide when to answer. However, existing proactive paradigms typically assume that the information required to answer a query is complete, leaving models to only wait or answer. In the real world, however, information is often incomplete due to uncertainty from either the video or the user. In proactive paradigms, such uncertainty can cause the model to wait forever or generate highly hallucinatory responses. We therefore argue that proactive interaction should be redefined with a third action: ask, allowing models to actively ask for missing information. To study when and what models should ask before answering, we introduce AskStream, the first multi-turn benchmark spanning video and user uncertainty for streaming video understanding, with four task categories and eight subtasks. It contains 438 videos with 2,714 manually annotated frame-level time windows across three types: wait, ask, and answer. Across both multiple-choice and open-ended settings, even the strongest model attains only 52.18% on our proposed Ask-F1 metric, highlighting substantial limitations in proactive information seeking under uncertainty.

Recent advances in multimodal large language models have increased interest in interaction paradigms for video understanding. The evolution from offline to streaming and proactive interaction has gradually shifted models from passive responders toward more proactive agents that can decide when to answer. Introduction
Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have made significant progress in video understanding and reasoning in recent years
(
Kimi Team, 2026
;
Qwen Team, 2026
;
Google DeepMind, 2026
;
OpenAI, 2026
)
. Beyond advancements in model architecture and training paradigms, research on
interaction paradigms
is equally important for advancing models toward more adaptive and generalizable intelligence in real-world environments. As shown at the top of Figure
1
, traditional video interaction primarily follows an
offline paradigm
, where the model observes the complete video before answering user queries.
In the real world, videos often arrive continuously as streams. This has driven the emergence of a
streaming paradigm
, where
models must continuously understand the incoming stream, maintain memory, and interact with users in real time.
Under both paradigms, the core task remains to determine
how to answer
. However, because the streaming paradigm primarily targets real-time responses, it is less suited to scenarios requiring delayed responses, such as anomaly alerts, procedural guidance, and continuous task monitoring. This motivates the
proactive paradigm
, where models continuously monitor the video and decide not only
how to answer
but also
when to answer
. Existing benchmarks
(
Lin et al., 2026b
;
Wang et al., 2025c
;
Azad et al., 2026
;
Li et al., 2026
)
progressively extend this paradigm by requiring models to wait for sufficient evidence, supporting multi-turn responses, modeling answer readiness, and adapting response timing under dynamic tasks, with a common focus on increasingly fine-grained response timing.
However,
the paradigm implicitly assumes that the information for answering is fully contained in the stream and will eventually become available, leaving the model only to
wait
or
answer
.
This assumption overlooks a key challenge:
information in the real world is often incomplete

article.headline: 视频理解模型不会主动提问，流式模型近乎失效
article.lede: 新基准 AskStream 把「提问」纳入动作空间：最强离线模型 Ask-F1 为 52.18%，流式模型仅 7.22%
article.problem: 现有的主动式视频交互范式默认「回答问题所需的信息一定会在流中出现」，因此模型的动作空间只有等待和回答两种。但现实中的不确定性既可能来自视频（画面模糊、证据缺失），也可能来自用户（指代不清），这会让模型无限等待或强行编造答案。作者因此主张把「提问」作为第三个动作引入，研究模型应当在何时、就什么内容发问。
article.method: 论文提出 AskStream 评测框架，把交互动作空间从「等待/回答」扩展为「等待/回答/提问」，并区分来自视频和来自用户的两类不确定性。评测分为离线与流式两种设定，覆盖多选与开放式两种回答形式，指标为 Ask-F1 以及分别衡量提问与回答的子分数 S_ask、S_ans；此外还用逐步加入 oracle 信息的消融实验，定位模型在何时提问、问什么、何时回答这三个阶段中哪一环出错。
article.results: 多选设定下，离线模型中 Gemini-3.8 Flash 表现相对最好，在 KVEM、WUQ、UPC 三个子任务上分别为 37.17%、43.10%、81.36%，总体 Ask-F1 为 52.18%，但其 S_ask 明显低于 S_ans，说明提问是瓶颈；流式主动模型在多数子任务上得零分，表现较好的 AURA 也只有 7.22% Ask-F1。开放式设定整体明显下降，Gemini-3.8 Flash 的 Ask-F1 为 29.19%（S_ask 23.34%、S_ans 38.97%），AURA 仅 4.01%。在不确定性分析中，Qwen3.5 9B 在 78 个视频的 130 个五选一事件上，输入模糊时准确率为 42.3%，在问出关键证据后升至 62.3%，接近完全清晰输入的 63.1%。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「主动提问」从概念口号变成可量化评测的能力维度，并用数据说明当前模型在信息缺失时基本不会求助，这对构建需要长时间监控、异常告警等真实场景的视频智能体是明确的短板信号。
article.limitations: 这是一篇以基准和评测为主的工作，论文没有提出能提升提问能力的新方法，因此只诊断问题、不解决问题。不确定性分析只在 Qwen3.5 9B 上、基于 78 个视频的 130 个事件完成，规模有限；开放式评测使用 Gemini-3.8 Flash 作裁判，作者仅用 300 轮人工标注做一致性校验，绝对分数的可靠性仍需谨慎看待。
article.figure_caption_zh: 交互范式的演进：AskStream 在原有的「等待」与「回答」之外加入「提问」动作，使模型在作答前能主动向视频或用户索取缺失信息。

figure.caption: Evolution of interaction paradigms. AskStream extends the conventional action space of {wait} and {answer} by introducing {ask}, enabling models to proactively seek missing information from the video or user before answering.

page_papers.title: A Broader Look into MLLM's Retrieval Heads
page_papers.abstract: Locating relevant evidence in long inputs is a core capability of Multimodal Large Language Models. Prior studies attribute this capability to retrieval heads, a sparse set of attention heads that transfer information from the context to the output. However, these analyses are confined to a limited set of modalities and the corresponding models. Moreover, how retrieval heads can be leveraged to enhance the model calls for further exploration. In this paper, we ask whether this mechanism expands together with the input modalities of the model. Taking audio-visual input as a newly added modality, we construct paired inputs in which the same answer is either spoken or shown on screen. With the evidence content fixed, retrieval heads remain sparse in the new modality and are shared to a large extent across modalities. Across 18 language, vision-language, and omni-modal checkpoints, omni-modal models largely preserve the retrieval heads of their backbones. Ablating these heads eliminates nearly all audio-visual retrieval. The heads shared across modalities make up fewer than 2\% of all heads, yet ablating them also degrades document understanding, spatial perception, and visual mathematics. Building on these findings, we turn retrieval heads into a target of optimization by training their attention with a ranking objective. This raises the page Recall@1 of Qwen3-VL-8B on MMDocIR by 6.03 points and improves document retrieval across three model families. Functional attention heads can thus serve both as a lens on multimodal models and as a target for improving them.

Abstract
Locating relevant evidence in long inputs is a core capability of Multimodal Large Language Models. Prior studies attribute this capability to retrieval heads, a sparse set of attention heads that transfer information from the context to the output. However, these analyses are confined to a limited set of modalities and the corresponding models. Moreover, how retrieval heads can be leveraged to enhance the model calls for further exploration. In this paper, we ask whether this mechanism expands together with the input modalities of the model. Taking audio-visual input as a newly added modality, we construct paired inputs in which the same answer is either spoken or shown on screen. With the evidence content fixed, retrieval heads remain sparse in the new modality and are shared to a large extent across modalities. Across 18 language, vision-language, and omni-modal checkpoints, omni-modal models largely preserve the retrieval heads of their backbones. Ablating these heads eliminates nearly all audio-visual retrieval. The heads shared across modalities make up fewer than 2% of all heads, yet ablating them also degrades document understanding, spatial perception, and visual mathematics. Building on these findings, we turn retrieval heads into a target of optimization by training their attention with a ranking objective. This raises the page Recall@1 of Qwen3-VL-8B on MMDocIR by 6.03 points and improves document retrieval across three model families. Functional attention heads can thus serve both as a lens on multimodal models and as a target for improving them.

1
Introduction
Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) increasingly process long, information-rich inputs spanning a growing range of modalities
[
17
,
32
]
. Within these inputs, the evidence needed to answer a question may occupy only a small part of the context, surrounded by unrelated content. Locating this evidence is therefore central to multimodal understanding. As the range of supported modalities expands, understanding the mechanisms that enable this capability becomes increasingly important.
Research on language models provides a starting point: a small set of attention heads, termed
retrieval heads
, transfers relevant information from the context to the output
[
25
]
. These heads occur across model families, and ablating them sharply reduces long-context retrieval accuracy. Subsequent work develops methods for analyzing retrieval heads
[
31
]
and extends this analysis to vision-language models, where visual retrieval similarly relies on a sparse set of heads
[
13
,
18
]
.
These findings raise two questions. First, does the same retrieval mechanism extend to new modalities as models expand beyond text and images? This involves examining whether retrieval heads are shared across modalities and retained during adaptation. Beyond explaining model behavior, understanding this mechanism may also guide model improvement. Prior work has focused primarily on analysis, while how to translate these insights into stronger multimodal capabilities remains less explored. We therefore ask a second question: can this mechanism serve as a basis for improving multimodal models?
To address these questions, we first study audio-visual input in omni-modal models. This setting allows the same information to be spoken or displayed, while related language and vision-language backbones allow comparisons across stages of modality adaptation. We construct paired inputs that place the same answer in a long video as either speech or on-screen text, holding the background, question, and answer fixed (
a,b). Together with text and image-text retrieval tasks, this design supports a unified question-to-evidence analysis across 18 checkpoints. Targeted head ablations then test the functional role of the detected heads. We obtain four findings:
•
Sparsity (
Sec.
4.1
).
Retrieval scores concentrate in a small set of heads for both spoken and displayed evidence.
•
Cross-modal sharing (
Sec.
4.2
).
Models largely reuse the same retrieval heads when the same information is presented in different modalities.
•
Preservation (
Sec.
4.3
).
Omni-modal models largely retain the retrieval heads of their language or vision-language backbones, and the retained heads remain necessary for retrieval.
•
Causal role (
Sec.
4.4
).
Ablating retrieval heads severely disrupts audio-visual retrieval. Ablating the subset shared across modalities, fewer than 2% of all heads, also substantially impairs performance on broader multimodal reasoning tasks.
Together, these findings identify retrieval heads as a compact, shared mechanism for evidence use, motivating direct optimization of their attention. We therefore turn to multimodal document retrieval (
Sec.
5
), where evidence localization provides a natural ranking signal. We select retrieval heads on document-related tasks and use their question-to-page attention to score candidate pages. A ranking objective trains these scores to favor relevant pages over distractors. On MMDocIR
[
7
]
, this improves Qwen3-VL-8B’s page Recall@1 by 6.03 points over the untrained scorer and also improves layout retrieval without layout supervision, with gains across three model families.
Our contributions are threefold:
•
A paired analysis of retrieval heads across evidence modalities and related model checkpoints, characterizing their sparsity, cross-modal sharing, and preservation as input modalities expand.
•
Causal evidence that retrieval heads support audio-visual retrieval and that a small subset shared across modalities also supports broader multimodal reasoning.
•
A ranking method that directly optimizes retrieval-head attention and improves multimodal document retrieval across model families.
2
Related work
Functional attention heads.
Early studies identified retrieval heads as a sparse, causally important component of evidence retrieval in long-context language models, using answer-copying behavior to characterize their function
[
25
]
. Query-focused scoring extends this analysis to attention between a query and relevant context, allowing retrieval heads to be identified on realistic question-answering tasks
[
31
]
. Further analyses reveal the dynamic nature of retrieval heads in evidence retrieval
[
15
]
. In vision-language models, functional specialization has been observed in text recognition, spatial grounding, and visual evidence retrieval, with causal interventions linking selected heads to evidence localization and downstream reasoning
[
1
,
10
,
18
,
21
]
.
Functional head utilization.
Despite growing mechanistic understanding, exploiting retrieval heads to improve model capabilities remains relatively underexplored. Existing efforts have focused largely on language models, ranging from attention-based retrieval and efficient inference to interventions that improve evidence use
[
31
,
26
,
12
,
16
,
14
]
. As mechanistic analysis extends to multimodal models, emerging applications suggest similar potential, but the broader use of these mechanisms to improve multimodal capabilities remains less explored
[
13
,
19
]
. Building on this perspective, we extend the analysis of retrieval mechanisms and explore their potential to improve multimodal evidence use.

Causal contribution of retrieval heads
Finding 4.
Retrieval heads are necessary for audio-visual retrieval, and the heads shared by audio and visual evidence also contribute to broader multimodal tasks.

The effect does not depend on the particular choice of the top-5% cutoff (

Main result.
Table
3

Ranking training then improves page retrieval by 6.03 Micro R@1 points, and the improvement holds in every one of the ten document domains. Layout retrieval also improves, although the training data contain no layout supervision. The trained model even scores above the published retrievers in

We next apply the same training to the other two model families. The results in

Finally, we vary the number of selected heads and compare retrieval heads with equally many random heads (

Random heads also benefit from training but remain far below retrieval heads, both before and after training. These results show that functional head selection remains important after ranking training.
6
Conclusion
In this paper, we investigated two connected questions: whether evidence-localization mechanisms extend as input modalities expand, and whether understanding these mechanisms can guide model improvement. Using paired audio-visual inputs and a unified analysis criterion across 18 checkpoints, we find that omni-modal models locate spoken and displayed evidence through sparse retrieval heads that are largely shared when evidence content is matched and retained from their backbones. These heads are necessary for audio-visual retrieval, and the small subset shared across modalities also contributes to broader multimodal tasks. This functional role motivates the design of treating retrieval-head attention as a target for optimization. Training selected-head attention with a ranking objective improves multimodal document retrieval across three model families, demonstrating how the mechanism identified through analysis can inform a practical method. Together, these results connect the understanding of multimodal evidence use with its improvement in a broader setting, positioning functional attention heads as both an interpretability lens and an optimization target.

article.headline: 多模态模型检索头：跨模态共享，也能被训练
article.lede: 研究者在18个模型检查点上追踪检索头，发现视听证据共用同一批头，并把检索头注意力当作优化目标提升了文档检索。
article.problem: 已有工作把长上下文中的证据定位归因于一小撮「检索头」，但这类分析基本局限于文本和图像，尚不清楚模型扩展到语音等新模态后该机制是否延续。另一方面，多数研究止步于解释现象，如何利用检索头反过来提升模型能力仍缺少系统验证。
article.method: 作者构造配对输入：把同一个六位数字以语音朗读或屏幕字幕的方式插入同一段长视频，其余背景、问题、答案与插入深度全部固定，从而只改变证据模态。他们在统一的查询—证据注意力打分下比较各层各头的排序一致性，并用定向消融（对照为同层同数量的随机头）检验必要性。随后把选定检索头的问题—页面注意力当作排序分数，用带难负例的排序损失只训练这些头上的 LoRA 适配器。
article.results: 跨模态共享明显：8个全模态模型中，69%到83%的音频与视觉top-5%检索头重合，全体头打分的Spearman相关系数在0.88到0.92之间；SALMONN系列与其视觉语言骨干的相关系数不低于0.97。消融top-5%检索头后，Qwen2.5-Omni-7B的音频精确匹配从98.3%跌到0，而匹配的随机消融仍保留96.9%。跨模态共享头不足全部头的2%，消融它们仍在8项下游任务中的4项上显著掉分（图像检索头最多1项）。在MMDocIR上，用排序目标训练后Qwen3-VL-8B的页面Micro Recall@1提升6.03点（Macro提升5.05点），布局检索在无布局监督下提升1.46点；Qwen2.5-VL-7B和Gemma3-12B的页面Micro Recall@1分别提升5.69和2.17点。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「检索头」从一个可解释性观察对象变成了可直接优化的训练目标，并说明这种优化在三个模型家族上都有效。对视听长输入和长文档检索这类证据稀疏的场景，这是一个改动量很小的介入手段。
article.limitations: 证据只覆盖文本、图像与视听三种模态，结论能否推广到更多模态尚不清楚；检索头本身依赖top-5%阈值和检测数据的选择，作者也给出了相应的敏感性分析。此外，与已发表检索器的对比因评测设置不同不可直接比较，作者自己只把同设置下相对未训练检索头的增益作为受控结论。
article.figure_caption_zh: 检索头得分图显示，无论证据以语音还是屏幕文字呈现，高分注意力头都集中在少数层和少数头上，音频与视觉条件选出的头高度重叠。

page_papers.title: WorkFactory: Turning Professional Intents into Executable Work for Scalable Agent Training
page_papers.abstract: Scaling supervised training for working agents requires diverse professional tasks that yield reliable expert demonstrations. However, missing or inconsistent task information can obstruct teacher execution and weaken the resulting supervision. We propose WorkFactory, a scalable framework for constructing coherent and executable professional tasks. Starting from professional intents, information-level planning builds an information support graph to guide task instantiation, explicitly representing the dependencies and locations of information required for the intended outputs. Probe executions then identify support failures and guide repairs while preserving the intended work. We construct 112,686 tasks spanning 612 occupations and use the collected teacher trajectories to fine-tune Qwen models at 4B, 27B, and 35B-A3B scales, yielding the WorkPilot family. All three models improve over their respective base models across four professional-work benchmarks, with WorkPilot-35B-A3B improving from 879 to 1565 Elo on GDPval-AA v2.1. Scaling analyses reveal model-dependent diminishing returns, with execution length first increasing and then decreasing. Controlled component analyses show that planning and repair reduce probe-diagnosed task environment defects and improve downstream performance. The data and models are available at https://github.com/IQuestLab/WorkFactory.
