Abstract
Scaling supervised training for working agents requires diverse professional tasks that yield reliable expert demonstrations.
However, missing or inconsistent task information can obstruct teacher execution and weaken the resulting supervision.
We propose WorkFactory, a scalable framework for constructing coherent and executable professional tasks.
Starting from professional intents, information-level planning builds an information support graph to guide task instantiation, explicitly representing the dependencies and locations of information required for the intended outputs.
Probe executions then identify support failures and guide repairs while preserving the intended work.
We construct 112,686 tasks spanning 612 occupations and use the collected teacher trajectories to fine-tune Qwen models at 4B, 27B, and 35B-A3B scales, yielding the WorkPilot family.
All three models improve over their respective base models across four professional-work benchmarks, with WorkPilot-35B-A3B improving from 879 to 1565 Elo on GDPval-AA v2.1.
Scaling analyses reveal model-dependent diminishing returns, with execution length first increasing and then decreasing.
Controlled component analyses show that planning and repair reduce probe-diagnosed task environment defects and improve downstream performance.
The data and models are available at
https://github.com/IQuestLab/WorkFactory
.
Figure 1
:
WorkPilot-35B-A3B consistently outperforms its Qwen3.6-35B-A3B base model across four professional-work benchmarks, with representative models shown for context.
1
Introduction
Language agents interleave reasoning and actions to interact with external environments
[
36
]
.
Working agents extend this paradigm to professional work in digital environments, executing workflows, coordinating tools, and producing deliverables across diverse occupations
[
23
,
17
]
.
This shift creates opportunities for agents to improve productivity and generate real economic value
[
18
]
.
A common approach to agent post-training is supervised fine-tuning on expert demonstrations of task execution
[
30
,
10
]
.
Scaling this approach to working agents requires diverse executable professional tasks spanning a wide range of occupational competencies.
Recent frameworks automate professional task construction by retrieving, reusing, adapting, or synthesizing task-relevant materials
[
12
]
, and then collect teacher trajectories for supervision
[
40
]
.
The value of scaling task construction, however, depends on whether the resulting teacher trajectories reliably demonstrate the target occupational competencies.
To produce effective demonstrations, a teacher agent needs access to
sufficient and consistent information
for carrying out the intended work.
Establishing this support is challenging because the information required for an intended output may be distributed across multiple artifacts and connected through intermediate calculations and judgments.
For example, a supplier-selection task may provide demand forecasts and vendor quotations in separate files but omit whether one vendor’s price includes freight.
Without this pricing condition, lifecycle costs cannot be computed and compared consistently; yet providing the computed costs directly would remove a substantive part of the work the teacher is expected to perform.
Constructing such an environment therefore requires a careful boundary: all necessary premises must be available, while intermediate and final results must remain for the teacher to derive.
Otherwise, the teacher may introduce unsupported assumptions or leave essential work incomplete, weakening the resulting trajectory as training supervision.
In this paper, we introduce WorkFactory, a scalable framework for constructing executable tasks that support reliable demonstrations of professional work.
We derive diverse professional intents by combining occupational knowledge, skill documentation, and professional artifacts, broadening the range of work that can be instantiated.
For each intent, WorkFactory plans backward from the intended output using an information support graph.
Rather than connecting artifacts alone, the graph captures what each output depends on and where the supporting information should be available across reused and synthesized materials, while leaving derived results to the solver.
To catch violations introduced during materialization, an isolated probe attempts the task from solver-visible inputs; its diagnoses drive repairs that must restore support without changing the intended work.
Only environments that pass this process are then assigned to an independent teacher, whose execution provides the training trajectory.
Using WorkFactory, we construct 112,686 tasks spanning 612 occupations and collect teacher trajectories for supervised fine-tuning.
Training Qwen3.5-4B
[
24
]
, Qwen3.6-27B
[
25
]
, and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B
[
26
]
on these trajectories yields the
WorkPilot
family.
All three WorkPilot models substantially improve over their respective base models across four professional-work benchmarks, including GDPval-AA
[
23
,
4
]
and JobBench
[
17
]
, demonstrating the training utility of WorkFactory data across the tested model scales.
Figure
1
illustrates the gains of WorkPilot-35B-A3B as a representative example.
Notably, WorkPilot-27B reaches a locally estimated 1612 Elo on GDPval-AA v2.1, placing it within the range of the compared frontier models.
Beyond aggregate performance, we study how working-agent performance and execution behavior evolve with training-data scale, observing model-dependent diminishing returns, an initial increase followed by a decrease in execution length, and changes in tool-use reliability.
Controlled component analyses show complementary benefits of information-level planning and execution-based repair in reducing probe-diagnosed environment defects and improving downstream performance, supporting the value of coherent task environments for effective expert supervision.
Our main contributions are as follows:
•
We propose WorkFactory, a framework that works backward from intended outputs to organize dependencies across reused and synthesized materials in an information support graph, then uses execution-based repair to preserve task executability after materialization.
•
We conduct a systematic empirical study of working-agent data scaling up to 110K tasks, characterizing diminishing performance returns across model scales and changes in execution length and tool-use reliability.
•
We train the WorkPilot family at 4B, 27B, and 35B-A3B scales, with WorkPilot-27B achieving frontier-level performance on GDPval-AA. We publicly release a subset of the task data and the model weights to support further research.
2
Related Work
Agent Task and Environment Synthesis.
Synthetic task and environment construction has become an important approach to scaling agent training.
Software engineering provides a favorable setting, where repositories offer realistic contexts and executable tests provide concrete supervision;
representative systems include SWE-Gym
[
22
]
, SWE-smith
[
35
]
, and R2E-Gym
[
14
]
.
Beyond coding, recent work synthesizes longer-horizon, multi-tool tasks through compositional expansion
[
34
,
29
]
, environment exploration and execution feedback
[
28
,
7
]
, and stateful interaction environments
[
11
]
.
These advances motivate synthesis for working agents, whose tasks require coherent workspaces that integrate heterogeneous information and domain-specific deliverables.
Professional Task Construction for Working Agents.
NexForge
[
40
]
translates capability requirements into task directives and instantiates them through workspace blueprints, while Synthetic Computers
[
12
]
plans dependencies among artifacts to guide workspace synthesis.
In concurrent work, GraphForge
[
31
]
constructs evidence graphs over real files to derive task statements and evidence-anchored rubrics, then revises these specifications using execution feedback.
WorkGenesis
[
42
]
synthesizes companion materials around retrieved files and uses rubric-based failure attribution to guide revisions to the request, synthesized materials, and rubric.
Whereas GraphForge compiles tasks and rubrics from an evidence graph over an assembled real-file workspace, WorkFactory works backward from intended outputs, using its graph to coordinate information dependencies and locations across reused and synthesized materials while leaving derived results to the solver.
Unlike WorkGenesis’s rubric-based audit, WorkFactory directly probes the solver-visible environment and constrains repair to preserve the intended work.
3
WorkFactory
3.1
Overview
WorkFactory constructs executable professional tasks for training working agents.
It first builds a diverse intent library from occupational knowledge, skill documentation, and professional artifacts, allowing task construction to cover both established workflows and realistic deliverables (§
3.2
).
For each intent, WorkFactory plans backward from the intended output using an information support graph, which coordinates dependencies and information locations across reused and synthesized materials while reserving derived results for the solver (§
3.3
).
Because these dependencies may be lost or contradicted when the environment is materialized, execution-based repair probes the task from solver-visible inputs and repairs blocking support failures without changing the intended work (§
3.4
).
Tasks that pass this process are assigned to an independent teacher for trajectory collection (§
3.5
).
Figure
2
illustrates the process through a supplier-selection example.
Figure 2

Appendix
C.4

3.2
Multi-source Professional Intent Synthesis
Professional intents specify meaningful work before its instance-specific materials are fixed.
To cover varied occupational competencies, WorkFactory draws on three different sources: (1)
occupational hierarchies
, which ground the work in roles and situations; (2)
documented skills
, which identify operations that can be composed into workflows; and (3)
real professional deliverables
, which provide cues about intended outputs and audiences.
The three synthesis routes reflect these roles: we expand occupations into roles situated in professional contexts, compose skills when one operation supplies inputs for another, and infer plausible objectives from deliverables through instruction backtranslation
[
16
]
.
An LLM-based review evaluates candidate intents from all three routes for internal coherence and feasibility, professional appropriateness, and plausibility as real workplace activities before adding them to the shared intent library
ℒ
\mathcal{L}
.
This offline library supplies intents for environment construction; Appendix
A

Each requested output must be supported by a complete chain of solver-visible premises, while the calculations and judgments that constitute the intended work must remain for the solver to perform.
This boundary is difficult to preserve when supporting information is distributed across the user request, reused artifacts, and synthesized files.

3.4
Execution-based Environment Repair
Execution-based repair tests the realized environment for missing or inconsistent support that remains after construction.
The loop consists of probe diagnosis, revision, and revalidation.
Diagnosing the realized environment.
A probe solver attempts the task using only the solver-visible request and resources, without access to the graph, construction plan, or prior execution outputs and diagnoses.
It grounds reported environmental issues in inspected sources and tool observations, identifies the affected operations and deliverables, and distinguishes them from solver mistakes and legitimate open choices.
Only issues judged to block task completion trigger repair; tasks without such blockers proceed to trajectory collection.
Appendix
C.1
details the reporting criteria.
Repairing and revalidating the environment.
A refiner uses the diagnoses to edit the request and existing reference files while preserving the files’ number, types, and dependency structure; the information support graph remains the initial construction specification.
For example, adding a missing USD 0.15-per-carton freight term for Supplier C restores the support needed for an NPV comparison without performing the comparison for the solver.
Each revision must pass construction checks and an LLM-based work-preservation review against the original intent and initial plan, assessing whether the core objective, essential operations, and substantive deliverable requirements remain intact.
Revised tasks that fail either check are discarded; those that pass undergo a fresh probe execution.
The loop stops when no blocker remains or the repair budget is exhausted, with unresolved tasks discarded.
Retained tasks form the candidate pool

4.3
Scaling Properties
We study how model performance and execution behavior scale with the number of distinct WorkFactory training tasks on GDPval under the GDPval-AA evaluation protocol.
Our primary sweep trains Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on nested subsets of 2K–110K tasks; we additionally evaluate Qwen3.6-27B and Qwen3.5-4B at 30K and 110K.

Performance improves with model-dependent diminishing returns.
Figure
5
(a) shows that GDPval-AA Elo increases with additional training data across all three models.
For Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Elo rises from 879 to 1565: the first 5K tasks contribute 447 points, whereas scaling from 75K to 110K adds only 13.
By 30K tasks, the 35B-A3B and 27B models have captured 88% and 94% of their respective gains from the base model to the 110K-task checkpoint, showing different patterns of diminishing returns across the sampled model scales.
The 4B model also gains 546 Elo by 30K tasks, showing strong early data efficiency at the smallest tested scale.
A two-checkpoint comparison on JobBench shows the same direction: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B improves from 58.80 at 50K tasks to 62.35 at 110K.
Execution length first expands and then contracts.
As shown in Figure
5
(b), the mean execution length of Qwen3.6-35B-A3B first rises from 24.87 turns at baseline to 162.88 at 2K tasks, then falls to 85.90 at 110K while Elo continues to improve.
The fraction of its GDPval-AA trajectories reaching the 250-turn limit also falls from 21.9% at 2K to 2.7% at 110K.
Across the sampled checkpoints, the 27B and 4B models also show an increase from their bases to 30K tasks followed by a decrease at 110K; the 4B model uses longer trajectories than the other two models at both data scales.
Figure
5
(c) further shows that, for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, code-execution failures decline from 16.0% at baseline to 6.3% at 110K.
After rising to 22.4% at 2K, web-search failures decrease to 10.4% at 110K, whereas web-fetch failures remain at approximately 40%–48%.
Together, these observations show that performance and execution length evolve differently as training data increases: longer attempts emerge at small data scales, followed by shorter executions and lower failure rates for some tool types at larger scales.
4.4
Component Analysis
We compare three 5K-task synthesis conditions: direct artifact-level planning, information-level planning, and information-level planning followed by execution-based repair.
The analysis asks whether explicitly planning and repairing task information improves both the conditions for teacher execution and the training utility of the resulting trajectories.
We assess task-environment quality using blocker- and correctness-level findings from a common probe solver (see §
3.4
) and downstream utility by fine-tuning the same Qwen3.6-35B-A3B base model under the shared training configuration.
For each defect category, incidence is the fraction of tasks whose report contains at least one hard defect in that category; categories may overlap.
We use the initial probe report for the first two conditions and the final report for the repair condition, including tasks later discarded for unresolved blockers.

Task-environment quality.
Replacing direct artifact-level planning with information-level planning reduces probe-diagnosed hard-defect incidence in six of the eight categories.
The largest reduction is in broken derivations, from 24.86% to 6.86%, while underspecified requests fall from 7.22% to 0.62%.
These changes are consistent with the graph’s role in making required information and its locations explicit.
However, the incidence of
leakage or shortcuts
and
self-inconsistency
increases by 1.44 and 1.18 percentage points, respectively.
We hypothesize that the former may arise when explicit dependencies lead the materializer to expose solver-derived information in the request, and the latter when denser constraints make it harder to maintain consistency across synthesized statements and values.
These regressions show that making information requirements explicit does not by itself ensure that materialization preserves them.
Adding execution-based repair reduces the reported incidence in all eight categories relative to information-level planning alone.
In particular, cross-file inconsistency falls from 25.74% to 4.84%, execution-feasibility defects from 6.64% to 0.48%, and leakage or shortcuts from 3.36% to 0.84%.
Taken together, these reductions show that execution-based repair complements information-level planning by addressing defects that remain in the materialized environments.

Downstream utility.
We train the same model separately on teacher trajectories from each synthesis condition.
Information-level planning raises GDPval-AA Elo from 1245 to 1293, while adding execution-based repair further raises it to 1326.
The cumulative 81-point gain over direct artifact-level planning accompanies reductions in probe-diagnosed defects, linking improvements in task construction to the downstream utility of the collected teacher trajectories.

4.6
Cost–Performance Trade-off
We estimate model-inference cost per GDPval-AA task from recorded input and output tokens using a common accounting formula and explicit mappings to provider prices.
The estimates use a shared cache-hit assumption and explicit price proxies where needed, and cover task-solving model inference only.
Under this standardized accounting, all three WorkPilot models lie on the non-dominated frontier among the models shown in Figure
6
; the estimated costs of WorkPilot-4B, WorkPilot-35B-A3B, and WorkPilot-27B are approximately $0.012, $0.031, and $0.396 per task, respectively.

5
Conclusion
We introduced WorkFactory, a framework for constructing executable professional tasks to support teacher demonstrations of occupational competencies.
Information-level planning specifies the dependencies and locations of required information, while execution-based repair addresses support failures exposed during task execution.
Using teacher trajectories from 112,686 tasks, we trained the WorkPilot family, whose three models improve over their corresponding bases across four professional-work benchmarks.
Data-scaling analyses reveal model-dependent diminishing returns and changes in execution length and tool-use reliability.
Controlled component studies connect reductions in probe-diagnosed environment defects to improved downstream training utility, supporting the value of coherent task construction for scaling working-agent supervision.
Limitations
First, GLM-5.3, our teacher model, accepts only text input. Consequently,
although the Qwen backbones include native vision and alignment components, we
train and evaluate them only through a text-only task-solving interface. This
work therefore does not examine learning from visual evidence directly. Future
work will extend trajectory collection and student training to multimodal
professional tasks.
Second, our training study focuses on supervised fine-tuning over teacher
trajectories.
Future work will leverage high-quality professional tasks and their execution
feedback to train working agents with reinforcement learning.
Ethical Considerations
WorkFactory trains agents to perform professional workflows and produce
realistic workplace artifacts. Such outputs may be incorrect, biased, or
misused in consequential settings, and should therefore receive appropriate
human review rather than replace qualified professionals. Dataset and model
release should also respect privacy, copyright, and licensing requirements.

Appendix A
Professional Intent Synthesis
Occupation-driven synthesis.
Starting from a public occupational hierarchy derived from the Standard
Occupational Classification
[
33
]
, we expand broad occupations
into fine-grained roles. These roles seed a search agent that retrieves
professional context from the web as needed and generates work situations
and objectives grounded in role responsibilities, business settings, and
motivating events.
Skill-driven synthesis.
We collect documented skills from a public skill directory
4
4
4
https://skills.sh/
and analyze each skill’s purpose, applicability conditions, prerequisites,
and operations to derive work situations and objectives. We combine skills
into candidate multi-step workflows when one skill’s output can supply inputs
required by another and the operations jointly serve a coherent professional
objective. For example, quotation extraction supplies supplier cost inputs for
annual cash-flow modeling, whose results feed NPV comparison and sourcing
recommendation.
Deliverable-driven synthesis.
Instruction backtranslation generates candidate instructions for existing
text
[
16
]
. Inspired by this, we use real
professional deliverables collected from the web as cues for plausible work
intents. We analyze their likely use, audience, content, and implied
production process to derive intents for producing, updating, reviewing, or
comparing such artifacts.
Intent review.
An LLM reviewer evaluates whether each candidate intent is coherent and
feasible, professionally appropriate, and plausible as a real workplace activity.
Candidates that fail this review are excluded from the shared intent library.

Appendix B
Information-level Planning and Task Instantiation
WorkFactory represents the information required by a task together with the
artifacts that provide or receive it. The representation distinguishes a
planned output or internal construction requirement from information already
available to the solver. Internal construction requirements serve only
as an intermediate specification during synthesis, connecting the intended
work to the request and supporting materials. They contain no instance-specific
facts and add no obligations unavailable to the solver.
All goals, constraints, and instance-specific information needed for completion
must be expressed in or obtainable through solver-accessible inputs.
B.1
Information Nodes and Relations
An information node records semantic content, entity and scope, and provision
status: supplied, externally acquired, solver-derived, or internal to
construction. It also records carrier bindings specifying where the content
is supplied, acquired, or produced. Solver-derived nodes describe quantities
or outputs to be derived and their supporting relations; their values remain
to be determined by the solver. Table

B.2
Carriers and Access
Carrier nodes identify where information occurs: the user request, reference
artifacts, external resources, future deliverables, or internal construction requirements.
A location binding records the carrier, provision status, and access
conditions. Before materialization it specifies a planned location; after
construction it can resolve to a file, sheet, cell range, page, or paragraph.
The same information may occur in several carriers. A shared identity and
scope link these occurrences and guide the worker in maintaining consistency
across files. Access metadata distinguishes solver-visible content from
internal construction requirements. Task-specific premises needed by the solver
must be supplied in accessible materials or obtainable from external resources.
Future deliverables are specified through their required content and supporting
relations, leaving their production to the solver.

Appendix C
Execution-based Environment Repair
C.1
Probe Reporting and Defect Taxonomy
Runtime quality assessment reports describe issues and assign severity labels.
A probe solver is informed that the task is synthetic and instructed to produce the best feasible deliverable.
It grounds each diagnosis in inspected sources and tool observations, identifies affected operations and deliverable requirements, and distinguishes environmental defects from solver mistakes and legitimate open choices.
Severity labels distinguish
blocker
findings that prevent completion
of the minimum required deliverable,
correctness
findings that identify
concrete task errors,
efficiency
findings that suggest better
processes, and
open
observations that record non-binding risks or
suggestions. Only blocker findings trigger repair, although a triggered repair
may also address correctness-level and other reported issues. Tasks with only
non-blocking findings skip repair; efficiency and open findings are advisory.
Non-blocking errors may therefore remain in retained tasks, and unclassified
findings do not enter the eight-category table.
For the component analysis, we retrospectively categorize the issues described in these reports by their content and supporting evidence.
The eight categories in Table

Blocker and correctness findings are treated as hard defects in the incidence
analysis. Task-level incidence counts a task once per category if its selected
report contains at least one finding labeled
blocker
or
correctness
in that category; a task may appear in multiple categories.
Classification uses the report’s stated evidence, not solver failure alone.

the conditions needed for completion; the initial plan is a reference for
the intended work, rather than a requirement to preserve every instance detail.

C.4
End-to-End Supplier-Selection Example
The following synthetic instance traces the running example from planning to
training. The intent is to evaluate lifecycle sourcing costs and recommend a
supplier for shipping cartons across four anonymous candidate vendors and a
three-year program. During instantiation, the planner specifies annual demand
of 48K, 60K, and 78K cartons and a 60:40 standard-to-insulated mix. Supplier
quotations provide unit prices, setup fees, and freight terms, while visible
rules specify an 8% discount rate for years 1–3, one-time setup costs in year
0, per-carton freight, USD-denominated constant prices, and no discounting of
the year-0 setup fees.
The graph marks the demand forecast, quotations, cost-timing rules, and vendor
profiles as supplied information. Transformation relations connect demand and
carton mix to annual carton volumes, then combine those volumes with each
vendor’s quotation to derive year-0 setup, annual spend, and vendor NPVs. The
NPVs and vendor profiles jointly support a cost–service recommendation.
Carrier bindings place the objective and rules in the user request, the
quotations and demand forecast in a reference PDF, and the inputs, model,
decision, recommendation, and assumptions in a future cost-comparison workbook.
The carton volumes, spending, NPVs, and recommendation remain solver-derived.
In the realized environment, Supplier C’s quotation does not state whether
freight is included or charged separately. A clean probe can diagnose that the
visible inputs do not support a comparable lifecycle-cost calculation. The
refiner adds a synthetic term specifying an additional freight charge of
USD 0.15 per carton to the quotation PDF, after which construction checks and
work-preservation review are repeated. A fresh probe then attempts the revised
task without seeing the earlier diagnosis. Neither initial construction nor
repair supplies the spending calculations, vendor NPVs, or final
recommendation.
Finally, an independent teacher completes the cost-comparison workbook across
all four vendors and produces a justified sourcing recommendation from the
solver-visible inputs. The resulting rollout is processed for training as described in
Appendix
D.3
.
Appendix D
Corpus and Training Details
D.1
Corpus Statistics
The final corpus represents 112,686 distinct tasks, each with at least one
training sequence. Before sequence construction, teacher rollouts undergo
lightweight validity filtering and, for selected long rollouts, rejection
sampling; overlength sequences are then removed during preprocessing. For teacher execution,
GLM-5.3 completes 94,077 of these tasks using GDPval Stirrup and the remaining
18,609 using Claude Code. The corpus spans 612
fine-grained occupations and contains 4.15 provided reference files per task
on average. Among file extensions occurring at least 10 times, it covers 317
reference-file extensions and 53 deliverable-file extensions.
Figure
7
shows that teacher trajectory
lengths are concentrated around 41–80 assistant turns, with a mean of 57.4,
a median of 56, and a 90th percentile of 91 turns.
Benchmark decontamination.
Evaluation tasks are not exposed to WorkFactory during intent synthesis or
task-environment construction. As a post-hoc safeguard, we encode the user
request of every retained training task and every evaluation task with
Qwen3-Embedding-8B
[
39
]
and flag pairs with cosine
similarity of at least 0.85. Separately, we flag pairs when shared 10-grams
cover at least 20% of the tokens in the shorter request. We also compare
hashes of the solver-visible files in the training and evaluation environments
to detect byte-identical artifacts. All request pairs flagged by either
text-overlap criterion are manually reviewed to distinguish reuse of an
evaluation task from benign similarity in domain, occupation, or deliverable
type. No reviewed pair constitutes task reuse, and no file hash is shared
between the training and evaluation environments.

Probe and teacher execution settings.
Every probe execution, including re-diagnosis after repair, starts in a clean
sandbox with the current visible request and resources. The probe runs in the
Claude Code harness with a 1M-token context window and no context compaction.
It cannot
access internal construction requirements, the information support graph, the construction plan,
or outputs and reports from previous executions. Teacher executions share this
task-information access boundary and use a 256K-token context window. We
collect trajectories for 94,077 tasks with the GDPval-AA Stirrup
harness

5

Code

2

official context-compaction mechanism
5

,

runs use its native tools and a compaction threshold of 0.7.
Their prompts differ: the teacher attempts the task, while the probe also reports
environmental issues encountered while solving.
Lightweight rollout filtering.
Every initial teacher rollout undergoes programmatic validity checks. We
exclude rollouts that contain repeated reasoning spans or repeated tool calls,
fail to produce a deliverable, or produce deliverables below a minimum content
threshold. These corpus-wide checks target degenerate or incomplete
executions; they do not provide task-specific judgments of deliverable
correctness.
Selective trajectory rejection sampling.
In addition to the corpus-wide filters, we select the longest 5% of initial
teacher rollouts for rejection
sampling using the 95th percentile of total interaction-turn counts.
Length is measured over the complete
rollout rather than individual training sequences, before pairwise
deliverable comparison. Initial rollout length serves as a heuristic for
allocating additional deliverable-quality checks.
For each selected task, the pairwise judge reads the user request, reference
artifacts, and both agents’ deliverables, without access to the internal
construction requirements. A DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 baseline deliverable is
generated once per task and held fixed across comparisons. A teacher win
retains the corresponding rollout. If the initial teacher attempt loses
or ties, we allow up to three additional attempts (four teacher attempts in
total), stopping at the first win. Each retry starts in a clean sandbox with
the same task inputs and generation settings, without access to previous
attempts or judge feedback. A task contributes no training episode if none
of its attempts wins; that task and its workspace are excluded from the final
corpus. Tasks outside the selected subset retain their initial teacher episodes
after lightweight filtering.

You are the pairwise evaluator for GDPVal-AA. Determine which blinded submission better fulfills the original professional task.
Evaluate both submissions using all available evidence from the initial task, reference files, extracted file text, rendered document images, native media, and submission files. Consider correctness, completeness, usability, professional quality, and faithfulness to requested deliverables.
Rules:
1. The identities of the systems are intentionally hidden. Never infer model identity from style, filenames, metadata, or self-description, and never favor Submission A or B because of its position.
2. Inspect both submissions independently before comparing them. Missing, empty, corrupt, or unusable deliverables are substantive failures.
3. For factual or pointable claims, rely on evidence actually present in the submitted artifacts. A submission’s claim that it is correct is not proof.
4. For visual deliverables, use rendered images as well as extracted text. When visible rendering conflicts with extraction, trust the visible artifact.
5. Use tie only when the submissions are genuinely equivalent overall or the available evidence cannot support a defensible preference. Do not use a tie merely because each submission has different strengths.
6. Check all material requirements in the original task, but keep the response concise. Return only the most decision-relevant comparisons.
Return exactly one JSON object containing (i) a winner in {A, B, tie}, (ii) a concise evidence-grounded overall explanation, and (iii) at most ten decisive comparisons. article.headline: WorkFactory：把职业意图变成可执行任务
article.lede: WorkFactory 用信息支撑图反向规划任务环境，探测执行失败并修复，构建 112,686 个任务、覆盖 612 个
article.problem: 训练能胜任专业工作的智能体，需要大量多样且可执行的专业任务，以及可靠的专家演示轨迹。但任务信息缺失或不一致时，教师模型会卡在执行环节，或引入缺乏依据的假设、漏做关键工作，使轨迹变成低质量监督。论文举的例子是供应商选择任务：报价文件没写某供应商的价格是否含运费，生命周期成本就无法一致计算；但若直接把算好的成本写进文件，又抹掉了本该由智能体完成的工作。
article.method: 作者从职业分类体系、公开技能文档和真实职业交付物三条路径合成「职业意图」，并用 LLM 评审其可行性与职业合理性。对每个意图，方法从目标输出反向构建信息支撑图，把信息单元、载体（用户请求、参考文件、外部资源、未来交付物）和支撑关系显式写出来，只提供前提信息，把中间推导与结论留给求解者。任务构建完成后，另一个独立的探测求解者在看不到任务构建图与计划的条件下执行任务，报告阻塞性缺陷；修复只能补充前提，必须通过「工作保留」审查，再经新一轮探测，只有通过的任务才交给 GLM-5.3 教师采集轨迹，用于掩码监督微调。
article.results: 最终语料包含 112,686 个任务、612 个细粒度职业、23 个主要职业组，平均每任务提供 4.15 个参考文件（平均 1.56 MiB），教师轨迹平均 57.36 个 assistant 轮次、62.95 次工具调用、136.18K token。微调后的 WorkPilot-35B-A3B 在四个基准上全面超过基座：GDPval-AA 从 879 升到 1565 Elo，JobBench 从 28.91 升到 62.35，Workspace-Bench 从 47.12 升到 56.53，OmegaUse-OfficeVal 从 7.14 升到 21.18；WorkPilot-4B 在 GDPval-AA 上从 661 升到 1375，WorkPilot-27B 从 975 升到本地估计的 1612 Elo。5K 任务的组件分析显示，信息级规划把 GDPval-AA Elo 从 1245 提到 1293，叠加执行修复后到 1326（累计 +81），同时跨文件不一致缺陷率从 32.82% 降到 25.74%、再降到 4.84%。数据规模方面，前 5K 任务贡献 447 Elo，而从 75K 扩到 110K 只增加 13 点；35B-A3B 的平均执行长度从基线 24.87 轮先升到 2K 任务时的 162.88 轮，再回落到 110K 时的 85.90 轮，代码执行失败率从 16.0% 降到 6.3%。
article.why_it_matters: 论文把工作型智能体数据合成的关键，落在「信息边界」上：哪些前提必须给、哪些推导必须留，并用执行探测把这一边界变成可检验的约束，而不是只堆砌看似合理的文件。它给出的规模、修复效果和跨模型尺度增益，为专业任务数据合成提供了可复用的流程参照，且公开了部分数据与模型权重。
article.limitations: 教师模型 GLM-5.3 只接受文本输入，因此训练与评测均为纯文本，骨干的视觉与对齐组件被冻结，多模态职业任务未被检验；研究也只做了监督微调，未涉及强化学习。多数 Elo 是本地两点锚定的估计而非官方评分（WorkPilot-27B 的 1612 即为本地估计），且成分分析用的探测报告在「信息级规划」条件下还出现泄漏/捷径与自不一致缺陷上升。

page_papers.title: Emotion Is Not External Knowledge: Internal Attention Signals for Affective State Reasoning
page_papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly operate in multi-turn interactions that require maintaining latent conversational states, not only explicit facts. We study affective state as an implicit state inferred from sparse contextual cues that remain relevant after topic shifts, and ask whether LLMs expose internal attention signals for routing such evidence at inference time. Prior attention interventions rely on labeled in-domain head profiles and externally specified target spans, limiting transfer across affective-evidence distributions. We propose Self-targeted Internal Attention Boosting (SIAB), which localizes sparse affective heads via causal localization (in detail activation patching) on synthetic minimal pairs and boosts, at the answer position, the content tokens these heads already attend to; both edited heads and target tokens are derived from the model's own behavior, enabling the same head set to be reused across tasks.We evaluate on ECC and GoEmotions across three LLMs and multiple prompting settings. Across settings, SIAB improves prompt-matched baselines by up to +10.3 macro-F1 on ECC and +5.5 on GoEmotions. Combined with PASTA-style external supervision, it achieves up to +13.84 accuracy points and +12.51 macro-F1 points, while mechanistic analyses trace the gains to sparse, emotion-enriched heads and show that layer proximity affects additivity.

Emotion is not External Knowledge:
Internal Attention Signals for Affective State Reasoning
Wenqiu Tang
Affiliation:
Nagoya University, Nagoya, Aichi, Japan

Abstract
Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly operate in multi-turn interactions that require maintaining latent conversational states, not only explicit facts. We study affective state as an implicit state inferred from sparse contextual cues that remain relevant after topic shifts, and ask whether LLMs expose internal attention signals for routing such evidence at inference time.
Prior attention interventions rely on head profiles derived from labeled examples across multiple profiling tasks and externally specified target spans, limiting transfer across affective-evidence distributions. We propose Self-targeted Internal Attention Boosting (SIAB), which localizes sparse affective heads across transformer layers in each model via causal localization (in detail activation patching) on synthetic minimal pairs and boosts the content tokens these heads already attend to. Both edited heads and target tokens are derived from the model’s own behavior, enabling the same head set to be reused across tasks. We evaluate SIAB on the ECC and GoEmotions benchmarks across three LLMs and multiple prompting settings. Relative to the corresponding settings without SIAB, macro-F1 improves by up to 7.67 points on ECC and 3.28 points on GoEmotions. Combining SIAB with PASTA further raises ECC macro-F1 by 12.51 points over the Gemma 3 zero-shot baseline.
1
Introduction
Conversation is inherently stateful; What a user means at any point
depends on what came before. As Large Language Models (LLMs) are
increasingly deployed in such multi-turn interaction, successful
responses must not only retain explicit factual context but also
maintain latent conversational states, such as a user’s frustration,
uncertainty, or trust
(
Fazzi et al., 2025
;
Følstad et al., 2024
)
.
Affective state is a challenging case. It is rarely given
as an explicit variable. Instead, it must be inferred from sparse
contextual cues whose relevance can persist across topic shifts. As
illustrated in Figure
1
, a model may therefore need
to use an earlier affective cue when making a later prediction.
Unlike knowledge-intensive failures, where retrieval or tool use can
supply a missing fact, affective continuity does not require adding new
information. Since the relevant evidence is already in the dialogue, the
difficulty is whether the model routes it to the final decision point.
Emotion recognition therefore provides a controlled proxy for studying
this routing problem at inference time.
Figure 1:
Long dialogues can bury early affective cues, turning affective prediction into a routing problem.
Inference-time attention intervention is a natural way to probe this
problem, since it reroutes existing contextual evidence during the
forward pass, without parameter updates or newly supplied facts. Existing
attention intervention methods, however, rely on external control
signals. Post-hoc Attention STeering Approach (PASTA)
(
Zhang et al., 2024a
)
profiles which heads to edit from labeled
in-domain data and steers attention toward externally specified spans.
Later variants reduce but do not remove this reliance on external
signals. These methods raise two questions. RQ1: Can internal attention signals
route affective evidence without external spans? and RQ2: Are
internal and external signals redundant or complementary?
We address these questions with Self-targeted Internal Attention Boosting
(SIAB), an attention intervention proposed for affective state reasoning. It first localizes a sparse
set of emotion-sensitive attention heads in different Transformer layers through causal localization via activation patching. It then uses these heads themselves
to select target tokens. At inference time, SIAB adds a scalar bias to
the pre-softmax attention logits of the localized heads, boosting the
content tokens they already attend to. Both the edited heads and the
target tokens thus derive from the model’s own behavior.
We evaluate on two Emotion Recognition in Conversation (ERC) settings with complementary distributions of affective evidence. In the Emotion-Cause Conversation benchmark (ECC;
He et al., 2025
), cues are dispersed across earlier turns and must survive later topic shifts. Meanwhile, in the GoEmotions benchmark
(
Demszky et al., 2020
)
, a single dense cue must instead be disambiguated among many fine-grained categories. The same head set is reused across both.
Since our goal is not only to improve recognition but to understand the
internal signal we exploit, we analyze when and why the localized heads
work. The gains come from a sparse set of heads; A few heads are sufficient,
and they attend more to affective words than random heads from early,
middle, and late layers. Whether SIAB succeeds further depends on logit
geometry and on whether the boosted tokens align with the final label
decision. Finally, the effects of SIAB and PASTA complement each other depending on their layer-band proximity.
Our contributions are threefold: (i) We propose SIAB, a self-targeted
inference-time attention intervention that requires no parameter update
or annotated span and composes with prompting and PASTA-style external
supervision, (ii) We show consistent gains across models, datasets, and
prompting settings, and (iii) We characterize its mechanism and boundary
conditions.
Figure 2:
Overview of the proposed Self-targeted Internal Attention Boosting (
SIAB
).
Causal localization via activation patching selects sparse emotion-sensitive heads (4–20 of hundreds).
SIAB adds a pre-softmax bias to the content tokens these heads already attend to
at final query positions —without training, parameter update, or external span.
2
Related Work
Existing attention-level methods externalize control to varying degrees,
relying on heads selected by testing each head’s steering effect on development examples with target tokens that are user-annotated
(
Zhang et al., 2024a
)
, heuristically extracted
(
Zhang et al., 2024b
;
Yu et al., 2024
)
, or applied at the head output rather
than its attention
(
Li et al., 2023
)
. Residual-stream steering operates at
a coarser granularity
(
Turner et al., 2024
;
Rimsky et al., 2024
;
Zou et al., 2023
)
. These
methods assume that the relevant evidence can be externally identified, an
assumption less natural for affective state, whose cues spread across
turns, often lack lexical salience, and shift as the conversation unfolds.
We instead derive both signals internally —heads from activation patching,
target tokens from each head’s own attention— and study how this internal
signal composes with external ones.
Mechanistic interpretability provides tools for discovering internal
structures that mediate model behavior. Activation patching
(
Wang et al., 2023
;
Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2023
)
has been used to localize
concrete circuit components, such as name-mover and S-inhibition heads,
through clean–corrupted activation contrasts, while direct logit attribution
(
Belrose et al., 2023
)
links intermediate contributions to
final-token logits. These tools fit our goal of identifying internal signals
for affective-evidence routing. Rather than specifying emotion-bearing spans
externally, we localize the attention heads that internally route affective
contrast.
Emotion recognition in conversation naturally probes affective state
across dialogue turns, yet existing mechanistic work operates at a
coarser granularity. It studies sentiment
directions
(
Tigges et al., 2024
)
, mid-layer multi-head
self-attention units
(
Tak et al., 2025
)
, or residual-stream
circuits for emotion
generation
(
Wang et al., 2025
)
, leaving
head-level recognition unaddressed. Other work improves accuracy through
retrieval, speaker modeling, or curriculum
learning
(
Lei et al., 2023
;
Xue et al., 2024
;
Fu et al., 2025
;
Li et al., 2026
)
,
but treats the model as a black box and ignores its internal attention
signal.
3

We introduce
SIAB
, an inference-time attention intervention with two components: Head-set construction via Activation Patching and
heads refinement introduced in §
3.1
and §
3.2

3.3

Conclusion
Affective state in dialogue depends on contextual cues that are already present but easily lost at prediction time. We showed that the proposed SIAB could route this evidence through internal model signals, without relying on externally marked spans or task-specific training. A fixed causally localized head set transferred across two contrasting attentional demands, whereas PASTA-style external profiles were competitive in-domain but transferred poorly. Their additive gains further suggested that internal and external signals capture complementary aspects of affective evidence. Future work should move from a fixed global intervention to sample-adaptive control, where intervention strength and target tokens vary with each example’s uncertainty and attention pattern, and test whether the same interface extends to other latent conversational states such as uncertainty, trust, or intent.
Limitations
Model scale.
We evaluated three open instruction-tuned LLMs spanning
4
4
–
8
8
B
parameters from distinct families (Gemma3, Qwen3, and LLaMA3). Whether the
internal signal continues to generalize at much larger scales
(e.g.,
70
70
B
+
+
) is an open question. Exhaustive activation patching at such
scales is computationally prohibitive in our setting.
Language coverage.
Both benchmarks (ECC and GoEmotions) were in English. Whether the recovered
head set transfers across languages, or whether language-specific
recognition circuits would emerge under multilingual evaluation, is
untested.
Dataset breadth.
The two benchmarks were selected to span complementary attentional
demands (long-context dialogue integration vs. wide-label distribution
shift over short inputs), and we reuse the same head set across them
without re-derivation. Generalization to non-emotion classification
tasks is left to future work.
Boundary on HARD samples.
A subset of test samples (HARD) remained unrescued even under stronger
interventions. As analyzed in §
5.3
, Both
scaling
β
\beta
and suppressing attention sink were insufficient. Whether these samples can be rescued by a more selective,
sample-adaptive intervention is left to future work.

Pair Construction for Causal Patching
Following the minimal-pair design of
Wang et al. (2023)
, each pair
(

and token length and differs only in affective content.
Coverage.
The set spans the six basic emotions of
Ekman (1992)
:
Anger, Disgust, Fear, Happiness, Sadness, and Surprise, 100 pairs each
(600 total), covering both valences and arousal levels to avoid a
polarity confound. Example (Anger): clean
‘‘During class, you
blamed me for the result, and I feel very’’
(Target
angry

vs. corrupted
‘‘…you praised me…’’
(Target
happy
). Within each category, pairs further vary the
syntactic locus of the cue —verb, predicate-adjective,
prenominal-adjective, or purpose-clause replacement— and distribute
it across multiple content words, so the discovered head set is not
tied to a single syntactic position.
Verification.
We constructed these datasets from approximately 25 templates authored by human annotators. Each template contains several replaceable slots, including names, times, locations, objects, and an emotion-bearing word or phrase. The emotion-bearing slots are shown in bold in the full template list. Example templates include:

Appendix G
Bootstrap
We use paired bootstrap resampling to quantify uncertainty arising from the finite evaluation sets. For each contrast, we draw

Table
11
reports the GoEmotions results, and Table
12
reports the ECC results. Across the two tables, all 18 prompt-matched the proposed SIAB settings yielded positive differences on both reported metrics. Equivalently, all 36 metric-level confidence intervals excluded zero. All 12 metric-level
PASTA+SIAB

The smallest positive lower bounds occurred under few-shot prompting, including the LLaMA3 model’s Mid / High on GoEmotions macro-F1 and the Qwen3 model’s High on ECC macro-F1, but remained above zero. In contrast, several stand-alone PASTA intervals included zero, indicating less consistent gains. The largest degradations occurred when ECC-profiled PASTA heads were transferred to GoEmotions, particularly for the LLaMA3 model, although LLaMA3’s in-domain

article.headline: 不靠外部标注，用内部注意力信号提升情感识别
article.lede: SIAB 用激活 patch 找出 4 到 20 个情感敏感注意力头，再放大这些头已关注的内容词；不训练、不更新参数、不
article.problem: 在多轮对话中，情感状态属于隐状态：它没有显式变量，只能从稀疏线索中推断，而且这些线索在话题转移后仍需保留。与知识型失败不同，相关证据已经在对话里，难点在于模型是否把它路由到最终决策位置。已有的注意力干预方法依赖标注数据来挑选注意力头，并依赖外部指定的目标 token，因此难以迁移到情感证据的分布上。
article.method: 作者先在合成的干净—损坏最小对比对上逐头做激活 patch，用归一化 logit 差恢复度筛出因果性情感头；再用 200 段 DailyDialog 对话做无标签精炼，按内容词上的注意力与 value 质量排序取 top-K，K 分别为 4、10、20。推理时，对选定头在最终 query 位置已经注意的 top-30% 内容词，在其 pre-softmax 注意力 logits 上加一个固定标量偏置 β，不重新定位、不访问金标签。
article.results: 在 Gemma3-4B、Qwen3-4B、LLaMA3-8B 三个模型、两个基准和多种提示设置下，18 个设置全部为正增益：ECC macro-F1 相对零样本最多提升 7.67 点（Gemma3 从 52.26 升到 59.93），GoEmotions 最多提升 3.28 点；ECC 上最大增益为 +10.27。把 SIAB 与 PASTA 组合后，Gemma3 在 ECC 上比零样本基线高 12.51 点 macro-F1。对照实验中，按任务内部配置的 PASTA 头迁移到 GoEmotions 时，LLaMA3 下降 7.19 点 macro-F1。
article.why_it_matters: 情感连续性不需要补充新事实，只需要把已有证据路由到决策点；这项工作给出了一个不训练、头集可跨任务复用的推理时接口。并且，内部信号与 PASTA 式外部信号在多数配置下近似可加，说明两者捕捉的是互补的方面。
article.limitations: 实验只覆盖 4 到 8B 的英语指令模型、两个英语情感基准，70B 以上规模、多语言和非情感任务均未验证。更难的一组样本仍然无法被挽救：把 β 加倍时，Gemma3 只多救 4.5%，Qwen3 与 LLaMA3 分别只有 0.4% 和 0.1%。

page_papers.title: WebAnything: From the Wild Web to Scalable Agent Environments
page_papers.abstract: Web agents require diverse, executable, and resettable website environments for reproducible training and evaluation. Human-assisted mirrors demand per-site engineering, while generative construction can diverge from specified real websites. Capture-and-replay preserves observations, with interaction coverage constrained by captured content and replay capabilities. We present WebAnything, a fully automated framework that reconstructs source-grounded, reusable Web environments from real URLs without per-site manual implementation or repair after initial setup and authorization. An Explorer-Builder collects browser-observable structures, resources, and interaction outcomes; an independent verifier checks frozen candidates and guides local repair or targeted source recapture. We construct 244 website artifacts across 14 application domains and 53 categories, supporting 12,984 executed and accepted tasks. Compared with human-assisted WebHarbor, WebAnything achieves higher aggregate scores on three fidelity metrics, with 12 wins, two ties, and no losses in a blind audit. Fine-tuning Qwen3.5-9B on 5,856 interaction trajectories improves REAL success by 9.9 percentage points, Odysseys-Easy Rubric Avg and Task Avg by 6.25 and 6.32 percentage points, and WebArena-Verified Overall success by 13.33 percentage points under the fixed harness. Code: https://github.com/china-qijizhifeng/Web-Anything

Abstract
Web agents require diverse, executable, and resettable
website environments for reproducible training and evaluation.
Human-assisted mirrors demand per-site engineering, while
generative construction can diverge from specified real websites.
Capture-and-replay preserves observations, with interaction
coverage constrained by captured content and replay capabilities.
We present
WebAnything
, a fully automated framework that
reconstructs source-grounded, reusable Web environments
from real URLs without per-site manual implementation
or repair after initial setup and authorization.
An Explorer–Builder collects browser-observable structures,
resources, and interaction outcomes; an independent verifier
checks frozen candidates and guides local repair or
targeted source recapture.
We construct 244 website artifacts across 14 application
domains and 53 categories, supporting 12,984 executed
and accepted tasks.
Compared with human-assisted WebHarbor,
WebAnything
achieves higher aggregate scores on three fidelity
metrics, with 12 wins, two ties, and no losses in a
blind audit.
Fine-tuning Qwen3.5-9B on 5,856 interaction
trajectories improves REAL success by 9.9 percentage
points, Odysseys-Easy Rubric Avg and Task Avg by
6.25 and 6.32 percentage points, and WebArena-Verified
Overall success by 13.33 percentage points under the fixed harness.

Web-Anything on GitHub
.
1
Introduction
Visual Web agents need stable, controllable environments in which they can explore, change state, recover from errors, and receive execution feedback. WebArena and VisualWebArena demonstrate the value of self-hosted websites for reproducible evaluation
(
Zhou et al., 2024
;
Koh et al., 2024
)
; WebGym and WebFactory further study scaling environments and interaction experience
(
Bai et al., 2026
;
Fan et al., 2026
)
. The real Web offers diverse structures and workflows, but live execution complicates state initialization, reproducibility, and safe isolation.
We investigate how specified real websites can be
automatically transformed at scale into
source-grounded, executable, and reusable Web agent
environments, without requiring manual
site-by-site reconstruction.
Existing approaches trade off
automation, source fidelity, and interaction coverage
(Figure
1
). Human-assisted mirrors provide controllable, source-corresponding environments but require per-site engineering
(
WebHarbor Team and Contributors, 2026
)
. Generative methods scale executable sites from specifications and references
(
Fan et al., 2026
;
Zhang et al., 2026
)
, but matching a specified source remains a distinct requirement. Capture-and-replay preserves source observations, with interaction coverage bounded by captured content and replay capabilities
(
Shi et al., 2017
;
Srivastava et al., 2026
)
; Weblica combines replay with source-grounded synthesis
(
Kar et al., 2026
)
. Scaling real-website environments requires both source correspondence and flexible, repeatable interaction.
A. Generative
Construction
Figure 1:
Trade-offs in real-website environment construction. Human-assisted mirrors require per-site engineering; generative methods need source correspondence; replay coverage depends on captured content and replay capabilities.
WebAnything
combines source-grounded reconstruction, independent verification, and iterative refinement.
Two technical challenges arise. The
Source-Grounding Gap
concerns reconstructing structures, resources, and behaviors when private backends and website internals are inaccessible. Screenshots and model priors alone can omit state relationships. Browser observations must instead be organized into evidence that constrains implementation. The
Verification and Feedback Gap
concerns detecting and correcting reconstruction discrepancies. Builder self-checks can overlook source-inconsistent defects, and a discrepancy may reflect either faulty implementation or insufficient observation. These cases require different actions: local repair or additional source capture.
We present
WebAnything
, a framework for
scalable, source-grounded Web agent environment construction
. Starting from real URLs, a coupled Explorer–Builder captures page structures, resources, and before/after interaction observations, then implements executable local routes and state transitions. An Independent Verifier checks frozen candidates in a separate context against source evidence and site contracts. Evidence-supported implementation errors trigger local repair; unresolved evidence gaps trigger targeted recapture. Updated candidates are frozen and reverified before release within their declared scope. Fixed initial states, reset mechanisms, and task evaluators support repeated interaction and trajectory collection.
Our evaluation covers construction scale, environment quality, and downstream utility. The resource pool contains
244 website artifacts
across 14 domains and 53 categories. On five matched WebHarbor sites and 14 historical states,
WebAnything
achieves higher automated fidelity metrics and 12 wins, two ties, and no losses in a blind overall-fidelity audit. Separate interaction tests characterize functional coverage. Historical analysis identifies evidence-supported discrepancies in
39 pairs across 22 sites
and independently reverified resolution of 18 issue records across six sites. The environments support
12,984 executed and accepted tasks
; SFT on earlier interaction trajectories improves Qwen3.5-9B on REAL, Odysseys-Easy, and WebArena-Verified Overall.
Our contributions are:
•
Fully automated, source-grounded reconstruction.
We introduce a unified Explorer–Builder that automatically
reconstructs executable Web environments from real URLs,
using browser-observable structures, resources, and behaviors
without per-site manual implementation or debugging.
•
Independent verification and evidence-aware refinement.
An independent verifier checks frozen candidates against
source evidence and site contracts, directing discrepancies
to local repair or targeted recapture, followed by
automated revision and reverification.
•
Scalable environment and task supply.
We construct 244 website artifacts across 14 domains,
supporting 12,984 executed and accepted tasks.
Historical construction records, independent quality
evaluations, and downstream SFT demonstrate automation,
source fidelity, and practical utility.
2
Related Work
Real-Web tasks and executable environments.
Mind2Web, WebVoyager, WebGym, WebLINX, SeeAct, Online-Mind2Web, and AssistantBench study tasks or interactions on real websites
(
Deng et al., 2023
;
He et al., 2024
;
Bai et al., 2026
;
Lù et al., 2024
;
Zheng et al., 2024a
;
Xue et al., 2025
;
Yoran et al., 2024
)
. WebArena, VisualWebArena, REAL, and WebShop emphasize controlled execution and state initialization
(
Zhou et al., 2024
;
Koh et al., 2024
;
Garg et al., 2025
;
Yao et al., 2022
)
. WorkArena, WorkArena++, and BrowserGym support enterprise workflows and common evaluation infrastructure, while OSWorld and AgentStudio extend executable evaluation to computer environments
(
Drouin et al., 2024
;
Boisvert et al., 2024
;
Le Sellier De Chezelles et al., 2025
;
Xie et al., 2024
;
Zheng et al., 2024b
)
.
WebAnything
connects real-source diversity with repeatable execution by constructing local environments for specified websites.
Website generation, replay, and mirroring.
WebFactory scales executable sites from specifications and references; InfiniteWeb uses task-centric test-driven development
(
Fan et al., 2026
;
Zhang et al., 2026
)
. VeriEnv provides cloned environments and deterministic SDK-based task verification; WebArena-Infinity iterates generation and testing
(
Chae et al., 2026a
;
Chae et al., 2026b
;
WebArena-Infinity Contributors, 2026
)
. WebGen-Agent combines VLM appearance feedback and GUI testing with backtracking and best-candidate selection for instruction-driven website generation
(
Lu et al., 2026
)
. Our refinement grounds frozen candidates in URL-specific evidence and routes discrepancies by evidence sufficiency. Screenshot-to-code methods include pix2code, Pix2Struct, WebSight, and Design2Code
(
Beltramelli, 2017
;
Lee et al., 2023
;
Laurençon et al., 2024
;
Si et al., 2025
)
. World of Bits and WARC-Bench preserve captured content through replay
(
Shi et al., 2017
;
Srivastava et al., 2026
)
; Weblica combines replay with source-grounded synthesis
(
Kar et al., 2026
)
. WebHarbor constructs mirrors through human–Coding Agent collaboration
(
WebHarbor Team and Contributors, 2026
)
.
WebAnything
jointly uses structural, resource, and behavioral evidence. Separate visual and interaction measurements complement image metrics such as SSIM and LPIPS
(
Wang et al., 2004
;
Zhang et al., 2018
)
.
Feedback and interaction-data supply.
Self-Refine and Reflexion use feedback for output revision and agent reflection
(
Madaan et al., 2023
;
Shinn et al., 2023
)
. Our feedback targets frozen website implementations and missing source evidence. AutoGUIWorld synthesizes GUI observations and trajectories, while WEFT studies coordination among environments, tasks, harnesses, and evaluators
(
Yang et al., 2026
;
Mao et al., 2026
)
. Synatra and AgentTrek derive demonstrations from indirect knowledge or tutorials; WebRL studies self-evolving task curricula
(
Ou et al., 2024
;
Xu et al., 2025
;
Qi et al., 2025
)
. OS-Atlas, UI-TARS, and OpenCUA expand GUI grounding or interaction data
(
Wu et al., 2025
;
Qin et al., 2025
;
Wang et al., 2025
)
.
WebAnything
supplies executable environments and collects interaction data with the fixed agent harness and a unified task/evaluator pipeline, measuring utility on external benchmarks.
3
Methodology
WebAnything
uses source evidence as the shared basis for construction and independent verification (Figure
2
). An Explorer–Builder reconstructs executable local pages and states; verification feedback then drives implementation repair or targeted source recapture.
Figure 2:
WebAnything
reconstruction pipeline. Source evidence guides executable construction. Independent checks of frozen candidates drive local repair or targeted recapture; verified candidates are released with repeatable interaction and task-evaluation interfaces.

3.2
Source-Grounded Reconstruction
State-associated evidence.
For each visited state, the Explorer–Builder associates page structures, computed styles, element geometry, screenshots, and resource references. Actions are linked to subsequent visible feedback and state changes. Distinct interaction states at the same URL remain distinct evidence: a closed menu and its expanded state, for example, constrain different implementation requirements.
Evidence-constrained implementation.
Structural observations constrain layout and component relationships; resource observations ground fonts, images, and media; behavioral observations constrain navigation, filtering, and state modification. The Builder organizes these into local components, routes, and shared object relationships. Screenshot references thus complement structural and behavioral evidence. A specific discrepancy can be traced back to its associated page state and action. When available observations do not establish a required outcome, the system seeks additional evidence rather than treating an inferred behavior as observed.
Coverage policies.
Full Coverage
expands accessible page types, interaction states, and neighboring branches from the entry URL and native navigation.
Just-in-Time Coverage
prioritizes dependencies of a given task set and expands them through construction and verification feedback. Both share the reconstruction and acceptance mechanisms, differing in exploration scope and expansion timing. Reported construction experiments use Full Coverage.
3.3
Independent Verification and Evidence-Aware Refinement
Verification decoupling.
The Builder implements and self-checks a candidate; an Independent Verifier then examines the frozen implementation in a separate context. It obtains rendering and operation results anew and compares them with source evidence and the site contract. Applicable checks cover pages, controls, resources, workflows, persistence, and restoration. The Verifier cannot edit candidate code. Stateful tests operate through local UI/API interfaces and restore the initial state. Candidate freezing binds findings to the inspected implementation and prevents verification-time repair from changing the target.
Evidence-aware refinement.
The model diagnoses each discrepancy using check results, source observations, the contract, and runtime conditions. If existing evidence establishes an expected outcome that the candidate fails to reproduce,
Local Repair
returns the affected page or control, executed action, expected and observed outcomes, and supporting evidence to the Builder. If evidence is insufficient to establish the target outcome,
Targeted Recapture
forms a concrete observation request and revisits the relevant source region. Newly captured structures, resources, or behaviors constrain the next implementation.
For example, Figma’s authorized source capture established a canvas-anchored comment composer. Independent checks found mismatched placement and appearance, providing a concrete target for local revision. The Builder read the feedback, changed the editor markup and styles, and submitted a new candidate; independent checks then confirmed the composer’s geometry and visibility. Existing source evidence supported repair in this case; an unresolved observation question instead becomes a bounded recapture request (Appendix
B.8
).
After either path updates the candidate, the controller freezes it again and the Verifier repeats affected checks and applicable regression tests. Verification therefore connects discrepancies to actionable revision, while source evidence constrains both initial reconstruction and subsequent refinement. Candidates passing checks within their declared scope can proceed to release. Implementation details and original prompts appear in Appendix
B.4
.
3.4
Environment and Verifiable Task Supply
Released environments package local implementations, resources, initial data, runtime configuration, and reset interfaces. Shared state connects related pages, and applicable creation, modification, and save operations affect later interactions. Fixed initial data and state restoration provide repeatable task starting conditions. The task pipeline generates instructions and matching success conditions for implemented capabilities. Agents execute tasks through a fixed browser-based computer-use agent harness shared across data collection and downstream evaluations; settings and execution budgets are specified in Appendix
E.1
. Evaluators check final answers or terminal environment states. Accepted trajectories are converted into step-level training examples. Task generation, executed acceptance, trajectory collection, and training export remain separate stages and counting units; Section
4.4
reports their outputs.
4
Experiments and Results
We study
RQ1: construction scale and efficiency
,
RQ2: environment quality and independent verification
, and
RQ3: task support and downstream learning utility
.
4.1
Experimental Setup
Objects and baselines.
The resource inventory covers 244 unique website artifacts as of October 9, 2026. Full Coverage construction records for 85 sites support automation and expenditure analysis. Quality comparisons use frozen artifacts and an independent evaluation pipeline: five WebHarbor sites with 14 historical reference states, and five VeriEnv artifacts for offline interaction tests. Historical VeriEnv fidelity references cover four LinkedIn states. Subsets and reference conditions are specified in Appendices
A.2
–
A.4
.
Measurements.
Pixel Similarity, SSIM, and Text F1 measure source-state correspondence, aggregated within sites and then averaged equally across sites. A blind audit of the 14 WebHarbor-matched states uses final labels agreed through discussion by three annotators, with randomized anonymous mirror order. Interaction tests disable external network access and report capability coverage, executed-test success, and all-test pass, keeping their denominators distinct. Explicit adapters restore initial states. Historical verification analysis links self-checks, independent findings, and repair traces; its definitions appear in Appendix
B.7
.
Tasks and training.
Two disjoint collections contain 6,172 accepted tasks across 74 sites and 6,812 across 229 sites. SFT uses earlier WebAnything interaction data: 5,856 trajectories associated with 5,167 unique training task IDs, converted into 60,517 step-level examples. Multiple trajectories or format variants can share a task ID. The newer 6,812 tasks are not used in this SFT experiment. We fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B for 473 steps (the fixed training endpoint), with global batch size 256 and learning rate

We present
WebAnything
, an end-to-end automated framework
for transforming real websites into source-grounded,
executable, and reusable Web agent environments.
Unlike human-assisted mirroring approaches,
WebAnything
automates source exploration, evidence collection,
website reconstruction, independent verification,
and iterative refinement, eliminating the need for
per-site manual implementation and debugging in
our audited construction runs.
By grounding reconstruction in browser-observable
structures, resources, and interaction behaviors,
the framework reduces reliance on incomplete visual
references or manually specified workflows.
Structural, resource, and behavioral evidence guides
reconstruction, while independent verification
directs discrepancies to local repair or targeted
recapture.
This separation enables the system to
distinguish implementation defects from insufficient
source evidence and refine reconstructed environments
accordingly.
The framework constructs 244 website artifacts
across 14 application domains and 53 categories,
supporting 12,984 executed and accepted tasks.
Experiments demonstrate source fidelity,
operational validity, and verification-driven
refinement, while also highlighting the importance
of evaluating functional coverage independently
from visual similarity.
Furthermore, supervised fine-tuning on 5,856
interaction trajectories improves Web agent
performance on REAL, Odysseys-Easy, and
WebArena-Verified, demonstrating the downstream
utility of the constructed environments.
Together, these results establish a practical path
toward scaling real-Web agent environments with
minimal site-specific human engineering.
More broadly,
WebAnything
connects automated website
reconstruction with reproducible interaction and
training-data collection, providing a foundation
for scalable Web agent development and post-training.
Limitations
Training validation with large-scale models.
Our supervised fine-tuning experiments with Qwen3.5-9B demonstrate the learning value of interaction data from reconstructed environments for downstream Web agent tasks. However, current training experiments primarily concern the 9B parameter scale. We have not systematically evaluated these data with larger foundation models, different post-training methods, or larger training budgets. Future work can examine relationships among environment scale, data diversity, and model capabilities to assess this approach in larger-scale agent training.
Continuous real-Web updates and environment maintenance.
Real websites continually change their page structures, resources, and interaction behaviors.
WebAnything
currently reconstructs and verifies source states at particular times, without systematically evaluating the timeliness of local mirrors or long-term maintenance efficiency under continuing source changes. Future research can investigate source-change detection, incremental evidence capture, and local environment updates to reduce maintenance costs while preserving source correspondence.
Copyright, content authorization, and environment distribution.
High-fidelity reconstruction of real websites involves page content, images, fonts, and branding that may be protected by copyright, trademarks, and terms of service. Public accessibility does not necessarily grant permission to reproduce, modify, or redistribute content. Environment construction, research use, and public release must therefore comply with applicable content authorization and compliance requirements. Future releases can prioritize the general construction framework, evaluation protocols, and de-identified research data, while determining the distribution scope of website mirrors and original resources according to their licenses.
Ethical Considerations
Exploring, capturing, and reconstructing real websites raises issues concerning terms of service, intellectual property, privacy, and security. The system should process only websites covered by authorization, public licenses, or research agreements, avoid collecting account credentials, cookies, personal information, and payment content, and run released environments in isolated networks and sandboxes. For websites or tasks that could facilitate abusive automation, reconstruction scope, public content, and model capabilities should be restricted.

Appendix A
Environment Construction and Quality Evaluation
The appendices provide protocols, implementation details, per-site results, and source inventories for the completed experiments.
A.1
Historical Construction and Cost Records
Construction reports for the historical 85-site subset record 59 passed sites, 15 source-blocked sites, 6 failed sites, and 5 sites with missing reports. These statuses reflect different versions of acceptance criteria, visual algorithms, and thresholds and serve to trace historical construction processes. After initial setup and authorization, this subset contains no recorded per-site manual implementation, debugging, or repair. Conclusions about human intervention and pricing are restricted to this historical subset and the recovered calls.
This construction experiment used the Full Coverage policy. In the recovered SDK records, the Builder and Verifier primarily used
gpt-5.6-sol
with
xhigh
reasoning; some Builder calls used
gpt-6-astra
, so the entire batch did not use a single model.
Recovered model-call and partial cost records cover 84/85 sites. Input tokens, including cached tokens, total 11.207 billion, of which 10.672 billion are cached input tokens; output tokens total 38.4318 million. Recorded, quantifiable model costs total $220.62, with recorded Builder and Independent Verifier costs of approximately $142.52 and $78.11, respectively. Across the 84 sites with records, the mean recorded per-site cost is approximately $2.63 and the median is approximately $1.60. Independently rounded components sum to $220.63, differing from the total by $0.01 due to rounding. Seven sites additionally contain unpriced Astra calls. These costs therefore provide only a lower bound for recovered, priceable model calls. They exclude unpriced calls, browser execution, and other system overhead, are not extrapolated to the total cost of 244 sites, and are not interpreted as the marginal cost of the Verifier under a controlled ablation.
Costs distinguish system development, initial authorization/setup, per-site implementation/debugging/repair, and research auditing. Neither the 244-site artifact pool nor the historical 85-site subset has a complete attempt cohort under uniform acceptance criteria, so we do not compute a unified construction success rate.

The resource inventory and environment-quality evaluation materials in this section use records frozen on October 9, 2026: resource scale comes from the frozen 244-site inventory, historical construction/cost audits from the 85-site subset, and quality results from two independent artifact comparisons.
