Conclusion
Co-Design Bench evaluates
273
273
real-user application revisions with runnable starting states and
2,331
2{,}331
hidden acceptance criteria. Its two tracks span localized multimodal edits and coordinated repository changes under a shared protocol of source evidence, browser execution, and adversarial review. Across ten endpoints, the strongest model reaches
69.9
%
69.9\%
mean strict completion but fully satisfies only
26.4
%
26.4\%
of tasks. Track-specific rankings, edit-breadth differences, and harness sensitivity show where reliable delivery remains difficult. Runnable baselines and criterion-level evidence support analysis of failures in request grounding, change propagation, and final-state verification. The benchmark provides a common setting for measuring progress toward complete delivery by coding agents, while retaining the task context and execution evidence needed to analyze unmet requirements and compare future solvers.

Appendix D
Implementation and Resource Accounting
Execution constraints.
Each trajectory has a three-hour wall-clock limit and a
120
120
-turn cap. A wall-clock timeout terminates execution and is recorded as an infrastructure failure. Reaching the turn cap instead triggers a build, render, and evaluation of the final workspace state.
Telemetry and token accounting.
Resource totals come from request-level API logs and include retries. For Anthropic routes, token totals sum prompt, completion, cache-creation, and cache-read entries. For OpenAI routes, reported prompt usage already includes cached input. The evaluated trajectories contain
135,370
135{,}370
tool calls. These accounting conventions distinguish actual requests from a count of unique attempted actions.
Trace integrity and final-state evaluation.
Tool invocations and returns are paired sequentially within the same assistant scope. This prevents identifiers reused by nested agents from merging unrelated events. Intermediate renders and edits remain available for inspection. Scores use the final candidate: earlier behavior earns credit only if it remains present in the final workspace.

Figures

connect solver inputs to evaluator checks. Each row shows the runnable page and relevant detail on the left, a summarized request in the center, and three selected acceptance criteria on the right. article.headline: 真实用户改码基准：最强模型仅完整通过26.4%
article.lede: 从26,314个真实编程会话筛出273个改码任务，最强模型平均通过69.9%的验收标准，全部通过仅26.4%。
article.problem: 现有网页编码基准多基于参考页面重建、合成编辑操作或版本历史抽取的改动对，缺少从真实用户编程会话中回收、同时覆盖局部多模态编辑与跨组件仓库协同修改的复合修订任务。论文还指出，执行方式会显著改变测得的完成度：在同样的150个WebCompass-edit任务上，qwen3.7-plus从单次执行的73.6%提升到agentic执行的95.1%，相差21.5个百分点，因此只报单一分数容易误读。
article.method: 作者构建Co-Design Bench，含273个任务与2,331条专家撰写、对解题者隐藏的验收标准，分多模态编辑（ME，100个任务）与仓库编辑（RE，173个任务）两条轨道，每个任务都配有可运行的编辑前应用、归一化请求和可选附件。评测采用judge-then-refute协议：先由固定的agentic评估器依据源码差异、渲染页面和Playwright轨迹对每条标准给出Pass/Partial/Fail，再由独立的LLM验证器专门反驳正向判定（查桩代码、硬编码、不可达入口等），最后做证据审计——视觉类声明必须有成功渲染与截图，交互类声明必须有录制的浏览器动作，缺证即在聚合前中止。
article.results: 在统一使用Claude Code harness、限时3小时与120轮的前提下，十个模型端点跑满2,730个模型–任务对。最强的gpt-6-astra平均严格完成度为0.699（69.9%），但只有26.4%的任务全部标准通过；分轨道看ME为0.754、全通过41.0%，RE为0.667、全通过17.9%，也就是说约73.6%的任务至少残留一条未满足的标准。RE轨道上，跨三或四种编辑类型的任务汇总严格完成度为0.591，低于只跨一或两种的0.654，差6.3个百分点，且十个端点在宽编辑组上无一例外更低。评估器敏感性检查中，换用三个替代评判模型后绝对分数最多偏移0.053，kimi-k3与Qwen3.8-27B在两条轨道上的相对顺序保持不变。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「通过多少条要求」与「整个任务是否交付」拆成两个指标同时报告，说明高分覆盖度可以掩盖大量未完成交付，为真实用户应用修订场景下的coding agent提供了可追溯到证据的评测口径。
article.limitations: 评分主体仍是LLM评判加LLM反驳，论文自承无法消除判断错误，人工只由两位前端专家抽查了200个任务–模型输出；任务使用固定请求，不模拟执行过程中的进一步用户反馈。此外跨harness实验显示模型排序会随执行框架反转（ME上Spearman ρ=-1.00，两模型差距在10.0至16.2个百分点间摆动），分数与harness强耦合；模态与编辑广度的分组比较也被明确称为描述性而非因果。
article.figure_caption_zh: 从产物到判定：先构建并渲染候选、采集源码与浏览器证据并给隐藏标准打分，再由独立验证器挑战正向判定、审计必需证据并聚合分数，并行的基线与可解性检查用于失败归因。

page_papers.title: VibeGame: Prompt-to-Game Development with AI-Native Engine and Self-Evolving Adversarial Agent Team
page_papers.abstract: Large language model agents have enabled software development through natural-language interaction, but extending this paradigm to end-to-end game development remains challenging. Building a playable game requires coordinating code, scenes, assets, animations, physics, and configurations, while allowing developers to validate their integrated behavior through interactive testing. We introduce VibeGame, a framework for creating complete 2D game projects from natural-language prompts and optional reference images. Its AI-native game engine represents project state as schema-validated structured text and provides frame-synchronous runtime control, enabling agents to inspect game states, execute actions, and verify behavior at their own pace. Built upon this interface, we design an Adversarial Agent Team of eight specialized agents to separate implementation from review, so that problems are found and fixed through multi-round loops. For each conducted and accepted project, we further introduce a training-free self-evolution mechanism to distill it into reusable skeletons, modules, and collaboration contracts for future development. We evaluate prompt-assets-to-game (PA2G), where agents are given an asset library, and prompt-to-game (P2G), where agents generate their own art. Engine and Self-Evolving Adversarial Agent Team

Abstract
Large language model agents have enabled software development through natural-language interaction, but extending this paradigm to end-to-end game development remains challenging.
Building a playable game requires coordinating code, scenes, assets, animations, physics, and configurations, while allowing developers to validate their integrated behavior through interactive testing.
We introduce VibeGame, a framework for creating complete 2D game projects from natural-language prompts and optional reference images.
Its AI-native game engine represents project state as schema-validated structured text and provides frame-synchronous runtime control, enabling agents to inspect game states, execute actions, and verify behavior at their own pace.
Built upon this interface, we design an Adversarial Agent Team of eight specialized agents to separate implementation from review, so that problems are found and fixed through multi-round loops.
For each conducted and accepted project, we further introduce a training-free self-evolution mechanism to distill it into reusable skeletons, modules, and collaboration contracts for future development.
We evaluate prompt-assets-to-game (PA2G), where agents are given an asset library, and prompt-to-game (P2G), where agents generate their own art.
On a GameCraft-Bench subset, VibeGame in P2G consistently outperforms a range of agent harnesses in either P2G or PA2G with the same underlying model, including GPT-6.1-Sol.
1
Introduction
Games are among the most demanding types of software to develop: they must sustain interactive worlds in real time, maintain a coherent visual identity, and enforce consistent, balanced rules.
Meeting these requirements has traditionally required months of collaboration among designers, programmers, and artists using game engines such as Unity
[
1
]
, Unreal Engine
[
2
]
, and Godot
[
3
]
.
The required time and resources put game development out of reach for many creators.
Artificial intelligence (AI) has begun to lower this barrier from two directions, yet neither fully supports practical game creation.
World models such as Genie
[
4
]
generate interactive experiences directly from video but produce no editable source code, while large language models (LLMs) integrated into commercial engines, as in DreamGarden
[
5
]
for Unreal, face project state scattered across graphical interfaces and binary assets that agents cannot consistently inspect or modify.
Neither produces a complete game project that can be built, played, inspected, versioned, and iteratively revised.
Meanwhile, LLM-based coding agents
[
6
,
7
]
have made “vibe coding” increasingly accessible, allowing non-programmers to describe software in natural language and refine it through iterative feedback.
Games are the natural next step, and we formulate this challenge as
Prompt-to-Game (P2G) Development
: given only a natural language description and optional reference images, the system must produce a complete playable game project, discovering and fixing its problems along the way.
Recent systems and benchmarks have made progress toward this goal.
AutoUE
[
8
]
and OpenGame
[
9
]
build games end to end with agents, and GameDevBench
[
10
]
and GameCraft-Bench
[
11
]
evaluate such abilities, the latter also with a provided asset library, a setting we call Prompt-Assets-to-Game (PA2G).
However, most of these efforts reserve runtime checks for final evaluation or limit them to verifying that a game builds and runs.
Yet many game issues emerge only during play, making interactive testing and refinement essential to playability.
Additionally, fixing one project artifact can introduce inconsistencies across interdependent code, scenes, assets, animations, physics, and configurations.
Addressing these challenges reliably and carrying validated solutions forward to future projects requires three tightly coupled capabilities.
First, an
agent-operable project state
must expose the structure and dependencies among scripts, scenes, assets, animations, physics, and configurations, because direct file access alone cannot prevent a seemingly local edit from violating hidden relationships elsewhere.
Second,
interaction-grounded verification
is needed because a structurally valid project can still fail at runtime when player input, physics, animation, and game logic interact; since execution unfolds faster than an agent can reason about it, verification requires controllable execution that can be paused, advanced, and examined.
Third, the system must
preserve validated development experience
: so that reusable project structures, features, and coordination procedures can guide subsequent work, while unverified or project-specific content must remain isolated.
To address these requirements together, we introduce
VibeGame
, a unified framework that connects project construction, runtime verification, and experience reuse within a development loop, as illustrated in Figure
3
.
(1)
An
AI-native game engine
exposes scenes, nodes, assets, scripts, and configurations as structured text with explicit references and schema validation, and its frame-synchronous runtime control lets agents inspect game states, inject actions, and observe their consequences.
(2)
Built upon this interface, an
Adversarial Agent Team (AAT)
separates implementation roles from auditor, player, and reviewer roles, which challenge the game from structural, behavioral, and project-level perspectives; the team iterates review and revision until the project satisfies the intended design and functionality.
(3)
Once the project is accepted, a
training-free self-evolution mechanism
distills its reusable experience into project skeletons, verified modules, and collaboration contracts (Section
3.3
), which subsequent projects adapt and revalidate rather than reuse blindly.
Figure 2
:
Games created by VibeGame from prompts across diverse 2D game genres.
Figures
1
and
2
present some examples produced by VibeGame.
And with the same underlying model, VibeGame in P2G outperforms a range of agent harnesses in either P2G or PA2G. Ablation studies further show that removing either the AI-native engine or the adversarial review roles substantially lowers the overall score, and that the experience distilled through self-evolution with a stronger model can be transferred to improve a weaker one.
In summary, our contributions are three-fold:
•
We introduce VibeGame, a framework for
prompt-to-game development
that transforms natural-language prompts into complete, playable game projects, enabling rapid game creation and subsequent iterative refinement.
•
At the core of our method is an
AI-native game engine
that enables coding agents to directly inspect and modify project state and control runtime execution without relying on graphical editors. Building on this engine, we introduce an
Adversarial Agent Team
that separates implementation from review, together with a
training-free self-evolution
mechanism that distills validated development experience into reusable knowledge for future projects.
•
We comprehensively evaluate VibeGame against other mainstream agent harnesses in both P2G and PA2G settings, demonstrating superior performance over all of them.
2
Related Work
Agentic software development and vibe coding frameworks.
Coding agents such as Claude Code
[
6
]
, Codex
[
7
]
, Cursor
[
12
]
, OpenHands
[
13
]
, and SWE-agent
[
14
]
, often with ReAct
[
15
]
-style reasoning and evaluated on benchmarks such as SWE-bench
[
16
]
, have moved LLM-based programming to repository-level development.
Vibe coding frameworks such as Trellis
[
17
]
externalize specs, tasks, and memory as persistent repository artifacts, and ChatDev
[
18
]
and MetaGPT
[
19
]
introduce role specialization into software development.
VibeGame extends these directions to game projects, where code, art assets, scene configurations, and runtime behavior must be maintained jointly and verified by running the game.
Engine-integrated game generation.
Prior work connects LLMs and generative models to game engines and 3D tools: Sketch2Scene
[
20
]
builds 3D game scenes from sketches; UnrealLLM
[
21
]
and DreamGarden
[
5
]
generate content and environments in Unreal Engine (UE); 3Dify
[
22
]
uses the Model Context Protocol (MCP)
[
23
]
or computer use to call Blender
[
24
]
, Unity, and UE toolchains, enhanced by retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)
[
25
]
; and
Hassan [26]
generate Unity templates from design documents.
AutoUE
[
8
]
chains five agents to generate 3D games in UE and uses play-testing for the final evaluation.
These systems mostly work around the graphical user interface (GUI) workflows of commercial engines, whereas web frameworks like Phaser
[
27
]
express projects fully in text.
OpenGame
[
9
]
builds on Phaser with templates and a debug protocol, generates its own assets from the prompt alone, i.e., the P2G setting, and repairs build and test failures until the game builds and runs.
VibeGame further adds an agent-oriented project representation, runtime control, and visual verification, and lets independent roles verify the running game inside the development loop.
3
The VibeGame Framework
Figure 3
:
System overview of VibeGame.
(a) The Adversarial Agent Team turns a user request into an accepted game through intention alignment, parallel development, and adversarial correction. (b) The AI-native game engine exposes a structured project representation and frame-synchronous runtime control for implementation and play-testing. (c) Training-free self-evolution extracts skeletons, modules, and collaboration contracts from accepted projects and returns them to future development as project priors.
VibeGame takes a natural-language request and optional reference images as inputs and produces a complete 2D game project that can be run, inspected, and modified through later requests.
Figure
3
presents the project lifecycle.
The AI-native engine provides the shared project representation and runtime interface on which all agents operate (Section
3.1
).
On top of it, the Adversarial Agent Team, eight specialized agents coordinated by an
orchestrator
, turns the request into an accepted game through intention alignment, parallel development, and adversarial correction (Section
3.2
).
After acceptance, the training-free self-evolution mechanism distills the project into skeletons, modules, and collaboration contracts that initialize future runs (Section
3.3
).
3.1
AI-Native Game Engine
A game engine provides the foundation on which a game project is constructed and executed, but traditional engines are designed for human-operated workflows.
We define a game engine as
AI-native
when it has three properties that remove the resulting barriers for coding agents.
(1) GUI-Independent
: the entire project is represented as plain-text files that agents can inspect and edit directly, rather than engine-specific identifiers or binary files that require graphical editors.
(2) Runtime-Accessible
: agents can pause, step through, observe, and intervene in the running game through code rather than GUI-based debugging tools, turning an asynchronous real-time system into a synchronously verifiable process.
(3) Source-Available
: agents can inspect the engine’s uncompiled source code rather than relying on documentation that may lag behind version changes or omit implementation details.
GUI-Independent.
We build our engine on Phaser because it expresses projects fully in text (Section
2
).
However, Phaser imposes little structure on how a project is organized, which makes agent-generated projects prone to fragmentation.
We therefore represent each game as a collection of scenes whose configurations are stored in type-checked JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) files.
Each scene is a hierarchy of nodes, the basic building blocks of the project; a node groups its visual appearance, collision geometry, behavior scripts, and configuration into one unit, declared explicitly in JSON fields rather than hidden inside constructors.
Nodes shared across scenes are stored as standalone definition files and instantiated at runtime.
This scene-node-asset hierarchy gives every artifact a clear location and makes cross-file dependencies explicit, so schema validation can detect invalid references, such as missing assets, before execution rather than as runtime failures.
Runtime-Accessible.
A structurally valid project may still fail when player input, physics, animation, and game logic interact during execution.
We therefore expose the running game through a frame-synchronous programmatic interface: agents can pause and resume execution, advance a specified number of frames, inspect or modify runtime properties such as node positions and velocities, inject semantic actions such as “press jump”, and capture screenshots.
With these controls, agents verify runtime behavior at their own pace through frame-by-frame inspection, scripted test sequences, or heuristic bots that react during real-time play.
Source-Available.
Even with structured project files and runtime control, agents may still encounter engine behavior that the documentation does not fully explain, particularly after an interface change or in uncommon functionality.
We therefore copy the engine’s complete, uncompiled source code into the project directory at initialization, so agents can look up the exact application programming interfaces (APIs), assumptions, and implementation details needed for the current task.

3.2
Adversarial Agent Team
The engine provides the interfaces required to construct and test a game, but it does not determine what should be built, how development should be organized, or when the result is satisfactory.
Assigning these responsibilities to a single agent would also require the same role to both produce and evaluate its own work, making behavioral failures and visual defects during gameplay easier to overlook.
VibeGame therefore introduces an
Adversarial Agent Team
(AAT) comprising eight specialized roles: orchestrator, designer, artist, architect, programmer, auditor, player, and reviewer.
We define each agent’s responsibilities through role-specific prompts and execution hooks, and use persistent project artifacts to preserve decisions and communicate them across the team.
As shown in Figure
3
(a), the team organizes development into three stages:
Intention Alignment
,
Parallel Development
, and
Adversarial Correction
.
Throughout this process, the orchestrator maintains the development state and coordinates the specialized roles.
3.2.1
Intention Alignment
Before development begins, the designer draws on game-design principles and genre conventions to expand requests such as “make a Hollow Knight-style boss fight” into a complete Game Design Document (GDD) that defines gameplay mechanics, progression rules, and numerical systems.
In parallel, the artist uses image-generation models to create concept art that establishes a consistent visual direction for subsequent assets.
After user confirmation, the GDD and concept art form the shared ground truth for all downstream development and evaluation.
During development, any task that introduces or changes a design decision returns to the designer, who drafts it, confirms it with the user, and merges it into the GDD.
3.2.2
Parallel Development
Code Workflow.
Code is implemented by a pipeline of four agents: architect, programmer, auditor, and player.
The orchestrator first decomposes the game into parallel components, retrieves relevant skeletons, modules, and contracts from the self-evolution repository (Section
3.3
) as project priors, and prepares a Product Requirements Document (PRD) that defines the scope and acceptance criteria of each component.
The architect then plans the implementation strategy and its verification procedure, and after the orchestrator approves the plan, the programmer implements it.
The auditor checks the result statically with the engine’s consistency-checking tools and against the design specification.
Finally, the player runs the game through the engine’s runtime interface under frame-synchronous control and uses a vision model to assess whether the rendered result matches the intended appearance.
A sub-task is complete only after it passes both static auditing and runtime play-testing.
Artist Workflow.
The artist agent converts visual requirements from the orchestrator into engine-ready assets.
It invokes image-generation models, including GPT-Image-2
[
31
]
and Nano Banana Pro
[
32
]
, to create the initial artwork, then applies post-processing operations such as background removal and size normalization.
It then registers the processed assets with the engine, recording their paths, dimensions, and usage.
3.2.3
Adversarial Correction
After all sub-tasks are completed, an independent reviewer acts as the final quality gate and evaluates the complete project on
functionality
(whether the game behaves as specified),
visual quality
(asset completeness, stylistic consistency, and screen clarity), and
playability
(e.g., control responsiveness and the clarity of combat feedback).
If the project fails any criterion, the reviewer rejects it with specific reasons, and the orchestrator converts them into new repair tasks; this build-review cycle continues until the project satisfies all acceptance criteria.
The process runs automatically by default, and the orchestrator incorporates any user feedback into subsequent development.
3.3
Training-free Self-Evolution
The AI-native game engine and AAT produce accepted game projects that reflect both agent-side implementation and user feedback.
VibeGame distills reusable experience from these validated projects with a training-free self-evolution mechanism and uses it to initialize future development runs, preserving implicit development knowledge that general-purpose agents lose across independent runs.
We organize the experience into three complementary forms: skeletons, modules, and contracts.
Skeletons.
A skeleton is a runnable project template associated with a particular game type.
It removes project-specific art assets but preserves the code architecture, tuning values, visual proportions, scene flow, and runtime structure of the original project.
Each skeleton also includes error notes and an art pack.
The error notes summarize recurring failures and their verified fixes, while the art pack records reusable visual-production recipes, including asset-generation prompts and post-processing conventions for the corresponding game type.
Modules.
A module is a self-contained behavior script that can be attached to any node (Section
3.1
) and implements functionality reusable across game types.
In addition to the underlying behavior, a module may include self-checking logic that converts previously observed runtime failures into static validation rules executed before the game starts.
Contracts.
A contract is a document that adapts the general AAT workflow to a recurring feature or development pattern.
It specifies the role-specific inputs, outputs, dependencies, and verification criteria required to implement that feature, enabling agents to coordinate through a validated procedure rather than relying only on the generic build-and-review loop.
For example, a map contract defines how the designer specifies map requirements, how the programmer represents the map in project files, how the artist supplies the required assets, and how the auditor and player verify the completed result.
4
Experiments
Figure 4
:
Results by game type and pairwise win rates.
(a) Gain of VibeGame over the strongest baseline of each model, Codex (P2G) for GPT-6.1-Sol and Qwen Code (P2G) for GPT-5.6-Luna, on each game type. (b) Win rate of VibeGame against each GPT-6.1-Sol baseline in the user study (top) and under the GPT-6.1-Sol judge (bottom); each bar stacks the win rates in the four rubric categories (M, D, V, A), and the number at its end is the overall win rate.
Figure 5
:
Qualitative comparison between VibeGame, Codex (PA2G), and Codex (P2G), all using GPT-6.1-Sol.
Left: Sports Skateboard Park. Right: Sports Boxing Gym. Red boxes mark the defects.
4.1
Experiment Setup
Benchmark.
We randomly sample two tasks from each of the 15 game types in GameCraft-Bench
[
11
]
, 30 tasks in total, as our
test set
(Appendix
7
), and adapt them to Phaser
[
27
]
, changing only the engine, the input setting, and a short hint on demo recording, leaving the game descriptions and evaluation rubrics untouched. We then evaluate a wide range of open-source agent harnesses on the test set under the PA2G and P2G settings, giving every harness, including VibeGame, a 24-hour budget per task with its model at the xhigh reasoning effort; in P2G, harnesses without native image generation are given the same image generation model as VibeGame.
Because GPT-5.5
[
33
]
, the judge used by GameCraft-Bench, makes various judgment errors, we use GPT-6.1-Sol
[
34
]
as the judge instead. Appendix
8
gives the full experimental details.
Ablation Settings.
We randomly sample 10 tasks from the test set as the
ablation set
and compare VibeGame with three variants: (1)
w/o Engine
, which removes the AI-native game engine and requires the agents to build on Phaser instead; (2)
w/o AAT
, which removes the adversarial review stage of the agent team, i.e., the auditor, player, and reviewer; and (3)
w/ Experience
, which adds the experience evolved by VibeGame with GPT-6.1-Sol on 5 tasks outside the ablation set to VibeGame with GPT-5.6-Luna.

Main Results.
As shown in Table
1
, under the same underlying model, general coding agents perform similarly to one another in the PA2G setting, with gaps of at most 2.50 points, and GPT-5.6-Luna
[
35
]
does not turn image generation into a visual advantage in the P2G setting.
OpenGame, although designed for game development, does not outperform general coding agents, suggesting that it may not generalize to tasks beyond its built-in templates or adapt well to the demo-recording requirements of GameCraft-Bench.
In contrast, with GPT-5.6-Luna, VibeGame leads in all four categories and improves the overall score over the strongest baseline by 11.70 points, showing that our harness substantially strengthens weaker models.
With the frontier model GPT-6.1-Sol, VibeGame trails Codex (P2G) by less than one point in Core Mechanics and Functional Visuals but leads it by 4.76 and 7.72 points in Content Depth and Art & Presentation, outperforming it by 4.19 points overall.
This suggests that frontier models can already implement core mechanics and reasonable visuals on their own, but still fall short in building games with deep content and polished presentation, which is where VibeGame adds its value.
Across game types (Figure
4
(a)), VibeGame outperforms the strongest baseline of each model on 13 of the 15 types.
User Study.
We further conduct a blind user study with 30 participants of diverse backgrounds, including students from fields such as mathematics and bioinformatics, information technology practitioners, and game enthusiasts. We pair VibeGame with each of the five GPT-6.1-Sol baselines on all 30 tasks, giving 150 pairs, and collect two judgments per pair, 300 in total. In each judgment, a participant reads the game description and the full evaluation rubric of the task, plays the two anonymized games, and picks the better game in each of the four rubric categories and overall. As shown in Figure
4
(b), human preferences broadly agree with the GPT-6.1-Sol judge, whose pairwise results come from comparing the two games’ scores on each task: under both, VibeGame wins against every baseline in every rubric category, with an average overall human win rate of 72.7%.
Ablation Study.
Table
2
reports the effect of the three coupled components. Removing the AI-native engine or the adversarial review roles of AAT lowers the overall score by 10.33 and 4.63 points, respectively, indicating that both the structured project representation with runtime control and the adversarial review substantially help prompt-to-game development. Adding the engine alone to Codex with GPT-6.1-Sol also raises its overall score by 2.69 points (Appendix
12
). Adding the experience evolved by GPT-6.1-Sol to GPT-5.6-Luna raises the overall score by 2.92 points, suggesting that the evolved experience transfers from a stronger model to a weaker one.
Qualitative Analysis.
We select the qualitative cases from GameCraft-Bench (Figure
5
).
The left case is Sports Skateboard Park, where the agent needs to implement a trick system in which the player chains flip, grind, and grab tricks into combos.
VibeGame presents aerial tricks such as board flips in a consistent and appealing visual style, while Codex (PA2G) draws the character and environment with programmatic shapes (i.e., simple shapes drawn in code), which gives the game a crude art style.
Codex (P2G) generates a coherent background, but its user interface (UI) overlaps the character, which is also assembled from programmatic shapes.
The right case is Sports Boxing Gym, where the task requires the opponent to telegraph each attack with a visible tell so that the player can read it and respond.
VibeGame fulfills this requirement with complete attack animations and mechanics that include wind-up tells.
Codex (PA2G) also draws its boxers with programmatic shapes and represents each punch by stretching a rectangular arm, which looks abstract rather than like a punching animation.
Codex (P2G) also produces polished visuals but does not show the opponent’s wind-up.
5
Conclusion
We present VibeGame, a framework for end-to-end prompt-to-game development that integrates an AI-native game engine, an adversarial agent team, and training-free self-evolution.
Under the same underlying model, VibeGame, without any provided assets, outperforms all evaluated agent harnesses; even with the frontier model GPT-6.1-Sol, it improves over the strongest baseline, Codex (P2G), by 4.19 points.
Limitations
While VibeGame delivers strong results across diverse game genres, we recognize that several directions remain open for future work.
First, we focus on 2D games and have not yet validated the framework in more complex 3D scenes or used it to develop complete commercial games that sustain long-term play.
Second, our AI-native design principles are implemented on a web-based 2D engine; bringing them to established engines such as Godot
[
3
]
, so that agents can also operate existing game projects, is a promising extension.

8.1
Setup
Every harness, including VibeGame, has a 24-hour budget per task and runs its model at the xhigh reasoning effort. In the P2G setting, harnesses without a native image generation tool are given GPT-Image-2
[
31
]
, the same image generation model used by VibeGame, as an external tool together with its documentation.
The judge GPT-6.1-Sol runs with medium reasoning effort, and scoring follows the original benchmark (Appendix

). All results are obtained from our own runs and evaluation rather than reused from GameCraft-Bench, because we changed the engine and modified the task instructions.
For w/ Experience, we let VibeGame with GPT-6.1-Sol build and self-evolve on 5 tasks randomly sampled from outside the ablation set, using the task rubrics and the vision-language model (VLM) judge scores in place of user feedback. We then add the evolved artifacts to the initial project of VibeGame with GPT-5.6-Luna and let it build the ablation tasks.

9.1
Game Creation
Game creation starts from a text request and optional reference images and exercises the full loop from intention alignment to project delivery. In this paper, we report results for both text-only and multimodal requests.
9.1.1
Text Input
To test creation driven by a compact text request, we asked the system to build a Sekiro-style 2D boss fight: a retro pixel-art duel recreating the reed-field battle between Sekiro and Genichiro.
The request specified the combat rules in a few sentences: the player can defend, perform frame-perfect deflections, attack, step-dodge, jump, slash in the air, and execute a deathblow once the boss posture is broken; the boss can defend and deflect, and special attacks are made readable through delayed wind-up frames.
The system started from an existing side-scrolling action skeleton, inheriting its scene structure and UI modules.
However, Sekiro’s core is a deflection-posture system entirely different from the skeleton’s simple hit-point-based combat, requiring the system to build the combat layer from scratch: both sides have independent posture gauges, defense distinguishes regular blocking from frame-perfect deflection, boss attacks are divided into blockable normal attacks and perilous attacks requiring specific responses, and a full posture gauge triggers a multi-stage deathblow animation.
The final output comprised 12 scripts, 2 character asset packs, 11 visual effect entities, and 1 UI asset pack.
This case demonstrates how a short request that names a genre convention is expanded into a complete, correctly tuned combat system.
The first row of Figure
9
shows the request and resulting combat sequence.
9.1.2
Multimodal Input
To test multimodal creation, we provided a text request together with an author-created concept image for a Hollow Knight-style 1v1 boss fight.
The text request specified the mechanical scope: the player has a basic attack, a charged attack, a dash, a jump, and an aerial attack, while the boss combines two melee skills with a ranged attack on a side-scrolling arena 1.5x the camera width.
The concept image anchored the character designs, the ruined-cathedral arena, and the overall visual atmosphere, which the generated assets were required to match.
The second row of Figure
9
showcases the multimodal input and resulting game.
We can observe that the delivered slice realizes both sides of this specification.
The boss gates its melee sweep, ground slam, and arcing projectile on the player’s distance, keeps its preferred range, and can be staggered out of idle; the player’s five actions cover the full movement-attack loop, including dash invincibility frames and aerial slashes; hit feedback combines screen shake, flash, and spark particles, with mask-style health icons and a full-width boss bar completing the heads-up display (HUD).
All character and arena art was generated to match the concept image, preserving its silhouette language and cold palette.
This case demonstrates how text can specify gameplay rules while the concept image anchors visual identity.
9.2
Game Edit
The next cases begin from accepted projects and alter different layers of the existing game.
Specifically, in this paper, we report three types of editing:
(1) intellectual property (IP) transfer that changes visual assets while preserving mechanics;
(2) genre transfer that replaces the central gameplay while preserving visual identity;
and (3) rule transfer that changes the roles of existing characters while reusing their abilities and animations.
9.2.1
IP Transfer
Starting from a completed side-scrolling boss fight project, we ask the system to replace the entire game’s visual theme with a Kung Fu Panda IP.
The system regenerates all art assets (including characters, effects, UI, and background), and then adjusts configurations for the new sprite size and frame counts. The delivered project retains the original combat logic, illustrating an edit concentrated on the asset and configuration layers. See top row of Figure
10
.
This validates the code-asset decoupling in the engine: when the project structure is well designed, IP transfer is accomplished primarily through asset replacement, with no need to rewrite core logic.
9.2.2
Genre Transfer
Starting from a completed turn-based card game project, we ask the system to change the core gameplay from card strategy to a real-time action boss fight.
This is a deep transformation: the turn-based card-playing mechanic was completely replaced with real-time melee, dodging, and shooting, while the system preserved the original project’s cyberpunk visual style and character designs.
Unlike IP transfer where only assets change, genre transfer requires the system to judge what can be preserved and what must be rewritten, demonstrating the system’s ability to perform selective deep modification while maintaining overall consistency (Figure
10
, middle row).
9.2.3
Rule Transfer
Starting from the Hollow Knight-style boss fight created from multimodal input in Section
9.1.2
, we tested the system’s ability to handle unconventional creative requests by asking it to swap the player and boss roles, requiring only that each character keep its existing abilities and animations.
In that source game, the player controlled a small horned warrior, while the antlered boss moved autonomously with a melee slam, a lunge, and a ranged thorn volley.
The edit enlarges the former player character into an AI-driven boss and shrinks the former boss into the player-controlled character, so the player now wields the former boss’s moveset while the former player character fights autonomously with its own dash, charged slash, and aerial attack.
This request is not a simple asset exchange: the system must convert the former boss AI into a player control scheme, turn the former player’s manual controls into autonomous boss AI, rebind inputs, and remap the HUD and win/lose flow, all without adding any new art or moves.
Our system completed this transformation (Figure
10
, bottom row), demonstrating that it can restructure gameplay roles in response to non-standard edit requests.

article.headline: VibeGame：从提示词生成可玩2D游戏
article.lede: 南京大学等提出VibeGame，用AI原生2D引擎和对抗智能体团队，把提示词变成可运行、可编辑的游戏项目。
article.problem: 游戏开发需要同时协调代码、场景、素材、动画、物理和配置，还要通过实际试玩验证整体行为。现有LLM智能体多把运行检查留到最终评估，或只验证游戏能否构建和启动，难以发现只有在游玩中才暴露的问题。
article.method: VibeGame把项目状态表示为带模式校验的结构化文本，并提供逐帧同步的运行时控制，让智能体暂停、步进、注入动作和截图检查。其八角色对抗智能体团队把实现与审计、试玩、评审分离，并在项目通过后以免训练自进化提炼骨架、模块和协作契约。
article.results: 在GameCraft-Bench子集30个任务上，以GPT-6.1-Sol为评审时，VibeGame（P2G）总体得分72.99，高于最强基线Codex（P2G）的68.80，提升4.19分；用GPT-5.6-Luna时总体49.99，比最强基线38.29高11.70分。消融显示去掉AI原生引擎总体从53.45降至43.12，去掉对抗评审角色降至48.82；加入GPT-6.1-Sol进化经验后GPT-5.6-Luna升至56.37（+2.92）。30人盲测共300次判断，总体人类胜率平均72.7%，15类游戏中13类超过各自模型最强基线。
article.why_it_matters: 它把“可运行、可检查、可迭代”的游戏项目作为智能体输出，并用运行时试玩补足静态代码检查看不到的问题，为游戏生成基准提供可复现的工程路径。
article.limitations: 仅在2D游戏上验证，未覆盖复杂3D场景或可长期游玩的完整商业游戏；作者也观察到连续开发不同类型游戏时，自进化积累的经验反而可能拉低智能体表现。此外，评审模型从GPT-5.5换为GPT-6.1-Sol会改变绝对分数和排名，且因引擎改为Phaser，结果不能与原始GameCraft-Bench直接比较。
article.figure_caption_zh: VibeGame从文本或多模态提示生成并编辑多种2D游戏类型的示例。

page_papers.title: AskStream: When and What to Ask Proactively under Uncertainty in Streaming Video Understanding
page_papers.abstract: Recent advances in multimodal large language models have increased interest in interaction paradigms for video understanding. The evolution from offline to streaming and proactive interaction has gradually shifted models from passive responders toward more proactive agents that can decide when to answer. However, existing proactive paradigms typically assume that the information required to answer a query is complete, leaving models to only wait or answer. In the real world, however, information is often incomplete due to uncertainty from either the video or the user. In proactive paradigms, such uncertainty can cause the model to wait forever or generate highly hallucinatory responses. We therefore argue that proactive interaction should be redefined with a third action: ask, allowing models to actively ask for missing information. To study when and what models should ask before answering, we introduce AskStream, the first multi-turn benchmark spanning video and user uncertainty for streaming video understanding, with four task categories and eight subtasks. It contains 438 videos with 2,714 manually annotated frame-level time windows across three types: wait, ask, and answer. Across both multiple-choice and open-ended settings, even the strongest model attains only 52.18% on our proposed Ask-F1 metric, highlighting substantial limitations in proactive information seeking under uncertainty.

article.headline: 视频理解模型不会主动提问，流式模型近乎失效
article.lede: 新基准 AskStream 把「提问」纳入动作空间：最强离线模型 Ask-F1 为 52.18%，流式模型仅 7.22%
article.problem: 现有的主动式视频交互范式默认「回答问题所需的信息一定会在流中出现」，因此模型的动作空间只有等待和回答两种。但现实中的不确定性既可能来自视频（画面模糊、证据缺失），也可能来自用户（指代不清），这会让模型无限等待或强行编造答案。作者因此主张把「提问」作为第三个动作引入，研究模型应当在何时、就什么内容发问。
article.method: 论文提出 AskStream 评测框架，把交互动作空间从「等待/回答」扩展为「等待/回答/提问」，并区分来自视频和来自用户的两类不确定性。评测分为离线与流式两种设定，覆盖多选与开放式两种回答形式，指标为 Ask-F1 以及分别衡量提问与回答的子分数 S_ask、S_ans；此外还用逐步加入 oracle 信息的消融实验，定位模型在何时提问、问什么、何时回答这三个阶段中哪一环出错。
article.results: 多选设定下，离线模型中 Gemini-3.8 Flash 表现相对最好，在 KVEM、WUQ、UPC 三个子任务上分别为 37.17%、43.10%、81.36%，总体 Ask-F1 为 52.18%，但其 S_ask 明显低于 S_ans，说明提问是瓶颈；流式主动模型在多数子任务上得零分，表现较好的 AURA 也只有 7.22% Ask-F1。开放式设定整体明显下降，Gemini-3.8 Flash 的 Ask-F1 为 29.19%（S_ask 23.34%、S_ans 38.97%），AURA 仅 4.01%。在不确定性分析中，Qwen3.5 9B 在 78 个视频的 130 个五选一事件上，输入模糊时准确率为 42.3%，在问出关键证据后升至 62.3%，接近完全清晰输入的 63.1%。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「主动提问」从概念口号变成可量化评测的能力维度，并用数据说明当前模型在信息缺失时基本不会求助，这对构建需要长时间监控、异常告警等真实场景的视频智能体是明确的短板信号。
article.limitations: 这是一篇以基准和评测为主的工作，论文没有提出能提升提问能力的新方法，因此只诊断问题、不解决问题。不确定性分析只在 Qwen3.5 9B 上、基于 78 个视频的 130 个事件完成，规模有限；开放式评测使用 Gemini-3.8 Flash 作裁判，作者仅用 300 轮人工标注做一致性校验，绝对分数的可靠性仍需谨慎看待。
article.figure_caption_zh: 交互范式的演进：AskStream 在原有的「等待」与「回答」之外加入「提问」动作，使模型在作答前能主动向视频或用户索取缺失信息。

page_papers.title: Your LR Schedule May Not Be Principled: Effective Learning Rate Scheduling in Weight-Normalized Training
page_papers.abstract: Weight-normalized (WN) training is emerging as a compelling alternative to conventional weight decay (WD), with recent studies reporting substantial pretraining loss gains. We show that these gains are driven primarily by the induced effective learning rate (ELR) trajectory rather than by normalization alone. Matching ELR trajectories largely collapses the training loss dynamics of WN and WD. Schedule design should therefore target ELR rather than the nominal learning rate (LR) alone. Building on this principle, we propose AIR (Affine Inverse-square-Root decay), which combines a theoretically derived $1/\sqrt{t}$ decay with an affine adjustment to satisfy prescribed peak and terminal LRs over a finite training horizon. We further identify late-stage ELR scheduling as a key source of its gains, because a shared late schedule attenuates the effect of earlier LR choices. Experiments on 128 B-token Mixture-of-Experts pretraining demonstrate that AIR outperforms cosine and other candidate schedules in training loss, downstream performance, and hyperparameter robustness, reducing terminal training loss by approximately 0.01 relative to cosine at matched cumulative LR. Applying the same ELR trajectory to WD reproduces the corresponding training dynamics, showing that the benefits extend beyond fixed-norm training and establishing ELR as the principled scheduling object.

We show that these gains are driven primarily by the induced effective learning rate (ELR) trajectory rather than by normalization alone. Matching ELR trajectories largely collapses the training loss dynamics of WN and WD. Schedule design should therefore target ELR rather than the nominal learning rate (LR) alone. Building on this principle, we propose AIR (Affine Inverse-square-Root decay), which combines a theoretically derived $1/\sqrt{t}$ decay with an affine adjustment to satisfy prescribed peak and terminal LRs over a finite training horizon. We further identify late-stage ELR scheduling as a key source of its gains, because a shared late schedule attenuates the effect of earlier LR choices. Experiments on 128 B-token Mixture-of-Experts pretraining demonstrate that AIR outperforms cosine and other candidate schedules in training loss, downstream performance, and hyperparameter robustness, reducing terminal training loss by approximately 0.01 relative to cosine at matched cumulative LR. article.headline: WN 预训练收益主要来自有效学习率轨迹
article.lede: 匹配有效学习率轨迹后，WN 与权重衰减的训练损失动态大幅重合；作者据此提出 AIR 调度。
article.problem: 权重归一化（WN）被视为权重衰减（WD）的替代方案，近期研究报告了可观的预训练损失收益。但这些收益究竟来自归一化本身，还是来自其诱导的有效学习率（ELR）轨迹，并不清楚。若只关注名义学习率，调度设计可能错过真正起作用的变量。
article.method: 作者通过匹配 ELR 轨迹比较 WN 与 WD，发现两者的训练损失动态大幅重合。据此提出 AIR（Affine Inverse-square-Root decay），将理论推导的 1/√t 衰减与仿射调整结合，在有限训练时程内满足指定的峰值和终端学习率。作者还识别出后期 ELR 调度是收益关键，因为共享的后期调度会削弱早期学习率选择的影响。
article.results: 在 128B token 的 Mixture-of-Experts 预训练中，AIR 在训练损失、下游性能和超参鲁棒性上优于 cosine 及其他候选调度；在累计学习率匹配时，终端训练损失相对 cosine 降低约 0.01。
article.why_it_matters: 若 ELR 是更原则性的调度对象，学习率调度器的设计、比较与复现都应以 ELR 为中心，而不是只看名义学习率；这也为把 WN 的收益迁移到 WD 提供了可操作路径。
article.limitations: ELR 匹配使损失动态大幅重合，但并未完全重合，材料也未拆解归一化本身可能残留的作用。实验只覆盖 128B-token 的 MoE 预训练，跨模型规模、架构与多种子方差的结果尚未给出。

page_papers.title: Intrinsic Distribution Matching
page_papers.abstract: One-step and few-step text-to-image generation must accurately render the details specified in the prompt despite limited opportunities for refinement. Distribution matching distillation (DMD) uses score differences to bring the generated distribution closer to a reference distribution. Following prior work, we estimate this difference with internal velocity branches, avoiding a separate fake-score network. We ask whether an explicit moment constraint improves this learned score supervision. A decomposition of the reverse-KL field into a Gaussian moment component and a non-Gaussian residual identifies statistics that can be constrained explicitly. We introduce Intrinsic Distribution Matching (IDM), which retains the full DMD correction and matches feature means and per-coordinate standard deviations using the generator's exponential-moving-average (EMA) copy, requiring no external feature encoder. Experiments use full-parameter and low-rank adaptation (LoRA) tuning on Z-Image-Turbo 6B and Qwen-Image 20B. At two network evaluations, IDM reaches 94.25% and 90.20% on Chinese and English LongText-Bench, the highest scores among the compared methods at this budget. Controlled ablations show gains from the added moment loss, while generator EMA features perform competitively with an external DINOv2 encoder across the five reported metrics. Code is available at https://github.com/inclusionAI/IDM.
page_papers.content:
Abstract
One-step and few-step text-to-image generation must accurately render the details specified in the prompt despite limited opportunities for refinement.
Distribution matching distillation (DMD) uses score differences to bring the generated distribution closer to a reference distribution.
Following prior work, we estimate this difference with internal velocity branches, avoiding a separate fake-score network.
We ask whether an explicit moment constraint improves this learned score supervision.
A decomposition of the reverse-KL field into a Gaussian moment component and a non-Gaussian residual identifies statistics that can be constrained explicitly.

Introduction
Diffusion and flow-matching models produce high-quality images, but their repeated network evaluations impose substantial inference cost
(
Ho et al., 2020
;
Song et al., 2020
;
Lipman et al., 2022
;
Liu et al., 2023
)
. One and few-step generation reduces this cost by learning a much shorter sampling process. The challenge is to accurately render the details specified in the prompt using only one or a few sampling steps. Long-text rendering makes this challenge concrete: many characters must remain legible and correct within a coherent image
(
Geng et al., 2025b
;
Wu et al., 2025a
)
. It therefore provides a demanding test of whether fast generation retains detailed conditional information.

article.lede: 论文把内部DMD损失与EMA特征空间的矩匹配结合，试图在一步/少步文生图中保留提示细节。
article.problem: 一步和少步文生图必须在很少的细化机会下准确呈现提示指定的细节，长文本渲染尤其能暴露这一难点。DMD用score差把生成分布拉向参考分布，但显式矩约束能否改善这种学到的score监督仍不清楚。
article.method: 作者将reverse-KL场分解为高斯矩分量与非高斯残差，从中识别可显式约束的统计量。方法沿用内部velocity分支估计score差，避免单独的fake-score网络，并在生成器的EMA特征空间加入特征矩损失，与内部DMD损失联合训练。
article.results: 实验在单张A100（BF16）上报告吞吐（batch=10）和延迟（batch=1），并比较约100-NFE的Z-Image基线与8-NFE的Z-Image-Turbo；两个提示在1和2 NFE下评估，GenEval按类别与总体打分。节选未给出GenEval、FID、CLIP的具体数值，论文未给出具体数字。
article.why_it_matters: 若显式矩约束确实补足DMD的监督，少步生成有望在降低推理成本的同时改善长文本细节。它也为分布匹配蒸馏提供了加入统计约束的训练思路。
article.limitations: 节选缺少GenEval、FID、CLIP等表格数值，系统比较和消融的增益无法独立核验；此外，协方差收缩命题只适用于实现条件均值的回归器，不能据此断言一步生成器普遍低估方差。

page_papers.title: Q-Learning with Scalar Adjoint Matching
page_papers.abstract: Flow policies capture rich and diverse action distributions, and fine-tuning them with off-policy RL to improve beyond the demonstrations has drawn growing interest. However, fine-tuning a flow policy against a learned value function is not trivial, because the policy generates its action over many flow steps. Adjoint matching offers a principled way to update the flow model itself by propagating value information from the final action back to each flow step, but it requires a vector--Jacobian product through the policy at every step, a cost that grows with the number of flow steps and the policy size. We observe that the batch-averaged velocity Jacobian of pretrained flow policies concentrates on its diagonal. Motivated by this finding, we derive a closed-form scalar adjoint that scales the value gradient at the final action by the flow time, eliminating the per-step vector--Jacobian products. We further find that controlling the critic's value at policy-generated actions is particularly important under the scalar adjoint. Based on these findings, we propose Q-learning with Scalar Adjoint Matching (SQAM), which combines the scalar adjoint with a value penalty at those actions. SQAM's gains concentrate on the four hardest OGBench domains, where its success rate exceeds that of the strongest baseline in each domain by 18 to 35 percentage points. To test whether SQAM extends to large pretrained policies, we also fine-tune a vision-language-action policy on a real bimanual robot. SQAM improves over supervised fine-tuning on all three tasks.

Abstract
Flow policies capture rich and diverse action distributions, and fine-tuning them with off-policy RL to improve beyond the demonstrations has drawn growing interest. However, fine-tuning a flow policy against a learned value function is not trivial, because the policy generates its action over many flow steps. Adjoint matching offers a principled way to update the flow model itself by propagating value information from the final action back to each flow step, but it requires a vector–Jacobian product through the policy at every step, a cost that grows with the number of flow steps and the policy size. We observe that the batch-averaged velocity Jacobian of pretrained flow policies concentrates on its diagonal. Motivated by this finding, we derive a closed-form scalar adjoint that scales the value gradient at the final action by the flow time, eliminating the per-step vector–Jacobian products. We further find that controlling the critic’s value at policy-generated actions is particularly important under the scalar adjoint. Based on these findings, we propose Q-learning with Scalar Adjoint Matching (SQAM), which combines the scalar adjoint with a value penalty at those actions. SQAM’s gains concentrate on the four hardest OGBench domains, where its success rate exceeds that of the strongest baseline in each domain by 18 to 35 percentage points. To test whether SQAM extends to large pretrained policies, we also fine-tune a vision-language-action policy on a real bimanual robot. SQAM improves over supervised fine-tuning on all three tasks.

Introduction
Flow policies represent rich and multimodal action distributions, and they have become a common
policy class for offline and offline-to-online RL
(
Park et al., 2025b
;
Li and Levine, 2026
;
Dong et al., 2026c
;
Chi et al., 2023
)
as well as the backbone of recent large pretrained robot policies
(
Intelligence et al., 2025b
;
Bjorck et al., 2025
)
.
Improving such a policy beyond the data it was trained on calls for fine-tuning it with off-policy RL
against a learned action-value function
(
Intelligence et al., 2025a
;
Wang et al., 2026
;
Dong et al., 2026a
;
Xu et al., 2026
;
Li et al., 2025b
;
Chen et al., 2025
)
.
However, fine-tuning a flow policy to maximize a learned value function is not a trivial problem because of its multiple sampling procedure
(
Park et al., 2025b
;
Zhang et al., 2026
)
. Most methods therefore freeze the policy and work outside it, adding a separately learned residual to the actions it produces
(
Dong et al., 2026b
;
Xiao et al., 2026
)
or learning with RL which input noise to feed the frozen policy
(
Wagenmaker et al., 2025
)
, which leaves the pretrained policy intact during training. The improvement then rests on a separately learned component rather than on the generative model itself, so it is either bounded by what the frozen policy can express or forfeits the expressiveness of the flow policy. On the other hand, adjoint matching
(
Domingo-Enrich et al., 2025
;
Li and Levine, 2026
;
Dong et al., 2026c
)
provides a theoretically grounded alternative for directly updating the flow model with value functions. It propagates value information from the final action back to each flow step to guide the model’s updates. However, this requires a vector–Jacobian product through the policy at every step, so the computational cost grows with the number of flow steps and policy size.
In this work, we observe that the batch-averaged velocity Jacobian of a pretrained flow policy concentrates on its diagonal (
Figure
2
). This suggests that the vector–Jacobian product adjoint matching
pays for at every flow step may not be necessary. Inspired by this finding, we approximate the
Jacobian by a scalar multiple of the identity, under which the propagation admits a closed form that
scales the value gradient at the final action by the flow time (
Proposition
1
). We call this
the scalar adjoint. It needs a single critic gradient at the sampled action and no vector–Jacobian
product through the policy, and
Section
4.2
shows that it preserves the qualitative trends
of the exact propagation.
We further find that the effectiveness of the scalar adjoint depends on the value-learning scheme. We investigate this dependence and identify the critic’s value at policy-generated actions as particularly important. Our regularization ablations isolate this dependency. Methods that regulate the
critic at these actions improve performance, while methods that act only on dataset
(
Kostrikov et al., 2022
)
or action distance
(
Tarasov et al., 2023
)
provide little improvement
(
Section
4.3
). Based on these findings, we propose
Q-learning with Scalar Adjoint Matching
(SQAM), which combines the scalar adjoint with a value penalty at policy-generated actions.
Through experiments on the
50
50
OGBench
(
Park et al., 2025a
)
tasks, SQAM outperforms prior methods in both offline RL and offline-to-online RL, and the gains concentrate where the benchmark is hardest. On the four hardest domains it adds
18
18
to
35
35
percentage points of offline success rate over the best
baseline in each, and it reaches
75
%
75\%
against
68
%
68\%
for the strongest baseline overall. To assess whether SQAM extends to large pretrained policies, we apply it to offline-to-online RL fine-tuning of a vision-language-action model
(
Kim et al., 2026b
)
on a real-world bimanual robot
(
Rainbow Robotics, 2024
)
equipped with two
20
20
-DoF dexterous hands
(
Wuji Technology, 2025
)
. We observe that SQAM clearly improves over supervised fine-tuning on all three manipulation tasks, while residual fine-tuning
(
Dong et al., 2026a
)
struggles in the same setting.

Comparison between Adjoints
Figure
4
explains why the scalar adjoint works even though it approximates the exact
adjoint. The approximation preserves the two properties the update relies on. In magnitude, both
adjoints contract in the same way as the flow time approaches zero, so the regression target in
Equation
2
has a similar magnitude at each flow step under either adjoint. In direction, the scalar
adjoint stays positively aligned with the exact adjoint at every flow time. These two properties allow
the scalar adjoint to stand in for the exact adjoint, but they do not make the two identical. The angle
between them is larger on the two manipulation domains than on the two locomotion domains, and these
are exactly the domains where the scalar adjoint alone underperforms (
Section
3.2
). Since
the scalar adjoint relies directly on the critic’s gradient, this correspondence led us to examine the
role of the value learning scheme in this framework, which
Section
4.3
presents.

5
Related work
Propagating value to intermediate flow steps.
A flow policy generates its action over many flow
steps, while the critic evaluates only the final action. Using the critic to steer the flow therefore requires propagating its value to each intermediate step, and existing methods differ mainly in how they do
so
(
Lee et al., 2026
)
. The most common approach evaluates the critic at a
Tweedie posterior estimate of the final action, and it is used for guidance at test
time
(
Chung et al., 2023
;
Kim et al., 2025
;
Zhou et al., 2026
)
.
Another line avoids the approximation and feeds the intermediate action to the critic directly, either
by matching the policy’s score to the critic’s action gradient at the intermediate
action
(
Psenka et al., 2024
)
or by learning a separate value at each noise
level
(
Oberai et al., 2026
;
Doo et al., 2026
)
. Adjoint
matching
(
Domingo-Enrich et al., 2025
;
Li and Levine, 2026
;
Dong et al., 2026c
;
Bergmeister et al., 2026
)
gives a theoretically
grounded answer, propagating the value gradient back to each flow step through the lean adjoint ODE.
For test-time guidance rather than fine-tuning, dropping the Jacobian has also been found to outperform
backpropagating through the exact Jacobian
(
Zhou et al., 2026
)
.
Critic regularization.
Many value learning schemes regularize the critic, and they differ
in where the regularization acts. CQL penalizes the critic’s value at the actions the policy prefers relative to the data
(
Kumar et al., 2020
)
, IQL fits a state value by expectile regression and trains the critic by TD regression toward it, using only dataset actions
(
Kostrikov et al., 2022
)
, and ReBRAC subtracts an action-distance penalty from the bootstrap target
(
Tarasov et al., 2023
)
. Fisher-BRC penalizes the action
gradient of the critic’s offset from a behavior model
(
Kostrikov et al., 2021
)
, which is close to the gradient-norm penalty we compare in
Section
4.3
, and Cal-QL calibrates the critic against a reference policy for offline-to-online fine-tuning
(
Nakamoto et al., 2023
)
.
Offline-to-online RL.
Pretraining a policy and a critic on offline data and then fine-tuning
them online is a standard recipe for sample-efficient
RL
(
Ball et al., 2023
;
Hester et al., 2018
;
Hu et al., 2024
;
Kostrikov et al., 2022
;
Kumar et al., 2020
;
Lei et al., 2024
;
Luo et al., 2024
;
Nair et al., 2021
;
Nakamoto et al., 2023
;
Rajeswaran et al., 2018
;
Vecerik et al., 2018
)
.
A central challenge is the distribution shift at the transition, which destabilizes the value
function and can make the policy forget what it learned
offline
(
Ball et al., 2023
;
Nakamoto et al., 2023
;
Wołczyk et al., 2024
)
.
6
Conclusion
We introduced SQAM, which fine-tunes flow policies with off-policy RL without a vector–Jacobian
product through the policy. Motivated by the diagonal structure of the batch-averaged velocity
Jacobian, it replaces the exact adjoint with a closed-form scalar adjoint and pairs it with a value
penalty at the policy-generated actions. SQAM improves most on the four hardest OGBench domains
and extends to a vision-language-action policy on a real robot.
Our results also suggest a broader point. A rough approximation of the adjoint suffices, while the
value learning scheme largely determines how well it performs. The bottleneck of
off-policy RL with flow policies may therefore lie less in the policy update than in the critic. We
hope this encourages further work on value learning for flow policies.

Ethics statement
This work fine-tunes robot policies with reinforcement learning in simulation and on a robot in a
controlled laboratory setting. The real-robot experiments involve no human subjects and no personal
data, and an operator supervised the robot throughout. As with any method that improves a policy
against a learned value function, deployment beyond a supervised setting calls for the usual
safeguards.
AI use statement
We used generative AI tools to assist with writing, editing, and routine coding and plotting. We did
not use them to generate research ideas, experimental results, or claims. The authors reviewed all
AI-assisted text and code and take full responsibility for the content of this paper.

Appendix E
Real-robot experiments: RB-Y1 with Wuji Hand 2
This appendix documents the real-robot experiments on a dual-arm RB-Y1
humanoid
(
Rainbow Robotics, 2024
)
equipped with two Wuji Hand 2 dexterous hands
(
Wuji Technology, 2025
)
. For
each of three manipulation tasks we follow the same pipeline: (i) behavior cloning (BC) of a
vision-language-action base policy on teleoperated demonstrations, (ii) collection of 30 rollout
episodes of the BC policy on the robot, (iii) offline RL for 15K steps on the demonstrations plus these
30 BC rollout episodes, (iv) online RL for a further 10K steps that continues from the offline
checkpoint while the robot collects new episodes, and (v) a 30-episode evaluation of every checkpoint.
The same protocol is run for our method (SQAM) and for the EXPO-FT
baseline
(
Dong et al., 2026a
)
.
E.1
Platform, observations and actions
Figure 9
:
Hardware setup: RB-Y1 humanoid with a Wuji Hand 2 on each wrist
and a head-mounted ZED Mini stereo camera.
Hardware.
We use a Rainbow Robotics RB-Y1
(
Rainbow Robotics, 2024
)
dual-arm humanoid with a 20-DoF Wuji
Hand 2
(
Wuji Technology, 2025
)
mounted on each wrist. The experiments use 54 of its degrees of freedom, the two 7-DoF arms and the
two 20-DoF hands, for bimanual tabletop manipulation. The torso and neck stay at fixed joint positions, and
the mobile base is not used. A single Stereolabs ZED Mini stereo camera
(
Stereolabs, 2018
)
mounted on the
head provides the visual input (
Figure
9
).
Observation space.
At every policy query the observation has three parts. The first is two ego-centric RGB images, the
left and right views of the ZED Mini stereo pair, captured at 30 Hz and resized to
192
×
320
192\times 320
. The
second is a 62-dimensional proprioceptive vector of measured joint positions. The third is the task instruction
(
Table
6
).
Action space.
Actions are absolute joint-position targets. The base policy predicts an action chunk of 24 steps, and
its first 16 steps are executed. RL acts only on these
16
16
executed steps and on the 54 arm and
hand joints. SQAM optimizes this sub-chunk by
updating the action head of the base policy, whereas EXPO-FT keeps the base policy frozen and adds a
residual to it through its edit policy.
Control loop.
The robot runs at a nominal control rate of 30 Hz and executes the policy synchronously. At each
policy query the current observation is sent to the actor and the returned 16 step chunk of
joint-position targets is executed step by step. A new observation is taken and the next chunk is
requested only after the chunk has been completed.

Appendix H
Limitations and future work
We see three directions that this work leaves open.
Value learning for flow policies.
Our results suggest that the value learning scheme largely
determines how well the scalar adjoint performs, and SQAM addresses this with a value penalty added
to a standard critic. A value learning method designed for flow policies from the ground up may make
this dependence more reliable than a penalty on top of an existing critic.
Multi-task fine-tuning.
Updating the generative policy itself, rather than a separately
learned component, should matter most when a single policy serves many tasks. Our real-robot experiments
fine-tune the policy on each task separately. Fine-tuning a single policy across many tasks, as in
Wang et al. (2026)
, would test this benefit more directly.
Why the Jacobian concentrates on its diagonal.
We observe that the batch-averaged velocity
Jacobian of pretrained flow policies concentrates on its diagonal on every domain we measured, but we
do not explain why. A theoretical analysis of when this structure arises would clarify the conditions
under which the scalar adjoint applies.

article.headline: SQAM：标量伴随匹配微调流策略
article.lede: 把流策略的精确伴随近似为标量形式，省去每步向量-雅可比积，并在OGBench最难任务和真实双臂机器人上验证。
article.problem: 流策略能表达多模态动作，但用离策略强化学习微调并不容易：策略要经过多步采样才产生动作，而critic只评价最终动作。伴随匹配可把价值梯度回传到每个流步，却要在每步计算向量-雅可比积，成本随流步数和策略规模增长。
article.method: 作者观察到预训练流策略的批平均速度雅可比集中在对角线上，于是把雅可比近似为标量乘单位阵，得到闭式标量伴随：只用最终动作处的critic梯度乘以流时间。进一步在策略自己生成的动作上给critic加价值惩罚，构成SQAM。
article.results: 在OGBench 50个任务、8个随机种子、离线1M步设置下，SQAM总体成功率75%，高于最强基线TRQAM的68%；在四个最难域上比各域最强基线高18到35个百分点，其中cube-quadruple从19%提到54%。真实双臂机器人上，SQAM离线到在线后在三个任务上分别成功25/30、15/30、13/30，SFT为15/30、7/30、4/30。
article.why_it_matters: 它说明流策略的强化学习微调未必要精确回传每步雅可比，粗略的标量伴随已够用，瓶颈可能更多在critic的价值学习。
article.limitations: 标量伴随依赖“批平均雅可比近似对角”的经验观察，论文未解释该结构何时成立；价值惩罚系数需逐域调，cube-double上还会降低离线表现，真实机器人也只验证了三个单任务。
article.figure_caption_zh: 三个真实机器人操作任务：翻塑料袋、把吸管放进杯子、把水果放进锅并盖上盖子。

figure.caption: Overview of the three real-world manipulation tasks. From top to bottom: flipping a plastic bag, placing a straw in a cup, and placing fruit in a pot and closing the lid. Each row illustrates the task progression from left to right.

page_papers.title: Honeycomb-Surfels: Compact Hexagonal Primitives for Efficient Scene Rendering and Reconstruction
page_papers.abstract: Novel view synthesis and 3D reconstruction have advanced rapidly with radiance fields and splatting, yet their memory and computational demands limit their use in resource-constrained settings. We introduce Hexels: novel planar hexagonal surface elements with a first-order spatial color field for efficient 3D scene and 2D image representation. Hexels exploit locally planar regions with smoothly varying appearance using fewer, larger primitives. Their hexagonal support provides an area- and boundary-efficient domain, while the local color field captures appearance variation within each primitive. Across 34 scenes, Hexels improve PSNR over memory-matched 2DGS by 4.53-7.38 dB across datasets while requiring lower training VRAM. We further ablate Hexels by showing that per primitive, Hexels outperform 2DGS by upto 4.74 dB while using lower training VRAM and having 2.31 times faster FPS. Even in unconstrained settings, Hexels offers complementary quality-memory trade-offs. For efficient 3D surface reconstruction, Hexels reduce error by 28.9% compared with memory-matched 2DGS across 15 DTU scans. On 6 Tanks and Temples surface scenes, Hexels achieves the highest mean F1 among compared methods (34.38%, versus 31.72% for 2DGS). We further also show that Hexels, as a general primitive, improves 2D image representation over Image-GS. Hexels push the Pareto frontier on the quality-efficiency trade-off of surface-aligned primitives.

Abstract
Novel view synthesis and 3D reconstruction have advanced rapidly with
radiance fields and splatting, yet their memory and computational demands
limit their use in resource-constrained settings. We introduce

Introduction
Novel view synthesis and 3D reconstruction have progressed rapidly,
from neural radiance fields
[
25
]
to explicit Gaussian
primitives that render in real time
[
18
]
to surface aligned planar primitives like 2DGS
[
14

[
13

These methods differ in geometry, but all face the same question: how much
of the scene can one primitive represent, and at what cost? This has led to the search for an overarching universal primitive which is efficient, expressive, and retains high geometric fidelity. This is even more important in resource-constrained settings, where efficiency includes not only rendering speed and model size but also the memory required during training.
Previous methods have often traded one aspect for another. For example, conventional Gaussian and triangle splats typically represent one view-conditioned color per primitive, so spatial variation emerges through many overlapping elements, leading to large
overdraw
. Others like BBSplat
[
33
]
add
per-primitive textures, or use shared neural appearance fields like NeST
[
39
]
and

Nexels
[
30

.
These methods increase per-element capacity, but move complexity into
textures, grids, or decoders. In contrast, we target the entire quality–efficiency trade-off at the primitive itself. For resource-constrained settings, this efficiency includes not only rendering
speed and model size, but also the memory required during training.
At constrained representation budgets, we seek a balance between geometric fidelity and appearance expressivity. Since agreement with training images alone does not guarantee accurate geometry
[
36
]
, we therefore target both surface reconstruction accuracy and novel-view rendering quality within a compact surface primitive.
We are motivated by the idea that natural images and scenes are highly structured: large regions are often locally planar with smoothly varying appearance. An efficient surface primitive should therefore be able to exploit this underlying structure, wherever possible, and do so in a compact and self-contained manner.

Method

Experiments
We evaluate novel-view synthesis under matched model memory, matched
primitive budgets and native baseline settings. As our focus is on fundamental parameter-based efficiency, all Hexels results do not utilize any post-quantization or compression. For initial runtime compression analysis, refer to Appendix

Fixed configurations retain the initial population; densified configurations
use mixed clone/split growth and contribution-based pruning, with a 2M limit.

Triangle Splatting, and MeshSplatting - provides the closest comparison to
Hexels, as these methods use explicit surface-aligned primitives without

among the original papers introducing the compared methods.

Resource-constrained reconstruction.
Compact, fixed-population Hexels retain high reconstruction quality while
requiring little model memory and training VRAM and supporting fast rendering.
These gains arise directly from the primitive and do not rely on texture
atlases, neural decoders, pruning, or quantization. This makes Hexels well
suited to reconstruction and rendering on memory-limited and edge devices.
Pruning and quantization remain optional extensions that could further reduce
deployment storage.
We have also developed an efficient renderer that directly evaluates the same
Hexel representation used during training, without baking or conversion to a
separate deployment representation. We will release it together with the
training code. This provides a direct path toward on-device NVS and surface
reconstruction, where captured images and reconstructed scene data can remain
local to the device.

Conclusion
We introduced Hexels, a general surface primitive, for 2D and 3D, that exploits the local structure of the data it represents: hexagonal support efficiently covers
coherent surface regions, while a first-order spatial color field models
appearance variation within each primitive. Across our three 3D benchmarks,
Hexels establish a new quality–efficiency frontier among the evaluated surface-aligned representations, improving PSNR by up to 7.38 dB at
matched model memory, using lower peak training VRAM and
up to 2
×
\times
less learned state at matched primitive count, while rendering up
to 2.31
×
\times
faster than 2DGS. The same primitive also performs strongly
for memory-constrained surface reconstruction and directly generalizes to
efficient 2D image representation. Hexels therefore move efficiency into the
primitive itself, opening a path toward high-quality novel-view synthesis
and explicit surface reconstruction on edge and resource-constrained
hardware.
Limitations and Future Work.
A first-order color model cannot represent arbitrary texture within a
single primitive. High-frequency or uncorrelated appearance requires
smaller primitives or a richer color model, reducing the expected benefit
of exploiting local smoothness. Sparse initialization can also leave parts of a scene
poorly covered, and the independent surface cells do not form a watertight
mesh. Sharper footprints do not by themselves prevent sampling artifacts,
especially at small projected sizes or grazing views.
Hexels does not outperform every baseline on every metric;
the appendix provides the full comparisons. Our current primitives are planar. A natural extension is developable Hexels: curved patches with zero Gaussian curvature that remain locally isometric to the planar canonical hexagon. Such primitives could bend along one principal direction, for example, as cylindrical or conical patches, while preserving the simple 2D footprint and affine appearance parameterization. This may allow individual primitives to cover larger regions of locally near-developable geometry without introducing additional overlap.

Hexels are also primitive-based renderers, but we try to solve a more

article.headline: 六边形图元Hexels：紧凑场景渲染与重建
article.lede: 论文提出以带一阶颜色场的六边形面片作为统一图元，在匹配模型内存下于三项三维基准上超过2DGS与Triangle Spla
article.problem: 辐射场与splatting类方法在新视角合成和三维重建上进展很快，但显存与计算开销限制了它们在资源受限设备上的使用。已有图元往往顾此失彼：普通高斯与三角splat每个图元只存一个视角相关颜色，空间变化要靠大量重叠元素堆出，造成严重overdraw；而引入逐图元纹理或神经外观场的方法又把这些复杂度转移到纹理、网格或解码器上。作者因此试图在有限表示预算下同时兼顾表面几何精度与外观表达能力。
article.method: 作者将图元本身作为优化对象，提出Hexels：一块仿射六边形平面片，内部用一阶（仿射）空间颜色场描述平滑的外观变化，从而以单个紧凑图元覆盖较大且近似各向同性的局部表面区域。训练从稀疏COLMAP点出发迭代30K次，固定配置保留初始图元数量。致密化配置采用混合clone/split生长与基于贡献的剪枝，上限为2M个图元；V1、V2、V3三种配置每个图元分别占80、116、260字节，且结果均未使用训练后的量化或压缩。
article.results: 在Tanks and Temples（10场景）、Mip-NeRF 360（9场景）和DTU（15场景）共34个真实场景上，匹配模型内存时Hexels V1的PSNR比2DGS高4.53–7.38 dB，比Triangle Splatting高1.70–2.90 dB，其中Mip-NeRF 360上平均增益为6.99 dB。渲染速度为377.8–830.8 FPS，是2DGS的1.54–1.87倍，峰值训练显存最多比2DGS少3.6倍。DTU表面重建的平均Chamfer距离为0.978 mm，而内存匹配与图元匹配的2DGS分别为1.375 mm和1.449 mm；每像素所需图元数与高斯类方法相比，平均混合次数减少71–80%。在匹配图元数量时，学习状态最多少2倍，渲染最多比2DGS快2.31倍。
article.why_it_matters: 它把效率改进落在图元设计本身，而不是依赖纹理图集、神经解码器、剪枝或量化，因此对显存受限的端侧新视角合成与显式表面重建更直接可用。作者还实现了直接评估训练时同一表示的渲染器，并计划与训练代码一并开源。
article.limitations: 一阶颜色模型无法表达单个图元内的任意纹理，高频或非相关的表观需要更小的图元或更丰富的颜色模型，从而削弱利用局部平滑性带来的收益；稀疏初始化还可能留下覆盖不足的区域，独立表面单元也不构成水密网格，小投影尺寸或掠射视角下仍可能出现采样伪影。作者也承认Hexels并非在所有指标上优于所有基线：例如无约束2DGS在DTU上的Chamfer距离为0.794 mm，优于Hexels的0.978 mm。

page_papers.title: CoSTA: Compressed Speech Token Adaptation for Efficient Spoken Dialogue Models
page_papers.abstract: Spoken Dialogue Models (SDMs) typically share a speech-token space for generation and synthesis, leading to long autoregressive sequences and costly inference. Lower-rate speech tokenizers shorten sequences but may introduce compression-quality trade-offs and costly replacement without breaking this coupling. To address this limitation, we propose CoSTA, a compatibility-preserving post-hoc framework that decouples generation and synthesis token spaces while retaining the original speech tokenizer and decoder. CoSTA extends the generation token space with compressed representations via mean-initialized vocabulary extension, pronunciation adaptation, and dialogue adaptation, followed by deterministic expansion back to the original speech-token space before synthesis. On bilingual speech-dialogue benchmarks, CoSTA achieves approximately $1.7\times$ expanded speech-token generation speed, lower full-response latency, and higher throughput while preserving response quality. Analyses show more sustained interaction under limited budgets and a practical trade-off among compression, decoding efficiency, and quality. Further experiments demonstrate cross-architecture transfer and complementarity to low-rate tokenization.
page_papers.content:
Abstract
Spoken Dialogue Models (SDMs) typically share a speech-token space for generation and synthesis, leading to long autoregressive sequences and costly inference.
Lower-rate speech tokenizers shorten sequences but may introduce compression–quality trade-offs and costly replacement without breaking this coupling.
To address this limitation, we propose CoSTA, a compatibility-preserving post-hoc framework that decouples generation and synthesis token spaces while retaining the original speech tokenizer and decoder.
CoSTA extends the generation token space with compressed representations via mean-initialized vocabulary extension, pronunciation adaptation, and dialogue adaptation, followed by deterministic expansion back to the original speech-token space before synthesis.
On bilingual speech-dialogue benchmarks, CoSTA achieves approximately
1.7
×
1.7\times
expanded speech-token generation speed, lower full-response latency, and higher throughput while preserving response quality.
Analyses show more sustained interaction under limited budgets and a practical trade-off among compression, decoding efficiency, and quality.
Further experiments demonstrate cross-architecture transfer and complementarity to low-rate tokenization.
