Introduction
Figure 1:
Overview of CoSTA. Existing SDMs couple generation and synthesis token spaces. CoSTA extends the generation token space with compressed representations and deterministically expands them back to the original space before synthesis.
Spoken dialogue models (SDMs) enable end-to-end speech interaction by modeling speech input and generating text tokens together with speech tokens, which are then synthesized into waveforms by a speech decoder
Défossez et al. (2024)
;
Zeng et al. (2024)
;
Xu et al. (2025a)
;
KimiTeam et al. (2025)
;
Wu et al. (2025)
.
Existing SDMs typically use the same token space for autoregressive generation and speech synthesis, tightly coupling generation with the representation required by the speech decoder.
These speech-token sequences are often overly long, increasing autoregressive generation cost, complicating text-speech alignment, and making long-context speech modeling more difficult
Shen et al. (2024)
;
Li et al. (2024)
.
In practical interaction, this inefficiency slows responses and consumes generation budgets faster, limiting sustained interaction and spoken-response duration.
One solution is to design speech tokenizers with lower token rates
Défossez et al. (2024)
;
Zeng et al. (2025)
;
Guo et al. (2024)
;
Wang et al. (2025c)
;
Guo et al. (2026)
.
However, aggressive rate reduction may introduce a compression–quality trade-off, and replacing the tokenizer of an existing SDM may require retraining or adapting the tokenizer, paired speech decoder, and SDM together.
More fundamentally, this route still couples generation and synthesis to the same representation.
We therefore ask a different question:
Can we decouple the token space used for autoregressive generation from that required for speech synthesis, while preserving the original speech tokenizer and decoder?
Speech-token sequences produced by existing tokenizers exhibit substantial redundancy and can be losslessly compressed using BPE
Gage (1994)
;
Sennrich et al. (2016)
;
Radford et al. (2019)
.
Across diverse tokenizer, data, and language settings, we uncover an empirical scaling regularity: BPE compression shortens speech-token sequences with increasing vocabulary size, following an approximate log-linear trend on held-out speech.
This persistent compressibility suggests a route to more efficient generation without altering synthesis: using a compact autoregressive representation while deterministically recovering the original speech-token sequence required by the decoder.

Method

Experiments
4.1

Experimental Setup
Implementation.
We use the 8B Step-Audio 2 mini
Wu et al. (2025)
as the SDM for its strong open-source support, simple architecture, and competitive dialogue performance; it uses S3Tokenizer V2 at 25 Hz.
For pronunciation adaptation, we sample 300 hours each of Chinese and English speech from Emilia
He et al. (2024)
and convert them to a unified timbre with Seed-VC
Liu (2024)
.
For dialogue adaptation, we follow OpenS2S
Wang et al. (2025a)
to construct approximately 50K speech-dialogue examples per language, with assistant speech synthesized by CosyVoice 2
Du et al. (2024b)
using a consistent voice.
We learn the BPE vocabulary from dialogue speech-token sequences and use 80K added units, supported by the vocabulary-size trade-off analysis in Section
4.4
.
Vocabulary extension adds only embedding and LM-head rows, about 6% of the original model parameters.
We train CoSTA-ZH, CoSTA-EN, and CoSTA-MIX for Chinese, English, and bilingual adaptation; further training details and data statistics are provided in Appendices
A
and
B.1
.

Bold
and
underline

Baselines and benchmarks.
We compare against the original Step-Audio 2 mini and Vanilla-
FT-ZH/EN/MIX, which use the same adaptation data and training configuration while retaining the original speech tokens.
This controls for training-data scale and isolates the effect of BPE-compressed token adaptation.
Qwen2.5-Omni
Xu et al. (2025a)
, Kimi-Audio
KimiTeam et al. (2025)
, and GLM-4-Voice
Zeng et al. (2024)
serve as external quality references.
We evaluate on 12 datasets from URO-Bench
Yan et al. (2025)
, covering aligned Chinese and English settings and spanning summarization, mathematical and common-sense reasoning, open-ended dialogue, and real-world conversation, providing broad coverage of realistic spoken-dialogue scenarios.

Conclusion
We uncover an approximate log-linear scaling regularity in speech-token BPE and introduce CoSTA, which decouples generation and synthesis token spaces while retaining the original tokenizer and decoder.

Additional Results
This section provides detailed quality results, initialization and data-scaling analyses, compression across corpus settings, first-packet latency, human evaluation, OpenS2S transfer, and vocabulary-size and adaptation analyses.
C.1

Detailed Main Results
In the main paper, we report per-dataset G-Eval scores and average ASR-CER/WER and UTMOS results for Chinese and English URO-Bench datasets. To provide a more complete comparison, Tables
14
and
15
further report the detailed values of all metrics on each dataset, including G-Eval, ASR-CER/WER, and UTMOS. These results detail the average quality trends discussed in the main paper and the variation across tasks; improvements are not uniform for every metric and dataset.
C.2

Data Scaling Analysis
We further analyze how the amount of adaptation data affects CoSTA. These scaling experiments were conducted in an early setting without progressive adaptation, and were mainly evaluated on four Chinese URO-Bench datasets: AlpacaEval-zh, APE-zh, Claude-zh, and MLC-zh. We study two scaling settings: varying the amount of pronunciation-adaptation data while keeping the dialogue-adaptation data fixed, and varying the amount of dialogue-adaptation data while keeping the pronunciation-adaptation data fixed.
Scaling pronunciation-adaptation data.

Table
16
reports the results when varying the amount of TTS data used for pronunciation adaptation, while fixing the dialogue-adaptation data to 50K examples. Increasing the amount of TTS data generally improves compressed-token learning, especially in terms of compression rate and speech-text alignment. However, the improvement becomes less pronounced as the TTS data size continues to increase. This suggests that pronunciation adaptation benefits from sufficient TTS data, while the marginal gain becomes smaller beyond a certain scale. Based on this trade-off, we use 300h TTS data as the default setting, which provides reliable compressed speech-token generation while keeping the adaptation cost moderate.
Scaling dialogue-adaptation data.

Table
17
reports the results when varying the amount of speech-to-speech dialogue data, while fixing the pronunciation-adaptation data to 300h. The results show that using 50K dialogue examples provides a strong balance between compression behavior and response quality. Therefore, we adopt 300h TTS data and 50K dialogue examples as the experimental configuration.
C.4
Compression Across Data Sources and Languages

Table
23
provides the complete AlpacaEval-zh results underlying Figure
7
, including generated-token compression and absolute decoding speed. The 0K row is the original Step-Audio 2 mini model; the 10K–160K rows are adapted CoSTA-ZH models. Thus, the vocabulary-size comparison among adapted models uses the nonzero settings.
Increasing the added vocabulary from 10K to 80K reduces
ρ
g
\rho_{g}
from 76.66% to 67.50% and raises expanded speech-token speed from 78.67 to 103.03 tokens/s. At 160K,
ρ
g
\rho_{g}
further decreases to 63.62%, but speed reaches only 104.18 tokens/s, a 1.1% increase over 80K. Meanwhile, G-Eval decreases from 81.36 to 78.87, and UTMOS decreases by 0.02. These results motivate 80K as a balance of speed, compression, and quality under the tested conditions, rather than the setting that maximizes every metric.
C.10
Computational Cost of Vocabulary Extension
Measurement setting.
Vocabulary extension affects inference asymmetrically.
The enlarged embedding table mainly increases parameter storage, while embedding lookup does not incur vocabulary-wide computation at each decoding step.
In contrast, the LM head projects each hidden state over the full vocabulary, and the subsequent token selection also grows with vocabulary size.
We therefore measure LM-head projection plus greedy argmax as the primary per-step computational overhead introduced by vocabulary extension.
Transformer computation is excluded because its cost depends on the evolving prefix length, which itself changes with token compression and is therefore difficult to attribute to vocabulary extension alone.

article.headline: CoSTA 解耦语音生成与合成词表
article.lede: CoSTA 保留原分词器与解码器，用压缩生成词表缩短语音 token 序列，实现约 1.7 倍生成加速。
article.problem: 现有口语对话模型通常让自回归生成与语音合成共用同一套语音 token 空间，序列过长导致推理成本高。降低 token 率虽能缩短序列，但可能带来压缩—质量权衡，且替换分词器往往需要连带重训解码器与模型。CoSTA 要回答的是：能否在保留原分词器和解码器的前提下，解耦生成词表与合成词表。
article.method: CoSTA 在生成端引入 BPE 压缩表示，通过均值初始化词表扩展、发音适配和对话适配，把压缩 token 加入生成词表。生成结束后，它再确定性展开回原始语音 token 空间，交由原解码器合成。默认新增 80K 词表单元，约占原模型参数 6%；适配使用中英各 300 小时 TTS 数据和每语言约 5 万条对话样本。
article.results: 在双语语音对话基准上，CoSTA 实现约 1.7× 扩展语音 token 生成速度、更低全响应延迟和更高吞吐，同时保持回复质量。词表从 10K 增至 80K 时，生成 token 压缩率 ρg 从 76.66% 降到 67.50%，扩展 token 速度从 78.67 升至 103.03 tokens/s；增至 160K 时 ρg 降至 63.62%，但速度仅比 80K 高 1.1%（104.18 tokens/s），G-Eval 从 81.36 降到 78.87，UTMOS 下降 0.02。
article.why_it_matters: 它提供了一条后处理式效率路径：不改原分词器和解码器，就能缩短自回归生成序列，并与低速率分词互补。对已部署的 SDM 而言，这降低了提速的替换成本。
article.limitations: 作者也承认改进并非在每个指标和数据集上一致，压缩率、解码效率与质量之间存在实际权衡：160K 词表虽把 ρg 降到 63.62%，但 G-Eval 从 81.36 降到 78.87，UTMOS 下降 0.02。主实验基于 8B Step-Audio 2 mini 和 URO-Bench 的 12 个数据集，跨架构迁移结果属于补充验证。

page_papers.title: Look Only When Needed: Certificate-Guided Visual Routing for Efficient Diffusion VLMs
page_papers.abstract: Diffusion vision-language models (DVLMs) process their entire input at every denoising step. Since visual tokens make up 89-97% of this input on the benchmarks we study, most of the decoding computation is spent repeatedly processing the same image. Visual token pruning methods partially relieve this burden by removing part of the visual tokens, but they lose the removed information and still process the remaining image at every step. To measure how often the image is actually needed, we compare LLaDA-V's predictions with and without the image at every decoding step and find that removing the image changes a token being unmasked at only 22.8% of steps on average and at as few as 7.9%. We therefore propose LOWN, a decoding method that decides at every step whether to process the image and how many tokens to unmask. LOWN predicts the masked tokens without the image and processes the image only when this prediction disagrees with the last image-conditioned prediction. Agreement certifies the earlier prediction for reuse, and the number of certified tokens sets how many are unmasked in that step. We further observe that the need for the image differs across benchmarks, so LOWN's adaptive decision is needed rather than a fixed schedule. Without training or a tuned threshold, LOWN retains 99.6% of LLaDA-V's score on ten benchmarks at 35.3% of the decoding FLOPs on average. LOWN also generalizes across LLaDA-based DVLMs, composes orthogonally with visual token pruning, and runs under key-value caching for further efficiency gains. Code and project page are available at https://hyeon9698.github.io/LOWN/

Visual token pruning methods partially relieve this burden by removing part of the visual tokens, but they lose the removed information and still process the remaining image at every step. To measure how often the image is actually needed, we compare LLaDA-V’s predictions with and without the image at every decoding step and find that removing the image changes a token being unmasked at only 22.8% of steps on average and at as few as 7.9%. We therefore propose LOWN, a decoding method that decides at every step whether to process the image and how many tokens to unmask. LOWN predicts the masked tokens without the image and processes the image only when this prediction disagrees with the last image-conditioned prediction. Agreement certifies the earlier prediction for reuse, and the number of certified tokens sets how many are unmasked in that step. We further observe that the need for the image differs across benchmarks, so LOWN’s adaptive decision is needed rather than a fixed schedule. Without training or a tuned threshold, LOWN retains 99.6% of LLaDA-V’s score on ten benchmarks at 35.3% of the decoding FLOPs on average. LOWN also generalizes across LLaDA-based DVLMs, composes orthogonally with visual token pruning, and runs under key-value caching for further efficiency gains. Code and project page are available at

Introduction
Recent diffusion language models match similarly sized autoregressive models while refining several masked positions in parallel over denoising steps
(
Nie et al., 2025
;
Ye et al., 2025a
)
. In diffusion vision-language models (DVLMs) such as LLaDA-V
(
You et al., 2026
)
and others
(
Yang et al., 2025a
;
Yu et al., 2025
)
, bidirectional attention prevents direct use of the exact key-value caching found in autoregressive models, so standard inference processes the full multimodal sequence at every step. Visual tokens dominate this sequence, accounting for 89–97% of LLaDA-V’s input across our benchmarks (Figure
1(b)
), while a forward without them costs only 3–10% as much. DVLM decoding therefore spends most of its compute repeatedly processing an unchanged visual input.
Existing methods reduce this cost through visual token pruning
(
Chang et al., 2026
;
Xu et al., 2026
;
Kim et al., 2026
)
(Figure
1(a)
), intermediate-state caching
(
Wu et al., 2026a
;
Liu et al., 2026
;
Nguyen-Tri et al., 2026
)
, or unmasking more tokens per step
(
Kim et al., 2025
;
Li et al., 2026b
;
Wu et al., 2026b
;
Wang et al., 2026
;
Lee et al., 2026
)
. These approaches make image-conditioned forwards cheaper, reuse their computation, or run fewer decoding steps, but none asks whether the current step needs the image. We ask whether removing the image would change the model’s decision at the current decoding state.
Comparing LLaDA-V’s predictions with and without the image along the same decoding trajectory reveals substantial redundancy (Section
3.2
). The two give the same top-1 token at 83.4% of the positions selected for unmasking, and 85.0% of final tokens had already appeared as top-1 predictions before unmasking. Within a trajectory, image-dependent steps tend to cluster early rather than recur periodically, while their overall share varies from 7.9% on MMBench to 43.8% on DocVQA. A fixed schedule therefore finds it hard to capture when the image is needed. These observations motivate deciding image access per input and step from predictions the model has already computed.
We propose LOWN (Look Only When Needed), a decoding method built on this redundancy. LOWN stores the top-1 predictions and confidences from the latest image-conditioned forward, which we call the FULL forward, as an anchor and tests it with a cheap TEXT-ONLY forward at each step. Agreement certifies the anchor prediction for reuse, while disagreement triggers a new FULL forward. The confidence-ordered run of agreements also determines how many tokens to unmask. LOWN requires neither training nor a task-specific threshold and can be added to visual token pruning or key-value caching because it reduces how often a FULL forward is needed (Figure
1(b)
).
We evaluate LOWN on ten benchmarks spanning multiple-choice, document and chart understanding, mathematical reasoning, and open-ended captioning. On LLaDA-V, it retains 99.6% of the baseline score at 0.35
×
\times
the decoding FLOPs (Figures
1(c)
and
1(d)
). Against accelerated methods given at least its FLOPs budget, it scores highest on eight of the ten benchmarks. Combined with key-value caching or visual token pruning, it further cuts the partner’s FLOPs by 1.8–2.5
×
\times
, and with the key-value cache the pair decodes 5.6–7.0
×
\times
faster than the model alone. The same rule transfers to LaViDa and VidLaDA.
Our contributions are as follows.
•
We show through paired FULL and TEXT-ONLY forward comparisons that most DVLM decoding steps can skip image access, while the necessary steps vary across trajectories and are not well captured by fixed schedules.
•
We introduce LOWN, a training-free and threshold-free method that uses prediction agreement to jointly decide when to process the image and how many tokens to unmask.
•
We validate LOWN across ten benchmarks and three DVLM backbones, retaining 99.6% of LLaDA-V’s score at 0.35
×
\times
its decoding FLOPs, composing orthogonally with visual token pruning, and running under key-value caching.
2

;

The image rarely changes a decision.
Of the positions the model unmasks, 83.4% receive the same top-1 token from the FULL and the TEXT-ONLY forward, averaged over the ten benchmarks, so at most steps the prediction follows from the text alone and the presence of the visual tokens rarely changes the token being unmasked. Moreover, 85.0% of the final tokens had already appeared as the top-1 prediction at the same position before the step at which they were unmasked. The baseline nevertheless continued to recompute those positions with the image until unmasking them.
The need for image access varies along the decoding trajectory.
On eight of the ten benchmarks, disagreement between the two forwards is largest in the early denoising steps and decreases as the response takes shape. This pattern is not universal, as illustrated by DeCapBench in Figure
2(a)
. The affected token positions also differ across tasks, and the share of image-dependent steps ranges from 7.9% on MMBench to 43.8% on DocVQA, 22.8% on average (Figure
2(b)
). Variation across steps, positions, and benchmarks therefore makes a fixed image-access schedule poorly matched to the observed trajectories and motivates input- and step-adaptive image access.
A method that skips the image therefore needs a test that runs at every step, and the TEXT-ONLY forward that exposed the redundancy is a natural candidate, since it costs 3–10% of a FULL forward. The next section turns the agreement between the two forwards into that test.

4
Method
LOWN separates two decisions that standard DVLM decoding makes with a single FULL forward, whether the current response state needs the image and how far decoding can advance (Figure

:
Qualitative comparison with visual token pruning (RedVTP).
In LOWN’s output, blue underlines mark tokens unmasked on FULL forward steps, while the remaining tokens are unmasked on TEXT-ONLY forward steps.
Visual information preservation.
Visual token pruning permanently removes part of the visual representation before decoding, whereas LOWN skips image access only at selected steps and can consult the complete image later. The distinction is most apparent on tasks that require reading or composing fine-grained visual evidence, where pruning incurs its largest quality losses (Figure
5
and Table
13
). In Figure
6
, LLaDA-V and LOWN use the relevant visual evidence and answer correctly, whereas RedVTP prunes that evidence and answers fluently but incorrectly. Here LOWN concentrates FULL-forward steps on visually grounded content, while surrounding language is handled by TEXT-ONLY forwards.
Certificate reliability.
On the baseline decoding trajectories of Section
3.2
, we compare each certified token with a fresh FULL prediction. With a one-step-old anchor, the disagreement rate is 4.1–11.0%, and it generally increases with anchor age, reaching 25.3% on DocVQA when the anchor is eight steps old. On LOWN’s own trajectories, the same rate is 2.2–4.7% for the tokens it unmasks on TEXT-ONLY steps. In practice the anchor rarely gets old, since every FULL forward replaces it and 92–97% of these tokens use an anchor from the preceding step, none older than five (Table
16
). An oracle schedule that uses the image only on the steps where it changes an unmasked decision costs 0.33
×
\times
the baseline against LOWN’s measured 0.35
×
\times
, and, since it still runs one forward per baseline step, it is not a lower bound. Appendix
F.2
gives per-benchmark results.
6
Conclusion
DVLMs need not process visual tokens at every denoising step. Along LLaDA-V’s decoding trajectories, most unmasked decisions agree between FULL and TEXT-ONLY forwards, but the steps requiring visual input vary across tasks, motivating adaptive rather than fixed image access. LOWN turns this agreement into a training- and threshold-free rule for deciding when to run a FULL forward and how many tokens to unmask. Across ten benchmarks, it retains 99.6% of LLaDA-V’s score at 0.35
×
\times
the decoding FLOPs. The same rule transfers unchanged to LaViDa and extends to VidLaDA under a controlled video protocol, while also composing orthogonally with visual token pruning and running under key-value caching. These results establish image-access scheduling as a broadly applicable axis for efficient DVLM decoding.
Limitations.
LOWN reuses anchor predictions that agree with the TEXT-ONLY forward, so a reused token can differ from a fresh FULL prediction, more often as the anchor ages (Appendix
F.2
). It also reduces cost less on chart and document reading, where visual dependence persists and more steps need a FULL forward (Appendix
E.5
). The same agreement decides how many FULL forwards a response needs, so its cost cannot be set before decoding. Combining LOWN with visual token pruning, however, partly addresses this, as its retention ratio gives some control over cost.

A.1
Measurement Protocol
We decode each benchmark with LLaDA-V’s released procedure, greedy at temperature zero with zero classifier-free guidance and low-confidence remasking, using the response lengths and step counts of Appendix
C
. At every step we run the TEXT-ONLY forward alongside the FULL forward on the same partially masked response, with the visual tokens removed and the position IDs of all other tokens kept. Only the FULL forward decides which positions are unmasked, and the TEXT-ONLY outputs never enter the decoding state, so the trajectory is the baseline’s by construction. At every masked position and step we log the top-1 token and its softmax confidence from both forwards, together with the positions the FULL forward unmasks.

C.4
Video Evaluation
We evaluate the 500-question EgoSchema subset and the 502-question MLVU test set. We use VidLaDA-8B with 32 frames per video, sampled at one frame per second and uniformly subsampled when needed. Each frame yields 210 visual tokens after spatial pooling. We adopt a controlled decoding protocol with a 128-token response, 128 baseline diffusion steps, and block length 32, following the efficiency-ablation setup of
He et al. (2026)
. Decoding is greedy, with zero classifier-free guidance and low-confidence remasking. The baseline’s parallel decoding is disabled, and LOWN uses adaptive acceptance within each block. We ask the model to reason inside
<think>
and
</think>
before answering with an option letter. This protocol differs from VidLaDA’s released 64-frame, two-token evaluation.
The two methods are evaluated on identical questions and frames. We score only the answer span after the closing tag, using the released task parsers. EgoSchema reports accuracy. MLVU reports the mean accuracy over its nine task types (M-Avg). For each benchmark, the FLOPs ratio divides LOWN’s summed decoding FLOPs by the baseline’s sum over the same questions. It includes the decoder and LM head and excludes the vision encoder.
Appendix D
Wall-Clock Measurements
D.1
Generation Time
All LLaDA-V timing experiments were run on the same server with NVIDIA H200 GPUs, with one experiment per GPU at a time. We measure per-example generation time at batch size 1 with a host clock around the model’s generation call. CUDA is synchronized before the timer starts and after generation returns. The interval includes decoding, multimodal preparation, and vision encoding performed within the call. Model loading and evaluation scoring are excluded. Each task mean averages all per-example times from one recorded execution of the full evaluation set. 2
includes 1,000 MathVista examples, 60 LLaVA-Bench questions, and 400 DeCapBench examples.

D.3
Cache Configuration and Composition
Fast-dLLM uses a block spanning the configured output, prefix refresh every 32 forwards, and its factor-based token selection with factor 1. The combined implementation retains these cache settings, maintains separate image-conditioned and TEXT-ONLY prefix caches, and takes the union of Fast-dLLM’s selected tokens and LOWN’s accepted tokens.

article.headline: 扩散VLM解码只在需要时才处理图像
article.lede: LOWN 每步先用仅文本前向检验图像条件下的锚点预测：一致就跳过图像，不一致才做一次完整前向。
article.problem: 扩散视觉语言模型在每一步去噪都对整个输入做一次前向，而在作者研究的基准上视觉 token 占输入的 89–97%，于是大部分解码算力都花在反复处理同一张图上。视觉 token 剪枝能减少每次前向处理的 token 数，但被删掉的信息无法找回，剩下的图像仍要每一步都处理。
article.method: LOWN 把最近一次带图像前向（FULL）的 top-1 预测和置信度存为锚点，每一步先跑一次仅文本（TEXT-ONLY）前向，按锚点置信度排序，取与锚点一致的最长前缀作为「认证」结果。当认证长度达到基线每步 unmask 的 token 数 k 时，该步跳过图像并直接 unmask 整个前缀；不足 k 时触发一次 FULL 前向刷新锚点，并优先 unmask 两次前向预测不一致的位置。整个规则不需要训练，也没有需要调的超参阈值。
article.results: 在十个基准上，LOWN 以 LLaDA-V 基线 0.353×（35.3%）的解码 FLOPs 保留 99.6% 的平均得分，在其中八个基准上优于给定同等或更高算力的加速方法，生成时间平均减少 57.4%、最多 73.2%。测量显示图像平均只在 22.8% 的步骤上改变被 unmask 的 token（MMBench 7.9%，DocVQA 43.8%），FULL 与 TEXT-ONLY 在 83.4% 的待 unmask 位置上给出一致的 top-1，85.0% 的最终 token 在被 unmask 前就已是 top-1 预测。规则原样迁移到 LaViDa 时以 0.174× FLOPs 保留 99.7% 得分；在 VidLaDA-8B 上，EgoSchema 与 MLVU 分别用 0.255× 和 0.272× FLOPs，得分 60.2 与 43.3（基线 60.6 与 41.8）。与 Fast-dLLM 缓存组合后 FLOPs 再降 44.1–58.9%，但三项任务得分均低于单独使用 Fast-dLLM，LLaVA-Bench 上低 5.0 分。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「这一步需不需要看图像」变成解码时可逐步判定的问题，与减少单次前向 token 的剪枝、降低单次前向成本的 KV 缓存正交互补。对需要在固定算力下部署扩散 VLM 的系统而言，这提供了一条不必牺牲视觉信息的新加速维度。
article.limitations: 认证复用的是与文本前向一致的锚点预测，仍可能与全新 FULL 前向不同：在基线轨迹上，一步旧锚点的认证结果有 4.1–11.0% 被推翻，锚点老到八步时 DocVQA 升至 25.3%，LOWN 自身 TEXT-ONLY 步骤上的接受误差为 2.2–4.7%。图表与文档阅读类任务视觉依赖持续，节省更少（DocVQA 上有一个样本只降到 0.90×），且 FULL 前向次数由解码过程决定，成本无法在解码前设定。
article.figure_caption_zh: LOWN 概览：TEXT-ONLY 前向与锚点预测一致即认证并跳过图像，认证前缀不足时触发 FULL 前向刷新锚点，并优先 unmask 两次前向分歧的位置。

figure.caption: {Overview of LOWN.} TEXT-ONLY agreement certifies anchor tokens for image-free unmasking, and an insufficient certified prefix triggers a FULL forward that refreshes the anchor and unmasks the positions where the two forwards disagree first.

page_papers.title: Your Benchmark Is an Empirical Measure Over Difficulty
page_papers.abstract: A benchmark is not merely a collection of test questions; it naturally induces an empirical measure over difficulty. In this work, we develop this measure-based view of benchmark evaluation. This perspective allows us to identify and formalize two central failure modes: measure mismatch, where the benchmark difficulty distribution differs from the intended difficulty distribution, and coverage gaps, where uncovered regions along the difficulty axis prevent benchmarks from detecting meaningful localized training progress. We propose two diagnostic metrics that capture these two failure modes and provide rigorous theoretical guarantees. Empirically, we analyze 25 popular benchmarks spanning 7 domains using carefully estimated item difficulties. Our results show that many benchmarks implicitly overweight certain difficulty regions, so their leaderboard conclusions should be interpreted with caution; others leave substantial portions of the difficulty axis uncovered, limiting their ability to monitor the model improvement process. Finally, we turn diagnosis into action by introducing BenchFill, a simple difficulty-targeted item rewriting algorithm that effectively reduces local coverage gaps.

Introduction
Benchmark evaluation looks simple: we run models on a set of questions and average the results. The resulting score is then used in two main ways: to compare models on leaderboards
(
Alzahrani et al., 2024

Wang et al., 2018
;
Liang et al., 2022
;

(

)
. But this simplicity hides a basic issue: the conclusion depends not only on how well models perform, but also on how benchmark questions are distributed
Siska et al. (2024)
;
Zhang et al. (2026)
.
Consider first the leaderboard setting in Fig.
1
(a), where we want to compare two models. Suppose they perform similarly on easy questions but differ substantially on hard ones. If the benchmark places most of its weight on easy questions, while the difficulty distribution of interest places more weight on harder questions, the two evaluations can lead to different conclusions for the same pair of models: the benchmark may suggest that the two models are nearly tied, even though under the desired difficulty distribution they are clearly separated. Now consider the training setting in Fig.
1
(b), where we want to track whether a model is improving. Suppose the model improves
substantially
over a local difficulty range. If the benchmark has few or no questions in that region, the benchmark score may barely change, even though the model has made real progress.
These two failure cases suggest that benchmark conclusions depend critically on how questions are distributed. To study this structure systematically, we organize benchmark questions along a
difficulty
axis, which provides a natural progression from easier to harder problems. The key conceptual step is to use difficulty as a way to define the distributional structure of the benchmark itself. This view recasts a benchmark from a collection of test questions into an
empirical measure
over difficulty, with each question contributing equal evaluation mass at its difficulty level.
This measure-theoretic formalization is useful because it turns the two failure cases above into precise and analyzable problems about the benchmark-induced difficulty measure. The first is a
measure mismatch
problem: the benchmark may distribute its mass differently from the target difficulty distribution that represents the intended evaluation objective, so benchmark conclusions can differ from the conclusions under the target difficulty distribution. The second is a
coverage gap
problem. Because the benchmark is an empirical measure supported only on finitely many difficulty points, there may be intervals of difficulty with little or no benchmark mass. A substantial performance gain concentrated in such an interval may therefore produce little or no change in the benchmark score. To our knowledge, this is the first work to identify and formalize measure mismatch and coverage gaps as two fundamental failure modes of benchmark evaluation.
These two problems naturally lead to two simple diagnostic metrics: the Wasserstein distance
Villani and others (2009)
between the benchmark measure and a target difficulty distribution, and the maximum gap between adjacent benchmark difficulty points. We provide theoretical results showing that these quantities directly characterize distributional mismatch and the detectability of localized improvements. Empirically, we analyze
25
popular benchmarks spanning
7
domains. We estimate question difficulty using Item Response Theory and compute the proposed metrics. Our results show that both issues are prevalent across benchmarks.
Our key contributions are summarized as follows:
•
We introduce a new measure-based perspective on benchmark evaluation, representing a benchmark as an empirical measure over difficulty. This perspective formalizes measure mismatch and coverage gaps, motivates two diagnostic metrics, and yields rigorous theoretical guarantees.
•

Human validation.
We ensure the reliability of the generated gap-filling items using a two-stage validation process. GPT-5.4 first serves as an automatic validity judge, checking whether each candidate is well-formed and whether its reference answer is correct; candidates that fail this check are discarded and regenerated. article.headline: 基准是难度上的经验测度：两类失效模式
article.lede: 论文把基准视为难度轴上的经验测度，形式化测度错配与覆盖空洞两种失效模式，并给出诊断指标与补洞方法 BenchFill。
article.problem: 基准分数既被用来做排行榜比较，也被用来监控训练进展，但结论不只取决于模型能力，还取决于题目在难度轴上的分布。如果基准的难度权重与使用者关心的目标分布不一致，同一对模型可能得出不同排名；如果难度轴某一段几乎没有题目，模型在该区间的局部进步就几乎不会反映到总分上。作者称这是首个把「测度错配」与「覆盖空洞」作为基准评估基本失效模式加以形式化的工作。
article.method: 作者把每道题看作在自身难度处贡献相等评估质量的点，于是基准成为难度轴上的经验测度：用基准测度与目标难度分布之间的 Wasserstein 距离衡量测度错配，用相邻难度点之间的最大间隔衡量覆盖空洞，并给出理论保证；题目难度用项目反应理论（最终采用 1PL）估计。诊断之后是 BenchFill：用 LLM 把已有题目改写为指定难度的新变体，迭代搜索并标注难度、更新记忆，默认填补当前最大间隔，候选先经 GPT-5.4 自动校验正确性，再由人类专家审核。
article.results: 实证覆盖 7 个领域的 25 个常用基准：其中 10/25 的难度分布偏差指标 DDM ≥ 0.10，意味着要把经验难度分布搬到同规模均匀参考分布，平均需移动至少 10% 的难度量程；8/25 的最大间隔 ≥ 0.10，9/25 的前五大间隔之和 ≥ 0.30，AIME24 与 AIME25 的前五间隔和接近 0.5。校准实验把源基准排名与留一参考排名的一致性从 Spearman 0.890 提升到 0.930、Kendall 0.802 提升到 0.848（Minerva-Math 原始仅 0.601）。补洞实验在 8 个基准上各针对 3 个最大间隔、共 24 个目标间隔，使用 MiniMax-M2.7（温度 1.0、最多 8 轮、每轮 4 个父题各改写 4 个子题）；24 个最终题目全部通过 GPT-5.4 校验与人工复核，其中 1 个因参考答案错误被重新生成。在轻度 SFT 后的小规模检验中，Original+BenchFill 在 3/3 个案例里以单侧分层随机化检验（p<0.05，每题 32 次采样）检出正向增益；至于每个基准仅插入 3 题时分数变化的具体幅度，论文未给出具体数字。
article.why_it_matters: 它提醒读者：排行榜分数是在基准自身的难度加权下做的比较，而用题目数量有限的小基准监控强化学习训练，可能系统性低估局部进步。两个诊断指标可以直接用来体检现有基准，或按目标分布做校准。
article.limitations: 全部结论都建立在 IRT 估计的单维难度上，1PL 的拟合诊断虽被作者认为最稳定，但难度估计误差会直接传导到两个指标；「目标难度分布」在很多场景下仍需人为指定，分布不均匀本身并不等于错误。补洞与增益检测的实验规模也很小——只有 8 个基准、24 个间隔、3 个增益案例，且改写全部由单一 LLM 完成，结论能否泛化到其他基准家族尚不清楚。

page_papers.title: SO-101 Bench: Accessible Spatial Manipulation
page_papers.abstract: Low-cost arms such as the SO-101 have become the most common entry point to robot learning, yet no released policy performs spatially constrained, language-conditioned tasks on them out of the box, and existing SO-101 benchmarks run only on physical hardware with simple tasks and few held-out objects. We introduce SO-101 Bench, a simulated benchmark for language-conditioned spatial manipulation built on an Isaac Lab digital twin of a real SO-101 setup. It has four tasks scored as five families, 138 objects in seen, unseen-instance and unseen-class splits, 916 evaluation episodes with subsets for held-out appearances, rotate-to-fit planning and occlusion memory, and 3,629 simulated demonstrations on which every learned policy is fine-tuned under an equal compute budget. The twin ranks policies as the real robot does: five policies trained without real data, four VLAs and an LLM agent, keep their exact ranking when the same weights run on the physical arm in an unseen environment with unseen objects (Spearman rho = 1.00, MMRV = 0.000), although simulation overestimates success. Across nine VLAs and world-action models, the best learned policies score near 61%, with spatial placement, unseen object classes and rotate-to-fit planning remaining open. An LLM agent that writes code and hands grasping to a learned policy scores 83.2%, and an ablation shows that this lead comes from the choice of harness and the choice of language model.

3  SO-101 Bench
SO-101 Bench evaluates language-conditioned tabletop manipulation with a single SO-101 arm
[
1
]
. It is designed to
test whether a policy can turn semantic understanding into precise physical execution: identifying the right
object among distractors, grasping objects of unfamiliar geometry, and placing them under (often precise) spatial constraints.
Every component below is shared by all evaluated policies.
3.1  Tasks
The benchmark comprises four language-conditioned tasks (Fig.
2
), scored as five task families.
•
Place each object in the plastic bin.
The pure grasping task: the policy must identify, grasp,
transport and deposit every object on the table. The bin moves between episodes. We evaluate a 1-object and a
4-object condition as separate families.
•
Place [object 1] next to [object 2].
The policy must place the target close to a referent without
disturbing other objects, adding semantic grounding and basic spatial placement.
•
Place [object 1] between [object 2] and [object 3].
The target must end centred between two
referents, which makes the task sensitive to object extent, orientation and fine placement; it is the most demanding task.
•
Move [object 1] [direction].
The policy must push or carry the target along a straight path in a
commanded direction until it reaches the boundary formed by the next object in its way.
The bin task stresses grounding, grasp strategy and grasp precision; the three spatial tasks additionally require
relational grounding, spatial reasoning, fine-grained placement and robustness to partial occlusion. To keep
language grounding nontrivial, distractors of the same class or colour are included so that class identity alone
is insufficient, and colour words are omitted from instructions unless necessary (i.e when two objects of the same class are on the table).

3.2  Objects and Generalization Splits
The benchmark uses 138 household objects in three generalization splits (Fig.
3
):
seen
(48 objects that appear in training),
unseen object, seen class
(43 objects whose class,
e.g. bowl or pen, appears in training but whose instance does not), and
unseen class
(47 objects of
entirely novel classes). The splits separate transfer across
instances

sports, toys), with priority on irregular shapes. Every object was verified through teleoperation to be
graspable by the SO-101, so that failures reflect the policy rather than the hardware. Of the unseen-class
objects, 37 are kept private to prevent test-set leakage.
All objects were created using the image-to-3D tools in 3D AI Studio
[
71

∼
\sim

from photographs of the real items and their simulated appearance and physical properties were tuned to match

3.3  Digital Twin
All evaluation runs in a digital twin of the original real-world setup, built in Isaac Lab
[
26
]
from a scan of the room
and the object assets of Sec.
3.2

camera and a wrist camera, both at
640
×
480
640\times 480
, and the arm’s joint positions. The twin includes 22 background
environments: 18 are used in training and in the varied evaluation episodes, and 4 are held out
(Appendix
F
). The robot is rendered in one of 6 training colours or one of 4 held-out colours.
The real arm’s joint calibration is aligned to the simulated kinematics so that the same policy weights can run in
both domains (Sec.
5

3.4  Scoring
Episodes are scored automatically from simulator state. Positions are measured in the tabletop plane from where
objects rest at the start of the episode. A success condition must hold continuously for 5 s; a failure condition
ends the episode once it has held for 5 s, so briefly undoing a mistake is allowed. The robot is considered to
touch an object when any link presses on it with more than 0.05 N. Episodes time out after 30 s (75 s for
4-object bins).
•
Bin:
every object ends with its reference point (the centre of its top-down bounding box) inside
the bin’s footprint and untouched by the robot. Fails if the bin moves more than 0.5 in.
•
Next to:
the target’s top-down outline ends within 2 in of the referent’s outline.
•
Between:
the target’s reference point ends within 1.75 in of the line through the two referents’
reference points, and closer to each referent than the referents are to each other.
•
Move:
with an object ahead of the target, the target’s leading edge ends within 2 in of that
object’s facing edge; otherwise the target advances at least 2 in. The target must stay within 2 in of the
straight path, and the boundary object must not move more than 0.5 in along the direction.
In all three spatial tasks the target must move at least 1 in and must not be touched by the robot at the end,
and the episode fails if any non-target object (referents included) moves more than 1 in, or if the target or a
held object stays in contact with another object for more than 5 s.

All learned policies are fine-tuned on
so101_bench_sim

recorded in the digital twin using seen objects only. It contains 1,892 bin episodes (including bin instructions
that name a single target among other objects), 1,150 next-to and between episodes, and 587 move episodes; 3,004
episodes have four objects on the table. Most episodes are rendered with randomized lighting, camera intrinsics and
extrinsics, background and robot colour; the canonical setup remains in the training distribution. A variant,
so101_bench_sim_WM

8  Conclusion
SO-101 Bench makes evaluation of language-conditioned spatial manipulation on a low-cost arm both repeatable
and predictive of the real robot. Its digital twin reproduces which conditions are hard and why policies fail there,
and it ranks five policies trained without real data exactly as the physical SO-101 does; policies developed
against the benchmark run out of the box in unseen real environments with unseen objects. The leaderboard shows
where current methods stand: learned policies grasp familiar objects reliably but struggle with spatial placement,
unseen object classes and rotate-to-fit planning, while an LLM agent that writes code and delegates grasping to a
learned policy leads both in simulation and on the real robot, largely because of its harness.
Limitations.
The sim2real study covers five policies and 45 layouts in one real environment, so its
intervals are wide (MMRV 95% CI
[
0.000
,
0.169
]
[0.000,0.169]
), and simulation overestimates absolute success by 9 to 31
percentage points; simulated success rates should be read as an upper bound and comparisons, not levels, as what
transfers. The learned policies are compared at a fixed 36 h fine-tuning budget, which left some of them
under-trained, so the leaderboard does not measure capability ceilings. The agents’ time limits count simulated or
control time only: the simulator pauses, and the real arm holds still, while the language model computes, which
hides their real-time cost. Finally, the benchmark covers rigid objects and a single arm. Extending the twin to
deformable objects and bimanual setups, adding real-time constraints for agents, and using the twin’s ranking as a
prior for cheaper real-robot evaluation are natural next steps.
A logical next step is to use repeated rollouts in the twin to refine control programs and accumulate validated,
reusable skills across episodes, as in ASPIRE
[
85

and RoboRSI
[
86
]
, while
keeping the held-out evaluation fixed.

Appendix E
Object Real2Sim Pipeline
Every object passes through the same pipeline, which produces a rigid body with separate visual and collision
geometry.
1. Asset generation.
We start from an image of the object: a photograph of the real object, an image
from the internet, or an image from a text-to-image model. An image-to-3D model accessed through 3D AI Studio
[
71
]
converts it into a textured mesh
(GLB) with physically based rendering (PBR) materials.
2. Mesh processing (Blender).
The mesh is scaled to the object’s real dimensions, oriented, and given
an origin at its base, which serves as the object’s root pose for the success conditions. Texture colours are
corrected towards the object’s real palette and brightness. The mesh is then duplicated into a
visual
and a
physics
mesh.
•
Visual mesh:
remeshed and decimated to a fixed visual budget, repaired (loose geometry removed,
duplicate vertices merged, no non-manifold edges), and the original colour and roughness are baked onto it.
•
Physics mesh:
cleaned and remeshed to a coarser physical budget, avoiding small crevices in which
the gripper could become caught. Over-faceted results are smoothed, remaining non-manifold regions are filled or
remeshed at a larger voxel size, and face normals are made consistent. The physics mesh is checked to align with
the visual mesh.
Both meshes are exported together as a USD file with packed textures.
3. Physics setup (Isaac Sim).
The root prim is made a rigid body with mass. The physics mesh is
given a collider, using a signed-distance-field (SDF) collider for complex non-convex shapes without thin walls
and a convex hull or convex decomposition otherwise. A physics material sets static and dynamic friction and
restitution, and the physics mesh is hidden from rendering.
4. Appearance tuning (Isaac Lab).
The visual mesh’s colour texture is adjusted, usually by tuning its
brightness and occasionally by repainting regions, until the object’s appearance under the benchmark cameras
matches the real object.

article.headline: SO-101 仿真基准：策略排名可迁移到真机
article.lede: SO-101 语言条件空间操作基准：五项策略在仿真与真机排名完全一致，但仿真成功率高出 9–31 个百分点。
article.problem: SO-101 这类低成本手臂（零件约 120–150 美元，而 ALOHA 单臂约 4,900 美元）已成为机器人学习最常见的入口，但据作者所知，没有任何已发布策略能开箱完成语言条件约束下的空间操作任务。今年发布的 SO-101 基准全部只在真机硬件上运行，任务简单、留出物体少，结果还受具体装配影响（舵机偏移、相机错位、物体磨损）；而 LIBERO 等常用仿真套件已接近饱和——一个 0.54M 参数策略就能达到 95.1%。
article.method: 作者在 Isaac Lab 中搭建真实 SO-101 装置的机械臂数字孪生，含 138 个家用物体，分 seen、unseen-instance、unseen-class 三档（其中 37 个未见类物体私有以防测试集泄漏），四类任务记为五个任务族，主评测为 916 个经可行性检查的回合，另设 ROBUST、PLAN、MEM 三个子集。所有学习型策略都在同一份 3,629 条仿真遥操示教上、以相同的 36 小时 × 4×A100 预算微调，并在独立的 39 回合验证集上选检查点。排名验证分两步：先比较独立训练的真机专用与仿真专用 GR00T N1.6 的难度结构（15 个任务×划分单元上 Pearson r=0.86），再用同一份权重在孪生与真机上跑五个策略。
article.results: 主评测 916 回合中，最好的学习型策略 InternW0-Δ 得 61.4（95% CI [58.5, 64.1]）、Galaxea 0.5 得 60.8（[57.9, 63.6]），统计上并列；它们在单物体装箱上达 90–93%，但 next-to 与 between 只有 34–44%，且没有任何学习型策略在需要旋转对位的 PLAN 子集上超过 17%。由 GPT-6.1 Sol 写代码、把抓取交给 Galaxea 0.5 的 LLM agent 得 83.2（[80.7, 85.7]），PLAN 达 75%。sim2real 方面，五个策略在 45 个匹配布局上仿真与真机排名完全相同（Spearman ρ=1.00，MMRV=0.000，95% CI [0.000, 0.169]），但仿真对每个策略都高估 9–31 个百分点；真机上 agent 为 64%（29/45），Galaxea 0.5 为 53%（24/45），McNemar p=0.30。60 个配对回合的 harness 消融显示：直接工具调用 35%（21/60）、PyRUA-Lean 67%（40/60）、再交给 Galaxea 0.5 抓取 85%（51/60），而 Galaxea 0.5 单独为 53%（32/60）。
article.why_it_matters: 它给出了一条可复现、成本远低于真机的评测流程，也是目前少数在“只用仿真数据训练的策略”上验证过 sim2real 排名的 SO-101 基准，意味着社区可以用孪生先筛策略、再用真机确认。对做 VLA/WAM 的读者，结论也很直接：抓取熟悉物体已基本解决，空间放置、未见类别和旋转对位仍是空白。
article.limitations: sim2real 研究只覆盖 5 个策略、45 个布局、单一真实环境，MMRV 的 95% 置信区间为 [0.000, 0.169]，作者自承这只能算“排名正确”而非精确校准，仿真成功率应读作真机性能的上界。所有学习型策略在固定 36 小时预算下比较，MolmoAct2 只跑了 0.5–0.6 个 epoch、FLUX 3 Action 只有 0.2 个 epoch，低分不代表能力上限；而且 agent 的时限只计仿真或控制时间，模型推理时机械臂静止，真机中位实际耗时 197 秒，而 Galaxea 0.5 为 38 秒，实时成本被掩盖。

page_papers.title: A-RSI: Adaptive Task Refresh for Zero-Data Multimodal Self-Improvement
page_papers.abstract: Recursive self-improvement requires models not only to acquire useful training experience, but also to decide when their current experience has ceased to be useful. Existing methods often focus on what experience to generate next, while paying less attention to when fresh experience should be introduced. Many also construct training targets through self-consistency or majority voting, making supervision depend on the model's own uncertain predictions. We address these two questions separately: training dynamics determine when to acquire new experience, while the answers to new tasks remain independently checkable. A-RSI monitors reward variation and accuracy in training logs to refresh a task pool when its learning signal declines, without consulting validation or test scores. A static library of model-authored programs produces multimodal questions and derives their reference answers; we specify the task-generation contract, automatically verify chosen properties of the reward and refresh rules, and separately audit the generated answers. The training loop uses no external training examples or human-written answer labels. On the primary eleven-benchmark suite, A-RSI raises the performance average from 57.77 to 61.05 with 800 fresh tasks.

Introduction
Recursive self-improvement depends on both acquiring useful experience and recognizing when the current experience is no longer useful. Recent methods have emphasized what to generate next, such as harder problems or tasks near the model’s estimated competence. Yet a system can continue spending updates on a pool whose learning signal has declined, while refreshing too often consumes new tasks that may not be needed. This makes the timing of replacement a distinct decision from the choice of replacement tasks.
The answers attached to self-generated tasks raise a separate reliability question. When training targets come from self-consistency or majority voting, errors in the model’s predictions can become labels for its next update. We therefore separate the source of a refresh decision from the source of answer correctness: training dynamics can indicate when to draw new experience, while the new tasks should have independently checkable answers.

Discussion
The simple version of the loop wins.
The cheapest policy we found for keeping a zero-data loop alive is to let the model’s training log say when the pool is spent and then supply random fresh tasks. Neither of the refinements we tried helped, and one made things worse. We read this as a statement about this setting, in which the tasks are programmatic and the checkpoint is a plateau.
Measured state is for diagnosis.
The ladder is useful for something other than selection. Because difficulty is measured, we can say what the model has learned, which tiers saturate first, and where a mismatch occurs: for example, three of six ladders never reached the promotion threshold, and hard multi-hop tasks are largely length exhaustion. Self-assessed difficulty (AUC near 0.50) could not support these statements.
Adaptation through observable training state.
The controller connects experience reuse to the model’s ongoing optimization. MiMo’s changing decisions across pools and the divergent Qwen–MiMo final-round replay show why elapsed training alone does not specify the action. A common fixed rule can respond to these differences through model-generated training feedback, without changing its thresholds or consulting evaluation performance.

Conclusion
An RSI loop stalls first where its data runs out, and its gains can look larger than they are.

article.headline: 不看测试分数：用训练日志决定何时换题
article.lede: A-RSI 只读训练日志里的奖励与准确率变化，在学信号衰退时换掉整个任务池；11 个基准平均分从 57.77 升到 61
article.problem: 递归自我提升不只取决于生成什么新任务，还取决于何时该换掉已经学不动的任务池；已有方法多关注前者，容易在信号衰退的池上继续消耗更新。另一处隐患是训练目标常来自自一致性或多数投票，模型的错误预测会变成下一轮的标签。作者把这两个问题拆开：训练动态决定何时换，新任务的答案则要能独立核查。
article.method: A-RSI 在训练前固定一套由模型撰写程序构成的任务库，程序生成多模态题目并直接算出参考答案，同时准备好互不重叠的替换池，每个池 400 题。训练时 Solver 用 GRPO 在活跃池上学，奖励由正确性、格式和终止三项组成。控制器只读训练侧的准确率和组内相对优势信号，判断保留当前池还是启用下一个未用过的池，换池时保留最新权重；全程不使用外部训练样本或人工答案标签，也不查验证集和测试集分数。
article.results: 主实验用 Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct，八个续训窗口、每窗 100 次更新，用 800 个新任务把 11 个基准的等权平均（Macro11）从 57.77 拉到 61.05。MiMo-VL-7B-SFT 上随机刷新终点为 60.71，持续复用为 60.01，差 +0.70 分，仅比每窗刷新高 +0.02、比周期刷新高 +0.18；作者明确指出这样小的单次运行差距不足以证明时机优势。在 MathVision 上该方法得 51.45 分、截断率 8.36%，其他刷新方案为 18%–22%。同一协议下，基于难度、控制器和 rollout 的选择器都没有跑赢随机选择；MiMo 的随机刷新端点也超过各对照臂。
article.why_it_matters: 它给出一个便宜的可复用判据：让模型自己的训练日志决定数据何时作废，而不依赖测试集或人工设计的难度曲线，这对持续学习的工程闭环有直接参考价值。同时它把奖励规则和生成答案分别做了自动验证与独立审计，为「自生成数据」的可信度提供了可操作的检查范式。
article.limitations: 每个实验臂只训练一次，作者自己承认 MiMo 上 +0.70 这类差距不构成时机优势，下一步需要跨随机种子复现和固定调度的随机对照，16k 评测也未完成。程序库只覆盖几何、图表、表格和计数，缺函数图像、数值估计与空间任务；参考解答审计中 hr 组仍有 5 例「第三高」并列，不能声称标签零歧义；部分零数据增益其实来自学会在长度预算内收尾。

page_papers.title: Disentangling Dual Image References in Frequency Aware Diffusion Models for Personalized Generation
page_papers.abstract: Personalized image generation aims to synthesize text-driven images conditioned on reference images, while mainly casting the generation as image customization for foreground and style transfer for background. Previous arts of diffusion models suffers from the text misalignment with background for image customization and foreground for style transfer during the denoising process. Such facts, as we observed, rooted from the entanglement among hybrid frequency bands during the denoising process. To address such salient limitation, in this paper, we study personalized generation based on dual references - customization and color and style reference - and propose a paradigm to disentangle these Dual image references within Frequency-aware Diffusion Models, dubbed Dual-FDM, to simultaneously tackle two crucial personalized image generation tasks: customization style transfer and color style transfer, by disentangling different frequency bands via mask strategy within frequency domain. For customization style transfer, we replace the mid-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from the foreground of the customized reference. For color style transfer, we substitute the low-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from both the foreground and background of the color reference. Both the substituted frequency bands are used as the key and value to reconstruct the query foreground and background of the denoised personalized image.Extensive experiments validate the superiority of Dual-FDM over the state-of-the-art diffusion models for personalized image generation. Our code can be accessed from https://github.com/htyjers/Dual-FDM.

Abstract
Personalized image generation aims to synthesize text-driven images conditioned on reference images, while mainly casting the generation as image customization for foreground and style transfer for background. Previous arts of diffusion models suffers from the text misalignment with background for image customization and foreground for style transfer during the denoising process. Such facts, as we observed, rooted from the entanglement among hybrid frequency bands during the denoising process. In particular, the low-frequency band primarily captures color information, mid-frequency band encodes global structure, while high-frequency band corresponds to local texture.
Besides, the early (high-noise) denoising stage mainly focuses on the low-and-mid frequency bands, while the late (low-noise) denoising stage progressively exhibits the high-frequency band, resulting in the dominance of low-and-mid over high frequency bands, especially when entangled within a single image reference, tends to reinforce each other at the early stage, hence the pitfall of overwhelming suppression of text prompt guidance. To address such salient limitation, in this paper, we study personalized generation based on dual references - customization and color and style reference - and propose a paradigm to disentangle these
Dual
image references within
F
requency-aware
D
iffusion
M
odels, dubbed
Dual-FDM
, to simultaneously tackle two crucial personalized image generation tasks: customization style transfer and color style transfer, by disentangling different frequency bands via mask strategy within frequency domain. For customization style transfer, we replace the mid-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from the foreground of the customized reference. For color style transfer, we substitute the low-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from both the foreground and background of the color reference. Both the substituted frequency bands are used as the key and value to reconstruct the query foreground and background of the denoised personalized image.
We further compute the ratio of information entropy of the substituted frequency bands to adaptively modulate the denoising timesteps between the early and late stages. Extensive experiments validate the superiority of
Dual-FDM
over the state-of-the-art diffusion models for personalized image generation. Our code can be accessed from

So far, neither image customization nor style transfer achieves satisfactory alignment between the generated image and the text prompt for diffusion models. Such facts, as we observed, rooted from the entanglement among hybrid frequency bands. Intuitively, as shown in Fig.
2
(c), the low-frequency and mid-frequency bands capture color and global structure, while high-frequency band focuses on local texture, where different frequency bands are mainly denoised during
different
stages of the denoising process. As we observed, the early (high-noise) denoising stage mainly focuses on the low-and-mid frequency bands, while the late (low-noise) denoising stage progressively exhibits the high-frequency band (See Sec.
A
of the Appendix), the dominance of low-and-mid over high frequency bands, especially when entangled within a single image reference, suggesting reinforce each other at the early stages, resulting in an overwhelming suppression of text prompt guidance.
To resolve the text misalignment for personalization generation, we propose to solve the problem upon dual references and develop a paradigm to disentangle these
Dual
image references within
F
requency-aware
D
iffusion
M
odels, dubbed
Dual-FDM
, for two classical personalized image generation tasks in a row: customization style transfer and color style transfer, by disentangling different frequency bands via mask strategy within frequency domain. Specifically:
•
We propose to map the foreground or background of image references into the frequency domain via Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT), where a mask is applied from left to right to progressively disentangle the low-, mid-, and high-frequency bands. Notably, for customization style transfer, we replace the mid-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from the foreground of the customized reference, named
Dual-FDM
cust
(Fig.
1
(a)). The style reference with the mid-frequency band substituted is used as the key and value to reconstruct the query foreground and background of the denoised personalized image in the decoupled cross-attention layer. For the color style transfer, we substitute the low-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from both the foreground and background of the color reference, named
Dual-FDM
cost
(Fig.
1
(b)). The style reference with the substituted low-frequency band is further utilized as the key and value to reconstruct the query foreground and background of the denoised personalized image in the decoupled cross-attention layer.
•
To pop up the foreground or background of the image reference, we utilize the key projection matrices in the decoupled cross-attention layer to represent the foreground, which are then reformulated through singular value decomposition (SVD) to derive the corresponding
background matrix
for the background.
•
For each task, we further compute the ratio of information entropy of the substituted frequency bands to adaptively modulate the denoising timesteps between the early and late stages, so as to achieve a well-balanced performance between text alignment and dual-image similarity.
Extensive experiments validate the superiority of Dual-FDM over the state-of-the-art diffusion models for personalized image generation.

Since CLIP is trained on real image–text (T) pairs, it is particularly sensitive to image style, which may distort text–image similarity. To alleviate this, we propose CLIP-TS by measuring similarity with style reference (S), thereby reducing the style influence . In addition, the generated background aligned with text prompts can interfere with the customized reference (C); hence we propose CLIP-TC, which incorporates text prompts to suppress such interference. We also provide CLIP-T (image–text similarity) and CLIP-CS (image–image reference similarity) for comparison.

4
Conclusion
In this paper, we study personalized generation based on dual references - customization and color and style reference - and propose a paradigm to disentangle dual image references within frequency-aware diffusion models, dubbed
Dual-FDM
, for two classical personalized image generation tasks in a row: customization style transfer and color style transfer, by disentangling different frequency bands via mask strategy within frequency domain. Extensive experiments validate
the superiority of
Dual-FDM
over the state-of-the-art diffusion models.

Appendix C
The algorithm of customization style transfer and color style transfer
Due to the page limitation, we summarize the process of customization style transfer in Algorithm
1
and color style transfer in Algorithm
2
.
To tackle the text-alignment issue in personalized image generation, in this paper, we study personalized generation based on dual references - customization and color and style reference - and propose a paradigm to disentangle these
Dual
image references within
F
requency-aware
D
iffusion
M
odels, dubbed
Dual-FDM
, for two classical personalized image generation tasks in a row: customization style transfer and color style transfer, by disentangling different frequency bands via mask strategy within frequency domain. For customization style transfer, we replace the mid-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from the foreground of the customized reference. For color style transfer, we substitute the low-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from both the foreground and background of the color reference. Both the substituted frequency bands are used as the key and value to reconstruct the query foreground and background of the denoised personalized image.
For each task, we further compute the ratio of information entropy of the substituted frequency bands to adaptively modulate the denoising timesteps between the early and late stages.

Appendix D
More details about the implementation details
As mentioned in Sec.3.1 of the mainbody, due to page limitation, we further provide more details about the implementation details as follows:
Datasets.
We evaluate
Dual-FDM
on combined datasets covering image customization, style transfer, and text-to-image (T2I) generation:
•
Image Customization
: 1)
DreamBench
Ruiz et al. (2023)
+
TI benchmark
Gal et al. (2022)
: a well-known single-object personalized image generation dataset comprising 38 subjects, covering unique objects and pets such as backpacks, stuffed animals, dogs, cats, sunglasses, and cartoons, with each subject associated with 25 prompts; 2)
DreamBench++
Peng et al. (2025)
: the latest human-aligned personalized image generation benchmark, comprising 65 object classes, 20 human classes, and 45 animal classes. For each image, 9 text prompts are generated by GPT-4o to span a range of difficulty levels.
•
Style Transfer
: 1)
IS-Plus benchmark
Wang et al. (2024b)
: a style evaluation benchmark containing 104 images across diverse styles; 2)
StyleBench
Gao et al. (2024)
: a style evaluation benchmark covering 73 distinct styles, ranging from paintings, flat illustrations, and 3D rendering to sculptures with varying materials. For each style, 5–7 distinct images with variations are collected. In total, StyleBench contains 490 images across diverse styles.
•
T2I generation
:
T2I-CompBench++
Huang et al. (2025a)
: an enhanced benchmark for compositional text-to-image generation. T2I-CompBench++ comprises 8,000 compositional text prompts categorized into four primary groups: attribute binding, object relationships, generative numeracy, and complex compositions. These are further divided into eight sub-categories.
Based on the above, we construct several combined datasets for different joint tasks: 1) for customization style transfer (small-scale), we concatenate
DreamBench
and
TI benchmark
as the customization references, and use
IS-Plus benchmark
as the style references; 2) for customization style transfer (large-scale), we take
DreamBench++
as the customization references and
StyleBench
as the style references; 3) for color style transfer, we combine
InstantStyle-Plus
and
StyleBench
as the color and style references, while text prompts are provided by
T2I-CompBench++
for stylized image generation.
Metrics.
We consider 9 evaluation metrics from three aspects to evaluate our
Dual-FDM
:
•
Text and Image Reference Alignment
: we follow previous methods and adopt two representative models,
CLIP
2
2
2
Since CLIP is trained on real image–text (T) pairs, it is particularly sensitive to image style, which may distort text–image similarity. To alleviate this, we propose CLIP-TS by measuring similarity with style reference (S), thereby reducing the style influence . In addition, the generated background aligned with text prompts can interfere with the customized reference (C); hence we propose CLIP-TC, which incorporates text prompts to suppress such interference. We also provide CLIP-T (image–text similarity) and CLIP-CS (image–image reference similarity) for comparison.
and
DINO
Caron et al. (2021)
, for evaluation. Specifically,
CLIP-T
measures the similarity between generated images and the given text prompts;
CLIP-TC
and
CLIP-TS
evaluate the similarity between generated images and customized (or style) reference images while jointly considering the text prompts; finally,
CLIP-CS
assesses the similarity between generated images and dual-reference images.
•
Image Generation Quality
: we employ Image Reward (
IR
)
Xu et al. (2023)
to model human preferences for image quality and
HPS V2
Wu et al. (2023)
that combines perceptual studies with deep learning for comprehensive visual and semantic assessment. Both metrics measure the semantics consistency of the high-quality image generation aligned with human standards;
•
Time Complexity
: We employ the inference time (
Times
) and Video Random Access Memory (
VRAM
) consumption to evaluate the computational efficiency and memory footprint of different methods during image generation.
Model Configuration.
Our main experiments are conducted on the pre-trained IP-Adapter-Plus
Ye et al. (2023)
with SDXL
Podell et al. (2023)
model as the text-to-image diffusion model, configured with 30 sampling steps and and a fixed random seed of 42, to ensure high-quality outputs. We use the recommended hyper-parameters for each method across all images to ensure fair comparison. All experiments are implemented in PyTorch and conducted on a NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU.

Limitations and Broader Impacts
Limitations.
As illustrated in Fig.
14
, for customization style transfer, when the style reference contains extremely sparse patterns (
e.g.
, line-based structures), the mid-frequency customized cues may
attenuate high-frequency style details, leading to incomplete style information
. We plan to address this issue in our future work.
Broader Impacts.
Our
Dual-FDM
can generate the personalized image according to the text prompt and reference images, our method may raise certain ethical concerns. The personalized image could potentially be misused in the creation of misleading information. We strongly advocate for the establishment of clear accountability in the use of such technologies, along with enhanced legal and technical oversight, to ensure they are applied responsibly.

article.headline: 用频域掩码拆解双参考图的个性化生成
article.lede: Dual-FDM 在频域用掩码替换中、低频分量，把定制参考与风格参考拆开，同时处理定制风格迁移与颜色风格迁移。
article.problem: 个性化图像生成包含两个子任务：图像定制要把参考图前景替换进文本提示，风格迁移要把参考图风格注入背景同时保持前景与文本对齐。已有方法在去噪过程中常出现文本失配：定制方法的稠密图像参考压制了稀疏的文本提示，风格迁移的稠密风格信息则泄漏到前景，布局类方法虽能保住前景身份，却因显式分割前景和背景而破坏整体一致性。作者认为这些问题的根源是去噪过程中多个频带纠缠：低频主要承载颜色、中频编码全局结构、高频对应局部纹理，而早期高噪声阶段主要由低频和中频主导，二者互相强化，形成对文本提示的压制。
article.method: 作者提出 Dual-FDM，把参考图的前景或背景经离散余弦变换映射到频域，用从左到右的掩码逐步分离低、中、高频带。为了取到参考图的背景，方法对解耦交叉注意力中的 key 投影矩阵做奇异值分解，并把奇异值取倒数构造背景矩阵，从而压制前景、增强背景。定制风格迁移（Dual-FDM_cust）用定制参考的前景替换风格参考背景的中频带；颜色风格迁移（Dual-FDM_cost）用颜色参考的前景加背景替换风格参考背景的低频带，替换后的频带作为 key 和 value 重建去噪图像的 query。此外，方法用替换频带的信息熵比值自适应划分早期与晚期去噪时间步。
article.results: 在 DreamBench、TI benchmark、DreamBench++、StyleBench 等组合数据上，Dual-FDM_cust 在六项指标上均取得最优：CLIP-T 0.3194、CLIP-TC 0.5031、CLIP-CS 0.6687、IR 5.3487、HPS 2.6007，相比最强的 [MS-Diffusion+CSGO] 组合（CLIP-T 0.3123、CLIP-TC 0.4680、IR 4.2023、HPS 2.5436）领先。颜色风格迁移在 T2I-CompBench++ 的 Color 类别上取得 CLIP-TS 0.5015、CLIP-S 0.7178、DINO-S 0.4970，均高于 InstantStyle、StyleAligned、StyleStudio 等八个基线。效率方面，单张推理耗时 10.26 秒、显存 12.48 GB，低于 MS-Diffusion 的 14.68 秒与 16.85 GB。附录的频域统计也支撑其观察：去噪过程中低频灰度均值仅从 119.5 变到 120.9，而平均梯度从 59.01 升到 233.88。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「文本对齐 vs 参考相似度」的权衡从经验性的结构设计转成可解释的频带操作，为同时处理定制与风格两类参考提供了统一的免训练框架。若频带与语义的对应关系成立，这套掩码替换思路也可迁移到其他多条件扩散生成任务。
article.limitations: 作者在附录承认，当风格参考只含极稀疏的线条状图案时，来自定制参考的中频线索会削弱高频风格细节，导致风格信息不完整。此外实验只在 IP-Adapter+SDXL、单张 RTX 4090、30 步采样下进行，未报告误差棒或显著性检验，频带划分的阈值也依赖人工设定与消融选择。

page_papers.title: Drift, Then Spread: Learning One-Step Generative Policies for Online Reinforcement Learning
page_papers.abstract: Generative policies offer expressive action distributions for online reinforcement learning (RL), but many diffusion- and flow-based policies require costly iterative sampling. We propose DriftSpread, a one-step generative policy based on Drifting for online maximum-entropy (MaxEnt) RL. To incorporate entropy without a tractable policy density, we build on an energy-based view of Drifting and derive critic-guided Drift and entropy-induced Spread from the negative MaxEnt objective. Our method learns these updates sequentially in the same actor, using action regression for value improvement and distribution matching to capture the effect of entropy. The actor updates require neither direct samples from the critic-defined Boltzmann target nor policy-density or score estimation. Under exact fitting with a fixed critic, we prove convergence to the Boltzmann target in the small-step limit followed by the long-time limit. On MuJoCo, DriftSpread achieves the highest aggregate normalized return among all evaluated methods, while outperforming the diffusion- and flow-based baselines in both training and inference efficiency.

Drift, Then Spread: Learning One-Step Generative Policies for Online Reinforcement Learning
Chunyu Luo
Hongyu Zhao
Guangyi Ni
Yue Song
Lingkai Kong
The University of Hong Kong  Beihang University
Harbin Institute of Technology, Shenzhen  Independent Researcher  Tsinghua University
Correspondence to:
lingkaikong@hku.hk
.
Abstract
Generative policies offer expressive action distributions
for online reinforcement learning (RL), but many diffusion-
and flow-based policies require costly iterative sampling.
We propose
DriftSpread
, a one-step generative policy based on
Drifting for online maximum-entropy (MaxEnt) RL.
To incorporate entropy without a tractable policy density,
we build on an energy-based view of Drifting and derive
critic-guided Drift and entropy-induced Spread from the
negative MaxEnt objective.
Our method learns these updates sequentially in the same
actor, using action regression for value improvement and
distribution matching to capture the effect of entropy.
The actor updates require neither direct samples from
the critic-defined Boltzmann target nor policy-density
or score estimation.
Under exact fitting with a fixed critic, we prove
convergence to the Boltzmann target in the small-step
limit followed by the long-time limit.
On MuJoCo,
DriftSpread
achieves the highest aggregate
normalized return among all evaluated methods,
while outperforming the diffusion- and flow-based
baselines in both training and inference efficiency.

Generative policies offer expressive action distributions
for online reinforcement learning (RL).
Diffusion- and flow-based policies can capture multimodal
distributions that are difficult to represent with a single
Gaussian
(
Dong et al., 2025
;
Celik et al., 2025
)
.
However, many of these approaches generate actions through
iterative sampling, requiring repeated network evaluations
during training and inference.
Recent MeanFlow-based methods reduce this cost through
few-step or one-step action generation
(
Dong et al., 2026
;
Chen et al., 2025
;
Kim et al., 2026
)
.
Drifting offers a different way to train one-step
generators
(
Deng et al., 2026
)
.
At each training iteration, it uses target data to
move generated samples toward the desired distribution,
then trains the generator to reproduce the moved
samples from the same inputs.
Through these repeated updates, the generator learns
to produce samples from the target distribution in
a single forward pass at inference.
This approach has shown better performance than
MeanFlow variants in one-step image generation on
ImageNet
(
Deng et al., 2026
)
.
These results motivate exploring Drifting for online
RL, where its use remains less studied.
We consider the maximum-entropy (MaxEnt) RL objective,
which balances expected return with policy entropy
to encourage exploration
(
Haarnoja et al., 2018
)
.
The critic defines a Boltzmann target distribution
for policy improvement, but does not directly provide
samples from it
(
Li et al., 2026
)
.
We therefore adopt an energy-based view of Drifting
(
Gretton et al., 2026
;
Han et al., 2026
)
,
using the negative MaxEnt policy-improvement objective
as the energy.
This energy guides updates to actions generated by
the current policy.
For the value term, critic gradients tell us how to
move actions toward higher values.
The entropy term is harder to use: an implicit actor
generates actions but does not provide a tractable
density for computing their distribution’s entropy.
We therefore need training targets that capture
the effect of entropy without explicitly computing it.
We propose
DriftSpread
, a one-step generative policy in the
Drifting model family for online MaxEnt RL.
Our key idea is to derive two updates from this energy
and fit them sequentially to the same actor through
repeated Drift–Spread cycles.
In each cycle, Drift uses critic gradients to move
generated actions toward higher values.
The actor then learns to reproduce these updated
actions from the same inputs through regression.
Spread captures the entropy contribution through
diffusion of the action distribution.
We approximate this diffusion by adding appropriately
scaled independent noise to actions from the updated
actor, then train the actor to match the resulting
distribution.
This allows the actor to learn the effect of entropy
without explicitly computing it.
For a fixed critic, we prove
that the learned policy converges to the Boltzmann
target distribution in the small-step, long-time limit.
Our main contributions are:
(1) We introduce
DriftSpread
, a Drifting model for online
MaxEnt RL with expressive policies and one-step action
generation.
(2) We develop sequential Drift–Spread training through
critic-guided regression and entropy regularization to
address the challenge of entropy computation for implicit
policies.
(3) On MuJoCo,
DriftSpread
outperforms 13 baselines
in aggregate normalized return, with lower training
costs than the diffusion, flow, and MeanFlow baselines
(Figure
1
).
2
Related Work
Generative policies for online RL.
Diffusion and flow models provide expressive action
distributions for online RL.
One line of work optimizes policies by backpropagating
critic gradients through diffusion or flow sampling
(
Wang et al., 2024
;
Lyu et al., 2025
)
.
DIME also differentiates through diffusion sampling
while optimizing a variational lower bound on the
MaxEnt objective
(
Celik et al., 2025
)
.
Another line of work constructs training targets
for learning critic-defined Boltzmann distributions.
DQS uses weighted averages of critic gradients
to construct score targets
(
Jain et al., 2025
)
.
SDAC and MaxEntDP instead use critic values to weight
denoising supervision and noise estimates, respectively
(
Ma et al., 2025
;
Dong et al., 2025
)
.
Reverse flow matching unifies these gradient-expectation
and noise-expectation formulations through posterior-mean
estimation
(
Li et al., 2026
)
.
These approaches use iterative action sampling,
motivating few-step and one-step policies for online RL.
MeanFlow was introduced for one-step generative modeling
and learns average velocities
(
Geng et al., 2025
)
.
Recent online RL methods use this formulation
to learn policies with fewer generation steps.
FPMD trains rectified-flow and MeanFlow policies
through policy mirror descent, with both variants
supporting one-step inference
(
Chen et al., 2025
)
.
MFPO trains few-step MeanFlow policies using velocity
estimates for critic-defined Boltzmann targets
(
Dong et al., 2026
)
, while SOM constructs velocity
targets from critic-based score estimates to train
one-step MeanFlow policies
(
Kim et al., 2026
)
.
Drifting models and policy learning.
Drifting learns one-step generators by repeatedly
moving generated samples and training the generator
to reproduce their updated positions.
This approach has achieved state-of-the-art performance
in one-step image generation on ImageNet
(
Deng et al., 2026
)
.
Subsequent work relates specific Drifting fields
to Wasserstein gradient flows
(
Gretton et al., 2026
)
and uses
optimal-transport couplings to construct sample
updates
(
He et al., 2026
)
.
W-Flow derives sample movements from an objective
over distributions and trains a one-step generator
on the resulting samples
(
Han et al., 2026
)
.
Drifting has also been applied to policy learning.
For offline RL, DriftQL combines critic-guided
policy improvement with a Drifting regularizer
based on the behavior distribution
(
Houssaini et al., 2026
)
.
For offline-to-online RL, Drifting Field Policy
derives a KL-regularized policy update through
Wasserstein gradient flow and constructs training
targets from actions ranked by the critic
(
Koo et al., 2026
)
.
Our work focuses on online MaxEnt RL from scratch.

Conclusion and Limitations
We introduced
DriftSpread
, a Drifting-based approach to
learning expressive one-step policies for online RL.
Building on an energy-based view of Drifting, we derive
critic-guided Drift and entropy-induced Spread from
the MaxEnt objective.
The two updates are learned sequentially by the same
actor: Drift moves actions toward higher values,
while Spread matches a broader distribution constructed
from the updated actor.
This design incorporates the effect of entropy without
estimating policy densities or scores, while allowing
each action sample to be generated in one forward pass.
Under exact fitting, our analysis establishes convergence
to the fixed-critic Boltzmann target in the small-step,
long-time limit.
MuJoCo experiments show that
DriftSpread
combines strong
control performance with efficient training and inference,
supporting Drifting as a practical approach to
generative policy learning.
Our work leaves two directions for future research.
First, our evaluation is limited to simulation
environments.
Testing on real-world control tasks would help
assess robustness to observation noise and changes
in system dynamics.
Second, we use a fixed spreading-noise distribution
and scale during training.
Adapting the spreading strength as learning progresses
may better balance exploration and value improvement.
