article.headline: 漂移再扩散：在线强化学习的一步生成策略
article.lede: DriftSpread 让同一个演员先沿 critic 梯度漂移、再做分布匹配扩散，推理一步出动作，MuJoCo 五个任
article.problem: 扩散与流式策略能表达多峰动作分布，但需要迭代采样，训练和推理的算力开销都大。最大熵强化学习里，熵项依赖策略密度或 score，而隐式演员网络不提供，critic 定义的 Boltzmann 目标分布也不直接给出样本。因此，如何在不估计密度和 score 的前提下让一步生成器学到熵的效果，是本文要解决的问题。
article.method: 作者把负最大熵目标当作分布空间上的能量，经 Wasserstein 梯度流拆成两项：critic 梯度驱动的漂移，和熵带来的拉普拉斯扩散项，后者用小步长下加零均值噪声来近似。训练时同一个演员顺序做两步：Drift 用动作回归拟合“当前动作 + η·∇Q”的停止梯度目标；Spread 用基于特征函数的 MMD 做分布匹配，去拟合漂移后分布与扩散噪声的卷积，从而避开策略密度和 score 估计。
article.results: 在 HalfCheetah、Hopper、Walker2d、Ant、Humanoid 五个 MuJoCo-v3 任务上，每个任务训练 10^6 次环境交互、5 个随机种子，DriftSpread 在 13 个基线中取得最高聚合归一化回报，并在 HalfCheetah-v3 与 Walker2d-v3 上取得最高的后期平均回报。平均推理时间降至 0.15 ms/动作，对比 DIME 的 1.24 ms 和两步 MeanFlow 策略 MFPO 的 0.36 ms；训练耗时低于扩散、流与 MeanFlow 基线，但 DFP 和 WPPG 的训练时间略低。二维高斯玩具实验里，顺序拟合的最终 KL 为 0.000422，联合拟合为 0.512165。
article.why_it_matters: 它给出一条不依赖策略密度、score 或目标分布样本的一步生成策略训练路径，同时保留最大熵带来的探索性，把生成式策略的推理成本压到与普通高斯策略同一量级。
article.limitations: 收敛到 Boltzmann 目标的证明要求 critic 固定、两个损失在每轮精确拟合到零，并且是“先 η↓0 再 τ→∞”的双重极限，实际训练未必满足。实验只在仿真环境进行；扩散噪声的分布与尺度全程固定，未随训练自适应；在训练时间上还略逊于 DFP 与 WPPG。
article.figure_caption_zh: DriftSpread 总览：(a) critic 学习与顺序的 Drift–Spread 演员更新交替进行，Drift 用动作回归、Spread 用分布匹配；(b) 在负最大熵目标面上，Drift 把动作推向更高 critic 值，Spread 再把漂移后的分布展宽以体现熵的作用。

figure.caption: {Overview of {}.} (a) Training alternates between critic learning and sequential Drift--Spread actor updates, using action regression for Drift and distribution matching for Spread. The maps $f_ $ represent the same actor at different training stages, each generating an action sample from reference noise in one forward pass. (b) The surface schematically represents the negative MaxEnt objective over policy distributions. The samples below illustrate how Drift moves actions toward higher critic values and Spread then broadens the post-Drift distribution to capture the effect of entropy.

page_papers.title: HairDeck: Animation-Ready Stylized Hair Cards from a Single Image
page_papers.abstract: The hair of stylized characters in games and avatars is built from hair cards: artist-placed ribbons whose geometry is the visible hair, animated by spring bones. Existing image-based methods produce realistic hair or a single fused mesh, while CHARM, the only generator of stylized hair cards, decodes a hairstyle autoregressively as a long sequence of control points. Observing that a card hairstyle is an unordered set of artist-defined primitives, we propose HairDeck, which generates it as one: each card is a single token, and a set diffusion transformer denoises all cards together. From a single image, HairDeck generates the cards and the spring-bone chains that drive them, yielding an animatable asset that exports to ready-to-use downstream formats. On CHARM's own test set, it lowers Chamfer distance by 44% and card-orientation error by more than half while running 33 times faster, and from single images it outperforms CHARM, image-to-3D pipelines and strand-based methods. Project page: https://hyzcluster.github.io/HairDeck

Abstract
The hair of stylized characters in games and avatars is built from hair cards: artist-placed ribbons whose geometry is the visible hair, animated by spring bones.
Existing image-based methods produce realistic hair or a single fused mesh, while CHARM, the only generator of stylized hair cards, decodes a hairstyle autoregressively as a long sequence of control points.
Observing that a card hairstyle is an unordered set of artist-defined primitives, we propose HairDeck, which generates it as one: each card is a single token, and a set diffusion transformer denoises all cards together.
From a single image, HairDeck generates the cards and the spring-bone chains that drive them, yielding an animatable asset that exports to ready-to-use downstream formats.
On CHARM’s own test set, it lowers Chamfer distance by 44% and card-orientation error by more than half while running 33 times faster, and from single images it outperforms CHARM, image-to-3D pipelines and strand-based methods.
Project page:
https://hyzcluster.github.io/HairDeck

Introduction
3D generators now produce convincing shapes from a single image
[
83
,
72
,
71
,
77
]
, but not the structure that artists build assets from.
The hair of stylized characters in games and avatars is a clear example.
It is made of
hair cards
: a few dozen to over a hundred ribbons, each placed by an artist, whose geometry is the visible hair.
Unlike the alpha-textured hair cards of realistic hair, flat strips whose texture stands in for many strands
[
20
,
88
,
60
]
, these cards have a rhombic or triangular cross-section whose width and thickness vary along the card.
Such hair is commonly animated with
spring bones
: short chains of bones hung from the head whose tips are simulated every frame, so that the hair sways and settles.
Similar simulations ship as Dynamic Bone in Unity
[
18
]
, PhysBones in VRChat
[
61
]
, Kawaii Physics in Unreal Engine
[
36
]
and a node in Godot
[
10
]
.
Artists place every card and rig every chain by hand.
Existing methods do not produce this asset.
Hair generators output realistic strands
[
49
,
13
,
42
]
, including recent ones that accept stylized images
[
28
,
31
,
44
,
65
]
, and card extraction turns such strands into alpha-textured cards for realistic hair
[
88
,
60
]
.
Image-to-3D generators
[
71
,
77
]
output a single fused mesh with no cards to animate.
CHARM
[
15
]
is the only generator of stylized hair cards and introduced the benchmark for them.
It generates the control points of a hairstyle one at a time, as a sequence of hundreds to thousands of discretized tokens.
We observe that a card hairstyle is an unordered set of artist-defined primitives, and we generate it as one.
Like CHARM, we describe each card by its control points (position, width and thickness), and we add its cross-section type and its root normal, the width direction at the root, so each card keeps the cross-section and the orientation the artist gave it.
What we change is the unit of generation, with two designs.
First, each card becomes one continuous token: a card VAE encodes its variable-length control points into a latent, and the token holds this latent with the card’s root position, root normal and cross-section type, so a hairstyle has one token per card, about 70 on average.
Second, all tokens of a hairstyle are generated together: a set diffusion transformer without positional embedding denoises them with flow matching
[
25
,
27
]
, and an existence flag on each token decides how many cards appear.
Each design makes generation more accurate and faster.
Together they amount to a simple rule for assets made of artist-defined primitives: one token per primitive, and no order among them.
A single image shows the hair relative to the head, so we predict the cards in a head frame anchored to the face, which improves where the hair sits without changing its shape.
Images also come in many drawing styles, so we widen the appearance of our training renders in two ways: synthetic style augmentation, which improves accuracy on stylized inputs, and renders restyled by an image-editing model
[
68
]
, which keep the card structure stable across styles.
Cards alone do not move.
We generate the spring-bone chains with the same recipe: each chain becomes one token holding its path, joint count and stiffness, and a second set diffusion transformer generates all chains of a hairstyle together from its card tokens.
With a fixed geometric skinning, the cards and chains form an animatable asset that exports to ready-to-use downstream formats.
In summary, our contributions are:
•
A card token for stylized hair: a representation that keeps the cross-section type and the root normal, and a card VAE that encodes the variable-length control points into one continuous latent and decodes the card by arc length.
•
A set formulation of hair-card generation: a set diffusion transformer without positional embedding generates all card tokens of a hairstyle together, and an existence flag on each token decides how many cards appear.
•
Single-image generation with a face-anchored head frame, synthetic style augmentation and restyled renders.
•
Spring-bone chains generated as a second set conditioned on the card tokens, which makes the output animatable.
We evaluate on CHARM’s test set with its protocol and also measure the orientation of every card against the original artist meshes.
HairDeck lowers Chamfer distance by 44% and card-orientation error by more than half while running 33 times faster.
From a single image, it outperforms CHARM, image-to-3D pipelines and strand generators.

3.4
Spring-bone chains
Cards alone are static, but the hair of game and avatar characters must move with them.
Artists achieve this with spring-bone chains, sequences of joints hung from the head whose simulated motion the cards follow, and rig them by hand for every hairstyle; we generate the chains so that the output can be animated directly.
Chain tokens.
A chain becomes a 27-dimensional token of its path (8 points by arc length), joint count, stiffness and existence flag, and a hairstyle a set of up to 48 chains.
Chain generation.
The chain DiT has the same block design as the set DiT and generates the chain tokens of a hairstyle in the head frame with flow matching, cross-attending to its card tokens (
Fig.
3
).
It is trained on the ground-truth card tokens and, at test time, reads the generated ones; cards from a point cloud are first mapped into the head frame (
Appendix
A
).
Skinning and simulation.
After generation, a fixed geometric skinning binds the cards to the chains.
We place the joints uniformly along each generated path.
A card follows the chain closest to the lower 60% of its centerline if their mean distance is below 0.4 face widths, and otherwise moves rigidly with the head; each of its points follows the nearest segment of that chain, blended linearly with the neighboring segment within half a segment of each joint, with a weight that rises from 0 at the chain’s root to 1 over 0.05 face widths of arc length.
We tune these two thresholds against the artists’ skin weights in the training data.
We simulate the chains with the VRM spring-bone update of UniVRM
[
62
,
63
]
, using the predicted stiffness and the drag and gravity of most VRoid chains.

4.1
Setup
Data.
We use the dataset of CHARM
[
15
]
, built from VRoid characters
[
39
]
: we take 36,440 of its training hairstyles and test on its 100 test hairstyles, with the point clouds CHARM released.
For single images, we render the front views of the 76 test characters whose complete models are available, and we collect 40 in-the-wild images, anime illustrations sampled at random and stratified by hairstyle.
Metrics.
On point clouds we follow CHARM’s protocol: it compares the generated cards with its ground truth, rebuilt from its card templates, by Chamfer distance (CD), earth mover’s distance (EMD), Hausdorff distance (HD) and voxel IoU.
As the templates estimate card orientations, we also evaluate against the original artist meshes.
Our orientation metric matches every generated card to the artist card closest in CD and averages the angle between their width directions over 32 positions along the card.
Root precision and recall are the shares of generated and ground-truth cards whose root position lies within 2% of the character height of a root position in the other set.
For single images, we align every output to the ground truth (
Appendix
D
) and report the aligned CD and IoU on surface samples.
The failure rate is the share of results that have fewer than 25% of the ground-truth cards (16 cards for in-the-wild images) or leave the scalp bare (hair covers less than 80% of the top or the back of the head); for the image-to-3D generators, whose output is one fused surface without cards, only the scalp criterion applies.
We time every method on one NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU (48 GB) with batch size 1, from the input to the cards, before meshing.

4.6
Applications
Interpolation.
The Dora encoder computes the condition tokens of a point cloud at query points that farthest point sampling picks from it, so the tokens of two point clouds have no correspondence.
To interpolate between two conditions, we match the tokens of the second to those of the first by Hungarian matching on the positions of their query points and blend the matched tokens linearly (
Fig.
9
).
Rigging existing hairstyles.
The chain DiT reads only card tokens, so it can also rig card hairstyles that an artist modeled without spring bones; its evaluation on the artists’ cards in
Sec.
4.5
measures this use.
5
Limitations and Conclusion
Limitations.
HairDeck learns from stylized VRoid hairstyles, so very short hair and the alpha-textured cards of realistic hair lie outside its training data.
It generates the geometry and UV coordinates of the cards but no textures.
Some VRoid characters model bows and hats with hair cards, so HairDeck generates them as cards when the input shows them; filtering such cards from the training data would avoid this.
The chain DiT follows the chain layouts common among VRoid characters and generates fewer chains for unusual ones, such as many chains radiating from the crown.
Figure
23
shows failure cases.
Conclusion.
HairDeck generates the stylized hair cards of a character and the spring-bone chains that animate them from a single image.
Treating a hairstyle as an unordered set of artist-defined primitives, with one token per card and all tokens generated together, makes generation more accurate and faster than autoregressive decoding, and the same recipe generates the chains.
Assets built from other artist-defined primitives, such as garments sewn from panels or drawings made of strokes, can be generated in the same way.

Export.
Every card mesh carries UV coordinates: the first runs across the width, so the two faces of a card mirror each other and need no seam, and the second is the arc-length fraction, from the root (0) to the tip (1).
To export to VRM, we replace the hair of a character model, its hair bones and its hair spring-bone groups with the generated cards, one spring-bone group per generated chain, and use the geometric skinning of
Sec.
3.4

Results from in-the-wild images are exported the same way, on the body of a test character with the hair color taken from the image.
Compute.
Each model trains on one NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU (48 GB): the card VAE in 4 hours, the point-cloud model in about 10 hours, the chain DiT in about 3 hours and the image model, starting from the point-cloud model, in about 27 hours.

Card VAE design.
Table
8
starts from a VAE that decodes the control points by index, as StrokeFusion
[
89
]
decodes the points of a stroke.
It takes the same inputs as our card VAE; its encoder sees the control points without their arc-length fractions, and its decoder adds
𝐳
\mathbf{z}
to 128 learned slot embeddings and predicts in each slot a control point and whether the slot holds one, with a squared error on standardized features.
Decoding at arc-length fractions instead cuts the reconstruction error by a factor of 4.3, and adaLN modulation
[
37
]
and the world-unit loss of
Sec.
3.1
, in place of a squared error on standardized features, together lower it by another 29%.
The raw token resamples a card to 64 points by arc length and holds their positions relative to the root position, widths and thicknesses (317 values) with the number of control points; the PCA token holds the first 64 principal components of these 317 values, fitted on 300,000 training cards and scaled to unit variance.
Width direction of the data.
Our cards keep the control point positions of CHARM’s templates; they differ in the width direction and in the widths and thicknesses, which we measure along the Bishop frame
[
1
]
.
Table
9
rebuilds the artist cards with each choice of control points, root direction and propagation, and measures both the width direction and the shape.
CHARM’s templates take the root direction from the first three control points and solve the rest of the card by least squares, which keeps each width direction perpendicular to the card and close to its neighbors.
On the control points quantized into CHARM’s tokens (512 levels per position axis), least squares rebuilds the shape more closely than a Bishop frame from the same start, as CHARM found for Bishop propagation from estimated normals
[
15
]
, but both leave the width direction far off (40.6° and 35.3°), because the quantization turns the root direction from the first three points by 23.6° (median).
Without the quantization, the Bishop frame is closer in both direction and shape, and with the root direction of the original mesh it is closer still, on artist and quantized points alike (7.5° and 8.2°, against 19.3° and 19.6° for least squares): given the right root direction, the quantization costs less than 1°.
Our cards take this route, with the root normal of the original mesh propagated by a Bishop frame; the card VAE adds 0.8°, and keeping the root direction constant along the card gives 11.9°.

Appendix D
Baseline details
Alignment.
For the aligned CD and IoU of
Tabs.
2
and
5
, every output is normalized to the bounding box of the ground truth and then aligned to it by ICP with scale, started from 24 axis-aligned rotations.
CHARM.
We run the authors’ checkpoints with greedy decoding: the point-cloud model on the point clouds of CHARM’s test set, and the image model on a line drawing of the hair made with CHARM’s pipeline.
Card-level autoregression.
The card-level autoregressive model of
Tab.
1
, with 182.1M parameters, uses our card tokens, card VAE, data, condition and training steps.
A 17-layer transformer of width 768 generates the cards in CHARM’s order, by the azimuth of each card’s mean point around the vertical axis, and a 6-layer per-token diffusion head, as in MAR
[
23
]
, samples each token with 50 steps and guidance scale 2; before each card, a stop head decides whether the sequence ends.
Retrieval.
Retrieval in
Tab.
1
compares the mean of the input’s condition tokens with those of the 36,440 training hairstyles by cosine similarity and returns the cards of the closest.
For the chains in
Tab.
4
, it returns the chains of the closest training hairstyle that has chains.
Procedural rig.
The procedural rig of
Tab.
4
places chains on cards by rules, with parameters from the spring bones of 300 training characters and lengths in face widths
W
W
.
Cards whose centerlines lie close (mean distance below 0.2
W
W
) and point the same way form a unit, which gets one chain per 0.23
W
W
of its width.
A chain follows the mean centerline of its cards, fitted by a quadratic Bézier curve, and starts 15% of the card length from the root.
Longer chains get more joints and a lower stiffness, as in the training characters; all chains use drag 0.4 and no gravity.
Mesh generators.
MeshAnything V2
[
6
]
, DeepMesh and BPT generate a mesh from a point cloud of the ground-truth hair mesh, with their official checkpoints and settings.
MeshAnything V2 and BPT sample it from the marching-cubes surface of the hair, and DeepMesh from the mesh itself.
The official sampler of DeepMesh mirrors its output, which we undo.
We sample 10K points from depth renders of each output over 100 views, as CHARM scans its data, and evaluate them with CHARM’s own scripts.
Image-to-3D generators and cascades.
TRELLIS.2 and Hunyuan3D-2.1 generate geometry only, from the image with all but the hair masked out.
For the cascades of
Tab.
5
, the mesh is placed in the median hair bounding box of the training set, scanned into 10K points as above and passed to CHARM or our point-cloud model.

We run the official checkpoints of DiffLocks
[

Its pipeline crops the image around a face box, which we take from our face mask on every input.

article.headline: 把发型当无序集合：单图生成可动画发卡
article.lede: HairDeck把风格化发型看作无序的发卡集合，每张卡编码成一个token，用无位置编码的集合扩散Transformer
article.problem: 游戏和虚拟形象中风格化角色的头发由美术逐张摆放的发卡（hair card）构成，并靠弹簧骨链做次级运动，这些都需要手工完成。已有的单图方法要么输出真实感发丝，要么输出一整块融合网格，没有可动画的卡片结构；CHARM是唯一的风格化发卡生成器，但它把发型当成数百到数千个离散控制点组成的长序列自回归解码。
article.method: 作者把每张卡用card VAE编码成32维潜变量，连同根部位置、根部法向、菱形或三角形截面类型和存在标志组成40维token，一个发型对应192个token槽位。集合DiT不使用位置编码，以flow matching对所有token一起去噪，存在标志在去噪中自行决定生成多少张卡（平均约70张），条件可以是点云或单张图像的DINOv3特征。第二个集合DiT以卡token为条件，在48个槽位中生成弹簧骨链，再用固定几何蒙皮把卡绑到链上，得到可动画资产。
article.results: 在CHARM的100个测试发型上，Chamfer距离从0.0117降到0.0066（降44%），相对原始美术网格的卡片方向误差从40.0°降到16.8°，单发型耗时从33.7s降到1.01s（约33倍加速）。单图任务上，对齐后的CD为0.0089，对比CHARM的0.0186、TRELLIS.2的0.0139、Hunyuan3D-2.1的0.0148和DiffLocks转卡的0.0174；在76个测试角色上失败率3.5%、在40张网络图片上10.0%，其他方法分别为13.2%–34.2%与17.5%–77.5%，每张图1.33s。消融显示去掉根部法向后方向误差升至26.4°，去掉存在标志后只生成62.8张卡（集合DiT为68.9，真值67.4）。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「一个美术原语一个token、原语之间无顺序」的集合式生成思路用到发卡上，同一套配方还复用到骨链，输出可直接导出为VRM等下游格式的可动画资产，而不只是给人看的网格。
article.limitations: 训练数据只来自VRoid风格化发型，极短发与真实感头发的alpha贴图发卡不在覆盖范围内，且只生成几何与UV、不生成贴图。此外蒙版内的道具（帽子、角、尾巴等）会被当作发卡生成，链DiT对头顶辐射等不常见链布局会生成偏少的链。
article.figure_caption_zh: 左：发型是一组发卡，每张卡编码成含根部位置、根部法向、card VAE潜变量、截面类型与存在标志的token；中：集合DiT用flow matching去噪整个token集合，跨卡注意并以点云或图像为条件，空槽位让模型自行决定卡数；右：card VAE解码出卡片，chain DiT再生成其弹簧骨链。

figure.caption: Overview. Left: a hairstyle is a set of hair cards. Each card, a polyline of control points with width and thickness, becomes one token holding its root position, root normal, card VAE latent $ {z}$, cross-section type and existence flag. Middle: the set DiT denoises the token set with flow matching, attending across cards and to the condition, a point cloud or an image. Empty slots let the model decide how many cards to generate. Right: the card VAE decodes the tokens into cards, and the chain DiT generates their spring-bone chains.

page_papers.title: Glance: The Generator Is Its Own Reranker
page_papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation commonly serves separate models for reranking and answering, duplicating model residency and passage processing. We introduce Glance, which equips the generator with a lightweight decision adapter and pointer head to score candidate passages from a shared prefill. Short relevance probes branch from the cached context, producing one score per passage without separately prefilling each query-passage pair. A single resident 9B backbone supports generation, general decisions and reranking, with approximately 0.1 GiB of additional memory per decision skill. After 39 minutes of MS MARCO fine-tuning, Glance achieves nDCG@10 of 0.741 on SciFact and 0.345 on NFCorpus, compared with 0.721 and 0.326 for bge-reranker-v2-m3. On 300 HotpotQA questions, its selected context improves answer F1 by 0.045 over cross-encoder-selected context under the same base generator (paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.014, 0.076]). In a scaling study, reranking quality keeps rising up to 200 candidates (43k tokens) scored from one shared prefill, where it exceeds the cross-encoder by 0.058 nDCG@10, and a probe-only activated adapter lets generation continue from the original passage cache. These initial results demonstrate generator-based reranking with one resident backbone; evaluation currently covers two retrieval datasets, one QA dataset and one backbone family.

Glance: The Generator Is Its Own Reranker
Adilet Metinov
Chingiz Arziev
Affiliation:
Airun Intelligence Labs
October 2026
Abstract
Retrieval-augmented generation commonly serves separate models for reranking and answering, duplicating model residency and passage processing. We introduce Glance, which equips the generator with a lightweight decision adapter and pointer head to score candidate passages from a shared prefill. Short relevance probes branch from the cached context, producing one score per passage without separately prefilling each query–passage pair. A single resident 9B backbone supports generation, general decisions and reranking, with approximately 0.1 GiB of additional memory per decision skill. After 39 minutes of MS MARCO fine-tuning, Glance achieves nDCG@10 of 0.741 on SciFact and 0.345 on NFCorpus, compared with 0.721 and 0.326 for bge-reranker-v2-m3. On 300 HotpotQA questions, its selected context improves answer F1 by 0.045 over cross-encoder-selected context under the same base generator (paired bootstrap 95% CI

In a scaling study, reranking quality keeps rising up to 200 candidates (43k tokens) scored from one shared prefill, where it exceeds the cross-encoder by 0.058 nDCG@10, and a probe-only activated adapter lets generation continue from the original passage cache. These initial results demonstrate generator-based reranking with one resident backbone; evaluation currently covers two retrieval datasets, one QA dataset and one backbone family. Adapters and code:
https://huggingface.co/airun-ai/GlanceRAG-MiMo-9B-Reranker

1
Introduction
RAG systems often assign evidence selection and answer generation to separate models. A cross-encoder reranker encodes each query–passage pair separately, typically in batches
[
13
,
6
]
; LLM-based rerankers improve quality further
[
19
,
15
,
25

at higher cost
[
1
]
. Either way, an additional model must be served and the candidate passages are processed before the generator reads the selected context.
The generator is going to read the passages anyway: can it judge all of them using computation shared across passages?
Glance equips the generator with a lightweight decision adapter. It prefills the candidate passages once, then evaluates short passage-specific probes that branch from the shared cache, and a 256-dimensional pointer head turns each probe into a relevance score. The same resident backbone then generates the answer (Figure
1
). In an activated-adapter variant, passage encoding uses the base weights, so generation can continue from the original cache.
Our contributions:
1.
Method.
Passage-specific relevance probes over one shared passage prefill, read by the generator’s own backbone through a small adapter and pointer head, including on hybrid linear/full-attention backbones (§
3
).
2.
Evidence.
Retrieval results on two BEIR datasets, zero-shot and after short MS MARCO training; downstream QA on HotpotQA under the same generator; and scaling to 200 candidates per shared prefill (§
4
).
3.
Unified serving.
Small decision adapters sharing one backbone, switched per request with outputs identical to each model loaded alone, and an activated variant whose answer continues from the reranking cache (§
4.6
, §
4.7
).
Glance removes the additional reranker backbone while delivering competitive retrieval quality and improved downstream answers in the evaluated settings; a dedicated cross-encoder remains faster per query.

Our 9B backbone interleaves Gated DeltaNet

We train the activated adapter for 150 steps (1,200 MS MARCO records, H100, 17 minutes) and a matched control with the LoRA on all tokens (same data, steps and seed). The activated adapter reaches 0.740 / 0.351 nDCG@10 on SciFact / NFCorpus (packed_all,

Chat.
Without probe tokens the activated model runs the exact base weights, so its greedy chat output is identical to the base by construction; the control adapter already changes the wording on one of two test prompts.
Cache reuse.
Because the state cache is now the base model’s own, generation can continue from it. On 100 HotpotQA distractor questions (10 paragraphs, median state 1.4k tokens, H100 not shared): the state pass takes 64 ms, the 10 probes fork from its cache in 85 ms (R@3 0.97), and the base model then answers by continuing the same cache with the question in the chat format. Continuing the cache gives EM/F1 0.61 / 0.750 against 0.59 / 0.754 for re-prefilling the top-3 passages, with a lower answer latency (138 ms vs. 181 ms median). On 5 checked questions the continued answer equals that of a fresh base-model prefill of the same text. Telling the model which passages scored highest added nothing at this scale, and a continuation without the chat turn markers is much worse (F1 0.577). In this mode the generator sees all passages; the reranking scores do not select its context. The passages are thus prefilled once for both reranking and answering; the continued cache still contains all 10 candidates. This is a 100-question, single-seed result.
4.8
Order sensitivity
In packed_all every probe sees all passages, so scores can depend on passage order. On 100 SciFact queries (220-word passages, as in Table
3

We serve the base model with the reranking LoRA registered as a vLLM adapter: chat requests use no adapter, decision rows are one-token requests with the adapter, and the residual stream at the readout positions is passed through the final norm and the 256-dimensional pointer head outside the engine. Rows of one request share the state through vLLM’s prefix cache on the hybrid model. In a single
generate

Production use needs a connector that exports only the readout positions and the head inside the engine.
5
Limitations
This is a proof of concept. Evaluation sets are small (hundreds of queries) and cover two BEIR datasets and one QA dataset. We test one backbone family (hybrid 9B). Latencies are from an unoptimised eager path; a dedicated cross-encoder remains faster per query. The shared-state construction itself is provided by the Kev runtime; our contribution is its use and training for reranking inside RAG with the generator’s own weights. In packed_all every probe sees all passages, so a passage’s score depends somewhat on its neighbours and on order (§
4.8
); averaging over orders is a simple remedy. BEIR differences are not significance-tested, and the per-passage baseline was not re-run with the trained adapter. Latencies come from different, partly shared GPUs (RTX PRO 6000, B200, H100), and speed-up ratios depend on load. The zero-shot adapter degrades beyond

The activated-adapter and cache-reuse results are single-seed, on 100 questions, the bitwise cache check used a 0.8B model, and with cache reuse the answer sees all passages rather than the reranked subset. Chat quality with the adapter on was checked on a handful of prompts, and specialising the adapter for reranking loses 9 JevBench items. Memory currently grows with

6
Conclusion
Glance shows that the generator can also serve as its reranker. Passage-specific probes share one candidate prefill, while lightweight adapters support ranking and general decisions on a single resident backbone. In the evaluated settings, the resulting rankings are competitive with a dedicated cross-encoder, and they improve downstream QA under the same generator. Probe-only adaptation further allows generation to reuse the original passage cache. The next questions are how these benefits extend across larger benchmarks and backbone families, how far a shared-cache implementation can push the candidate count toward 128k-token contexts, and how optimized serving systems change the latency trade-off against small cross-encoders.

article.headline: 生成器兼任重排器：一次预填充打分
article.lede: Glance 用单一 9B 主干共享预填充候选段落，再由轻量适配器和指针头给每个段落打分。
article.problem: RAG 常把重排和回答交给不同模型，导致模型驻留和段落处理重复。交叉编码器逐对编码查询-段落，LLM 重排器质量更高但成本更大。问题是：生成器本来就要读这些段落，能否用跨段落共享的计算同时完成判断？
article.method: Glance 在冻结的 9B 生成器上挂 rank-16 LoRA 决策适配器和 256 维指针头，先对候选段落做一次共享预填充，再让每个段落专属的短探针从缓存分叉并输出相关性分数。主流程用适配器打分后关闭适配器、重预填充 top-n 再生成；Glance-Activated 则只在探针 token 上启用适配器，使生成可从原始候选缓存继续。训练在 4,000 条 MS MARCO 查询上进行 39 分钟（55,598 个带标签探针），未使用 BEIR 或 HotpotQA 数据，每项决策技能约增加 0.1 GiB 显存。
article.results: 39 分钟 MS MARCO 微调后，Glance 在 SciFact 和 NFCorpus 上的 nDCG@10 分别为 0.741 和 0.345，高于 bge-reranker-v2-m3 的 0.721 和 0.326。300 道 HotpotQA 上，同一基础生成器使用 Glance 选出的 top-3 上下文，答案 F1 比使用交叉编码器选出的上下文高 0.045（配对 bootstrap 95% CI [0.014,0.076]）。在 200 个候选（43k token）的扩展实验中，Glance 的 nDCG@10 比交叉编码器高 0.058。
article.why_it_matters: 如果成立，RAG 不必再单独驻留重排器，生成、通用决策和重排可共享同一 9B 主干与候选段落缓存，简化多模型服务。
article.limitations: 这是概念验证：评测仅覆盖两个 BEIR 数据集、一个 HotpotQA 和一种 9B 混合主干，BEIR 差异未做显著性检验。专用交叉编码器每查询仍更快（31–60 ms），当前实现显存随候选数×上下文长度增长（k=100 时 56 GiB），且激活适配器与缓存复用仅为 100 题单种子结果。
article.figure_caption_zh: 图 1：单一常驻主干先共享预填充所有候选段落，段落专属探针经指针头输出 k 个相关性分数；主流程重预填充 top-n 后生成，激活变体则从原缓存继续生成。

page_papers.title: RynnWorld-Latent: A Cross-Embodiment World Model Conditioned on Universal Latent Actions
page_papers.abstract: Learning controllable world dynamics from heterogeneous interaction videos is challenging because robot embodiments use incompatible action spaces, while human videos lack native control labels. We present RynnWorld-Latent, a cross-embodiment video world model that uses the 3D-grounded latent actions introduced by RynnLAM as a shared conditioning interface. This representation enables joint pretraining on human interaction videos, robot demonstrations, and simulation rollouts without requiring a common native action space. Built on a pretrained video transformer, RynnWorld-Latent combines global action tokens with an identity-initialized local pathway that aligns actions with future video latents. We pretrain on 23 datasets comprising approximately 553.5M frames and adapt the model to target robots through post-training. The framework supports two data-generation routes: digital teleoperation uses target robot commands to generate action-video demonstrations, while latent-action synthesis transfers source motion to an edited initial frame and pairs the resulting rollout with retargeted pseudo robot actions. Experiments show improved video prediction metrics on public benchmarks and two real-robot platforms, alongside qualitative action following when different action sequences share the same initial observation. Synthetic mid-training improves policy success rates on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, and both generation routes improve real-world policy success rates over real-demonstration-only training in the evaluated settings. These results support universal latent actions as a scalable interface for learning controllable visual dynamics across heterogeneous embodiments.

Abstract
Learning controllable world dynamics from heterogeneous interaction videos is challenging because robot embodiments use incompatible action spaces, while human videos lack native control labels. We present RynnWorld-Latent, a cross-embodiment video world model that uses the 3D-grounded latent actions introduced by RynnLAM as a shared conditioning interface.
This representation enables joint pretraining on human interaction videos, robot demonstrations, and simulation rollouts without requiring a common native action space. Built on a pretrained video transformer, RynnWorld-Latent combines global action tokens with an identity-initialized local pathway that aligns actions with future video latents. We pretrain on 23 datasets comprising approximately 553.5M frames and adapt the model to target robots through post-training. The framework supports two data-generation routes: digital teleoperation uses target robot commands to generate action-video demonstrations, while latent-action synthesis transfers source motion to an edited initial frame and pairs the resulting rollout with retargeted pseudo robot actions. Experiments show improved video prediction metrics on public benchmarks and two real-robot platforms, alongside qualitative action following when different action sequences share the same initial observation. Synthetic mid-training improves policy success rates on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, and both generation routes improve real-world policy success rates over real-demonstration-only training in the evaluated settings.
These results support universal latent actions as a scalable interface for learning controllable visual dynamics across heterogeneous embodiments.

Introduction
World models, which predict future states conditioned on actions, have long been theorized as a cornerstone of generalist robot intelligence
(
Sutton, 1991
;
LeCun et al., 2022
;
Richens et al., 2025
)
. The recent progress of large-scale video generation has catalyzed a new class of video world models, in which future dynamics are represented directly in visual space
(
Zhao et al., 2026b
;
Zhao et al., 2026c
;
Agarwal et al., 2025
;
Ali et al., 2025
;
Zhao et al., 2026e
;
Zhao et al., 2026a
;
Zhao et al., 2025
)
. These models achieve impressive visual fidelity and provide a promising substrate for learning physical dynamics from large-scale video corpora. However, when applied to robotic manipulation, language-conditioned video generators face an interface mismatch: their primary control signal is a task-level description, while physical interaction is governed by continuous, frame-level causal interventions.
Language describes semantic intentions at a coarse temporal granularity. An instruction such as “pick up the cup” specifies a task outcome, but does not determine the precise trajectory by which the outcome is achieved. In contact-rich manipulation, small differences in timing, contact order, gripper state, or camera motion can lead to substantially different futures.
Without fine-grained motion or action conditioning, a text-conditioned model must represent multiple plausible trajectories for the same instruction, making precise control over manipulation dynamics challenging.
Moreover, natural language alone is not a convenient interface for specifying temporally precise interventions, such as closing the gripper earlier while maintaining the same preceding motion.
These limitations motivate an explicit action-conditioning interface for controllable video world modeling.
A natural solution is to condition world models on robot actions
(
Gao et al., 2026
)
. However, directly using raw robot actions introduces a severe alignment bottleneck. Different embodiments operate in heterogeneous kinematic spaces, with different joint counts, coordinate conventions, control frequencies, and hardware limits. As a result, a world model conditioned on raw actions is difficult to scale across platforms. At the same time, large-scale human videos contain abundant interaction dynamics without robot-specific control labels, while simulation actions need not match a target robot’s control space. What is needed is not a stronger action encoder for a particular robot, but a shared action interface that represents interaction-related visual change while abstracting away platform-specific control conventions.
We argue that latent actions provide such an interface. Instead of representing actions as robot commands, latent actions describe what changed between observations. Distilled from video in a self-supervised manner, continuous latent actions provide a shared description of visual transitions without requiring identical hardware control interfaces. Human hands, robot grippers, and simulated agents may differ drastically in their low-level control signals, yet their visual transitions can share motion and interaction patterns.
By encoding heterogeneous videos into a shared latent-action representation, a single world model can be pretrained on human interactions, robot demonstrations, and simulation rollouts under a unified action-conditioning objective, without requiring their native control spaces to be aligned.
In this work, we introduce
RynnWorld-Latent
, a cross-embodiment video world model built upon
RynnLAM
(
Zhao et al., 2026d
)
, the 3D-grounded latent-action representation introduced in RynnVLA-Latent
(
Zhao et al., 2026d
)
. While RynnVLA-Latent
(
Zhao et al., 2026d
)
uses these descriptors as supervision targets for policy pretraining, our work investigates their complementary role as conditioning signals for learning controllable visual dynamics. RynnWorld-Latent predicts future video from an initial observation and a sequence of continuous latent actions, without requiring text conditioning or a common native robot action space. Technically, we combine global action tokens with an identity-initialized, frame-aligned local conditioning pathway within a pretrained video diffusion transformer. The local pathway exploits the temporal correspondence between latent-action extraction and video-latent compression, allowing each action descriptor to condition its corresponding future video latent.
A central idea of this work is that RynnWorld-Latent should not be viewed only as a future predictor, but as a
data-generation engine
for scalable robot learning. This leads to two complementary generation modes. First, after target-robot post-training, RynnWorld-Latent can be conditioned on target robot actions and support interactive digital teleoperation
(
Zhao et al., 2026c
)
: operator control signals are mapped to target actions and drive video generation, producing paired action-video data without requiring additional physical robot execution. Second, the latent-action-conditioned model enables data synthesis from existing videos. Given a source video, we extract its latent-action sequence, edit the first frame to replace the embodiment or environment, and generate a new rollout conditioned on the edited first frame and the original latent actions. First-frame editing specifies the new visual embodiment or environment, while the latent-action sequence guides the interaction dynamics. The resulting rollout has motion close to the source video, but appears under a new embodiment or environment. These generated rollouts can be paired with retargeted pseudo robot actions for downstream VLA training.
We evaluate RynnWorld-Latent from three complementary perspectives. First, we assess action-conditioned video prediction on public world-model benchmarks and held-out demonstrations from two real-robot platforms, measuring prediction fidelity after target-robot adaptation. Second, we investigate latent-action controllability through qualitative comparisons that vary the supplied latent-action sequences while holding the initial observation fixed, and illustrate cross-embodiment motion transfer through first-frame editing. Third, we examine the utility of world-model-generated data for downstream policy learning. Synthetic mid-training improves success rates on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, while both latent-action-driven synthesis and digital teleoperation improve observed closed-loop policy success on the evaluated real-world manipulation tasks. These evaluations jointly characterize prediction fidelity, qualitative action following, and downstream training utility.
Our main contributions are as follows:
•
We present RynnWorld-Latent, a text-free, latent-action-conditioned video world model,
which uses frozen RynnLAM descriptors as a shared conditioning interface for learning visual dynamics from human interaction videos, heterogeneous robot demonstrations, and simulation rollouts without aligning their native control spaces.
•
We design an action-conditioning mechanism that combines global action tokens with locally identity-initialized, frame-aligned injection, associating transition descriptors with the corresponding future video latents.
•
We enable latent-action-guided generation under edited robot embodiments and environments, and adapt the world model to native robot-action conditioning. The resulting latent-action synthesis and digital-teleoperation pipelines generate data that improves downstream policy learning in the evaluated settings.

Related Work
2.1
World Models
World models predict how environments change under actions and support planning and policy learning through simulated experience
(
Finn et al., 2016
;
Ebert et al., 2018
;
Hafner et al., 2019
;
Hafner et al., 2020
)
. Advances in video generation have enabled large-scale pretraining of visual dynamics models and their adaptation to interactive simulation
(
Agarwal et al., 2025
;
Yang et al., 2024
;
Wu et al., 2024b
;
Rigter et al., 2024
;
Huang et al., 2025
)
. Language-conditioned video and image generation have also been used to produce visual plans and synthetic demonstrations for robot control
(
Du et al., 2023
;
Zhou et al., 2024
;
Black et al., 2024b
;
Jang et al., 2025
)
. However, task-level instructions leave the timing and trajectory of individual movements largely unspecified. To simulate fine-grained manipulation, action-conditioned world models incorporate robot controls into future prediction
(
Zhu et al., 2025b
;
Guo et al., 2026
;
Wang et al., 2025b
)
. Such predictions support policy evaluation
(
Li et al., 2025a
;
Quevedo et al., 2026
;
Wang et al., 2026c
)
and planning
(
Ebert et al., 2018
;
Zhou et al., 2025
;
Assran et al., 2025
;
Kim et al., 2026
)
, while related approaches combine future prediction with action learning to improve robot policies
(
Wu et al., 2024a
;
Cheang et al., 2024
;
Zhu et al., 2025a
;
Ye et al., 2026
;
Sun et al., 2026
)
.
Extending action-conditioned modeling across embodiments requires handling differences in action dimensions, coordinate conventions, and control semantics. Existing approaches address this through heterogeneous action modeling
(
Wang et al., 2025b
)
or geometric motion representations shared by humans and robots
(
Wu and Gao, 2026
;
Zhao et al., 2026c
)
. For pretraining on diverse robot and human videos, a further challenge is that many data sources lack corresponding control labels. More closely related to our setting, latent-action pretraining infers conditioning variables from observed transitions, allowing videos without native action labels to contribute to world-model learning
(
Gao et al., 2025
;
Garrido et al., 2026
;
Gao et al., 2026
;
Liu and Shorinwa, 2026
)
. Building on this direction, RynnWorld-Latent uses continuous latent actions as a shared conditioning interface for cross-embodiment world-model pretraining, without requiring direct alignment of embodiment-specific control spaces.
2.2
Latent Action Learning
Learning across embodiments requires representations that connect different forms of observation and control. Prior work studies shared policies trained on heterogeneous robot data
(
O’Neill et al., 2024
;
Octo Model Team, 2024
;
Kim et al., 2024
;
Wang et al., 2024
)
and action-space alignment using recorded controls
(
Zheng et al., 2025
;
Zhang et al., 2025c
)
. For videos without corresponding robot actions, transferable skills and geometric motion cues provide intermediate representations for learning
(
Xu et al., 2023
;
Kim et al., 2025
;
Wen et al., 2024
;
Bharadhwaj et al., 2024
;
Collins et al., 2025
)
. Latent action learning instead infers compact action variables from transitions between observations
(
Rybkin et al., 2019
;
Schmidt and Jiang, 2024
)
. These variables have been used as supervision for policy pretraining and transfer
(
Ye et al., 2025
;
Chen et al., 2025b
;
Bu et al., 2025b
;
Chen et al., 2025a
;
Li et al., 2025b
;
Tharwat et al., 2025
)
, as well as conditioning inputs for predicting future states
(
Menapace et al., 2021
;
Bruce et al., 2024
;
Alles et al., 2025
;
Bi et al., 2025
;
Garrido et al., 2026
)
.
Both discrete codes
(
Bruce et al., 2024
;
Ye et al., 2025
;
Chen et al., 2025b
)
and continuous representations
(
Gao et al., 2025
;
Liang et al., 2026
;
Yang et al., 2026a
;
Garrido et al., 2026
;
Gao et al., 2026
)
have been explored. Recent work further studies alignment with available action supervision
(
Zhang et al., 2026a
;
Luo et al., 2026
)
, the separation of motion from appearance
(
Yang et al., 2026a
;
Xu et al., 2026
;
Zhang et al., 2026b
)
, and geometric constraints on the learned action
space
(
Yang et al., 2026b
)
. These distinctions matter because visual changes can include camera motion, background variation, and other effects unrelated to the agent’s control
(
Nikulin et al., 2025
;
Zhang et al., 2025a
;
Garrido et al., 2026
)
.
Building on these studies, we use a pretrained and frozen encoder RynnLAM
(
Zhao et al., 2026d
)
to extract 3D-grounded continuous latent-action descriptors from heterogeneous visual transitions. Unlike methods that require native control annotations or explicit motion retargeting during world-model pretraining, our approach uses these descriptors as a shared conditioning interface for human, robot, and simulation videos. This enables joint learning of visual dynamics without requiring the original action parameterizations to be aligned across embodiments.

Overview
RynnWorld-Latent is a cross-embodiment latent-action-conditioned video world model that can further serve as a data-generation engine for robot learning. It predicts future video latents from an initial latent frame and a sequence of continuous latent actions, without relying on text conditioning. The pretraining corpus is summarized in Tab.

The framework consists of three stages:
(i) cross-embodiment pretraining, where human egocentric videos, robot teleoperation data, and simulation rollouts are relabeled into a shared latent-action space;
(ii) target-robot post-training, which adapts RynnWorld-Latent to a target embodiment and introduces a robot-action conditioning interface;
and (iii) data generation, where the post-trained model supports interactive digital teleoperation when conditioned on target robot actions, and enables latent-action-driven data synthesis when conditioned on transferred latent actions.

To generate trajectories for policy learning, we combine the world model with interfaces for capturing interaction intent and producing action-video episodes. In our design, RynnWorld-Latent provides action-conditioned visual dynamics, while the surrounding pipeline provides target-robot adaptation, action retargeting, temporal alignment, and filtering. Compared with asset-based simulation, this generative pipeline can reduce the need for explicit 3D assets and manual system identification: scenes are specified implicitly by a conditioning image, visual outputs are produced in a learned video distribution, and interaction priors are drawn from large-scale video pretraining. We instantiate two complementary data-generation pipelines: interactive digital teleoperation and latent-action data synthesis.

The data engine requires a reference scene frame

ref

We therefore synthesize scenes featuring the target robot from large-scale egocentric human hand videos. Our pipeline shown in Fig.
3
consists of egocentric data preprocessing followed by two alternative routes for generating robot-centric initial scenes: robot inpainting like Ego2Robot
(
Wang et al., 2026b
)
and image editing using an end-to-end model. During preprocessing, we verify the integrity of the input videos and motion data, standardize their formats, and extract egocentric frames and human hand poses. We temporally align the video and motion sequences using zero-order hold or interpolation. We also use SAM3
(
Carion et al., 2026
)
, prompted with human hand keypoints and text descriptions, to segment the hands and combine the resulting masks. In the robot inpainting route, we perform video inpainting within the hand masks to reconstruct the background after removing the human hands. We retarget the extracted human hand motion to the robotic hand and estimate the robot base pose and joint configurations through motion post-processing and inverse kinematics with base-pose search in MuJoCo
(
Todorov et al., 2012
)
. We then render the robot in the estimated poses and composite the rendered images onto the inpainted background to obtain robotic manipulation observations corresponding to the original human demonstrations. In the image editing route, we instead provide the original egocentric image and its hand mask to an end-to-end image-editing model, like Qwen-Image-Edit
(
Wu et al., 2025a
)
, which replaces the human hands with robotic counterparts to generate an initial scene. The two routes thus produce synthetic robot observations through explicit retargeting and rendering or direct image editing, respectively. Finally, we apply quality gates to filter the generated observations and retain accepted samples as initial scenes for subsequent world-model-based data generation.

Action relabeling, synchronization, and filtering.
For interactive digital teleoperation, target robot actions can be logged directly. For latent-action data synthesis, robot actions can be obtained by relabeling the source motion. When the source video already has robot actions compatible with the target embodiment, those actions can be reused after temporal alignment. Otherwise, we derive pseudo robot actions by estimating the relevant source motion, retargeting it to the target robot workspace, and applying inverse kinematics; implementation details are provided in Appendix
C
. The pseudo actions are temporally aligned with the generated video in frame-index space. We emphasize that temporal synchronization does not by itself establish physical consistency: the actions come from retargeting or inverse kinematics, while the observations are produced by an independently trained generator. We therefore treat the derived actions as pseudo-labels and filter episodes based on joint limits, motion smoothness, visual quality, temporal consistency, and plausibility of object interactions. The resulting synthetic episodes can be combined with real robot data for downstream VLA training.

Real-world policy tasks.
We evaluate downstream policy learning on four tasks that span varying levels of bimanual coordination, contact richness, and precision. These tasks are distributed across two distinct dual-arm robotic platforms:

, a stationary dual-arm robot equipped with dexterous hands, and

Tasks performed on Marvin-WUJI (Dual-Arm Dexterous Hands):
•
(1) Plate-Placement:
The robot reaches toward a shelf, uses its dexterous hands to securely grasp a plate, and places it beside the oven on the tabletop, requiring precise spatial alignment and stable grasping of thin, fragile objects.
•
(2) Plate-Wiping:
A highly dexterous bimanual coordination task in which one hand grasps and stabilizes a plate while the other hand holds a cloth to wipe the plate’s surface before returning the plate to the shelf, requiring coordinated bimanual manipulation.
Tasks performed on Astribot-S1 (Wheeled Mobile Dual-Arm Grippers):
•
(3) Steak-Serving:
The robot approaches the dining area, uses its dual grippers to stably lift a plate containing a cooked steak, and accurately serves it onto the designated spot on the dining table, integrating mobile navigation with precise placement.
•
(4) Plate-Retrieval:
Following the meal, the robot identifies and grasps used, dirty plates left on the dining table, collects the associated cutlery, and returns the items to their designated positions.

Beyond interactive teleoperation, we use RynnWorld-Latent as a scalable data engine that converts large-scale human interaction videos into robot-action-labeled data.
Synthetic corpus.
Given a source human video, we extract its latent-action sequence using the frozen RynnLAM, edit the first frame to replace the human embodiment or original environment with the target robot embodiment or a robot-compatible scene, and condition RynnWorld-Latent on the edited frame and the original latent-action sequence to generate a robotized rollout. 5
Conclusion
We presented RynnWorld-Latent, a cross-embodiment video world model that uses shared continuous latent actions as a conditioning interface for learning visual dynamics from heterogeneous interaction videos. Building on the 3D-grounded RynnLAM representation, the model combines global action tokens with temporally aligned local conditioning to connect motion descriptors with future video latents. This enables world-model pretraining across human, robot, and simulation videos without requiring their native action spaces to be aligned, followed by target-robot adaptation through an embodiment-specific action encoder.
Experiments show strong video prediction fidelity on public benchmarks and two real-robot platforms, while qualitative comparisons demonstrate that generated motions respond to different supplied latent-action sequences under the same initial observation. The model also supports approximate cross-embodiment motion transfer and native-action-conditioned digital teleoperation. Synthetic data generated through both routes improves downstream policy success in the evaluated settings. Together, these findings support shared latent actions as a practical interface for cross-embodiment world-model learning and controllable robot-data generation.
Limitations.
Latent actions are inferred from observed visual transitions and may encode camera motion or appearance information as well as manipulation. Qualitative action following and image-based prediction metrics therefore do not establish causal identification or physical correctness. In the synthesis pipeline, retargeted robot commands and generated observations are obtained through separate processes; temporal alignment and filtering cannot guarantee their physical consistency. The reported real-world success rates use 35 trials per task, and small differences should be interpreted accordingly. Moreover, synthetic mid-training adds both data and optimization compute, whose contributions are not separated by the current comparisons. Future work will address long-horizon consistency, action-observation alignment, and broader transfer across embodiments.

Appendix A
Teleoperation Setup
For Marvin-WUJI, we collect real-world demonstrations through the teleoperation system shown in Fig.
8
. The hardware setup consists of dual Tianji 7-DOF robotic arms and dual Wuji 20-DOF dexterous hands, yielding a total of 54 degrees of freedom.
For arm control, the human operator wears five HTC Vive trackers (mounted on the chest, both wrists, and both upper arms). The system computes wrist-to-chest relative transforms at 100-120 Hz and feeds them into a Pinocchio-based inverse kinematics solver running in a separate process. The resulting joint commands are further smoothed by a Ruckig trajectory generator with velocity, acceleration, and jerk constraints before being sent to the robot arms at 200 Hz.
For hand control, the operator wears Manus data gloves. The raw glove signals are converted to a 21-point MediaPipe hand skeleton format and retargeted to the 20-DOF Wuji hand joint space via a dedicated retargeting module, with an exponential moving average filter applied for motion smoothing.

(

4
. Tab.

Thus all chunks from a held-out episode remain outside the post-training split, and the test tasks themselves are represented in training. Appendix C
Details of Pseudo Robot Action Relabeling
For source videos without target robot actions, we estimate the relevant hand or end-effector trajectory from the source motion. The estimated trajectory is retargeted to the target robot workspace through coordinate mapping, workspace scaling, and embodiment-specific retargeting. We then solve inverse kinematics to obtain target robot joint commands. During IK solving, we enforce joint limits, velocity limits, and temporal smoothness. The resulting actions are treated as pseudo-labels rather than ground-truth robot commands. These pseudo-labels are subsequently filtered together with the generated videos before being used for policy training.
Appendix D
Baseline Implementation Details
Ego2Robot.
We reproduce Ego2Robot
(
Wang et al., 2026b
)
in our pipeline. Specifically, we audit each raw video and its corresponding HaWoR
(
Zhang et al., 2025b
)
motion-capture trajectory, geometrically retarget the HaWoR hand poses to the 20-degree-of-freedom (DoF) Wuji hand, and resample the trajectories using zero-order hold or interpolation. At the source resolution, we use the projected HaWoR keypoints as prompts for SAM3
(
Carion et al., 2026
)
to segment both hands and refine the segmentation using text prompts. We then take the union of the left- and right-hand masks, dilate it by 4 pixels, and remove the hands using a video object removal model, such as MiniMax-Remover
(
Zi et al., 2026
)
or ProPainter
(
Zhou et al., 2023
)
. In parallel, on the CPU, we estimate the robot base pose through a coarse-to-fine inverse kinematics (IK) search in MuJoCo, evaluating 81 candidates in the coarse stage. The visual strategy is decoupled from the segmentation masks, and this branch outputs
qpos54
and an IK report. Finally, we render the TIANJI M6 arm and Wuji hand using MuJoCo’s EGL-based off-screen rasterization and composite the rendered robot onto the inpainted video using an end-effector-locked projection strategy.
We further introduce quality gates for sample selection. article.headline: 跨具身世界模型用潜在动作统一异构数据
article.lede: 阿里达摩院提出 RynnWorld-Latent，以 3D 接地潜在动作为共享条件接口，在 23 个数据集约 5.5 亿
article.problem: 语言条件只能描述任务级意图，无法指定抓取时机、接触顺序等帧级因果干预，同一指令对应多条可能轨迹。直接用原始机器人动作又会遇到关节数、坐标约定、控制频率各异的对齐瓶颈，而大规模人类视频根本没有原生控制标签。
article.method: 模型用冻结的 RynnLAM 从相邻帧提取 608 维连续潜在动作（512 维运动 token、64 维全局动作、32 维相机分量），把 576 维操作描述作为统一条件接口。在 Cosmos3 视频扩散 transformer 上，它把全局动作 token 送入联合自注意力，并额外加一条零初始化、与未来视频 latent 逐帧对齐的局部注入通路。目标机器人后训练阶段再引入轻量动作编码器，使模型可被原生机器人指令驱动，用于数字遥操作与潜在动作数据合成两条数据生成路线。
article.results: 在 DreamDojo 的 GR-1 三个评测集上，PSNR、SSIM、LPIPS 均优于所列基线，例如 EgoDex Eval 上 LPIPS 从 DreamDojo-14B 的 0.21 降到 0.19。真机评测中 Marvin-WUJI 上 PSNR 21.86、SSIM 0.80、LPIPS 0.12（Cosmos3-Edge 为 20.03/0.78/0.31），Astribot-S1 上为 15.96/0.60/0.34。消融显示换成文本条件后 Marvin-WUJI PSNR 降至 19.80、LPIPS 升至 0.30。策略侧，合成数据 mid-training 使 π0 在 LIBERO 上从 94.4% 升到 96.1%、LIBERO-Plus 从 53.6% 升到 79.4%；真机上 π0.5 的 Steak-Serving 从 40.00% 升到 60.00%，Plate-Retrieval 从 45.71% 升到 68.57%，每任务 35 次试验。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「动作」从硬件指令换成从视频自监督学到的视觉转移描述，让人类视频、异构机器人和仿真数据能在同一条件下联合预训练，并把世界模型直接当作合成机器人数据的引擎。
article.limitations: 潜在动作从视觉转移推断，可能混入相机运动与外观变化，图像指标和定性跟随都不能证明因果识别或物理正确；合成管线里重定向动作与生成观测来自两个独立过程，时间对齐与过滤不保证物理一致，且真机结果每任务仅 35 次试验，合成 mid-training 的数据量与额外算力贡献也未分离。
article.figure_caption_zh: 世界模型数据引擎总览：上方由源人类视频提取潜在动作并把首帧编辑成目标机器人以生成 rollout 与重定向伪动作，下方数字遥操作把人类控制信号重定向为机器人动作、以生成帧作为操作者视觉反馈。

figure.caption: {Overview of the world-model data engine.} {Top: Scalable data editing.} extracts latent actions from a source human video, while its first frame is edited to depict the target robot. Conditioned on the edited frame and the original latent actions, generates robot video rollouts. The generated observations are paired with pseudo-actions obtained through motion retargeting and inverse kinematics. {Bottom: Digital teleoperation.} Human control signals are retargeted to robot actions, which condition together with a reference scene. Generated frames provide visual feedback to the operator, while the recorded actions and generated observations form synthetic demonstrations without physical robot execution.

journals.title: Could your chatbot tip off a scientific rival? It’s possible, researchers say
journals.blurb: 《Science》第394卷第6823期（2026年10月）第476-477页的简讯讨论了一个值得关注的问题：聊天机器人可能向科研竞争对手泄露信息。对机器学习研究生而言，这提示在使用基于大模型的科研助手时，需要重视数据与想法的保密边界。

journals.title: Even stupendous black holes can’t explain dark matter
journals.summary:
Nature, Published online: 29 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03386-4

The theoretical objects would have left a larger imprint on cosmic radiation if they were a source of the invisible force pulling together the galaxies.
journals.blurb: 《Nature》刊文指出，即使极其巨大的黑洞也无法解释暗物质。若这类理论天体是维系星系的神秘引力来源，它们应在宇宙辐射中留下更明显的印记。该结论对把暗物质归因于原初黑洞的模型构成限制。
